skills.title: Design information architecture
skills.description: Design or review a website or product's navigation, sitemap, labels, content taxonomy, or URL structure. Use for findability and structural design requests; file cleanup, private source routing, and database schemas are outside this skill.

guide.what: Organize navigation, content labels, and site structure.
guide.when: A website or product needs better findability.
guide.inputs: The audience, content inventory, tasks, and current navigation.
guide.outputs: A sitemap, taxonomy, navigation proposal, or structural review.
guide.example: Reorganize this site’s navigation around the tasks visitors need to complete.
guide.expect: It reads the current content inventory and navigation before proposing anything, then gives a sitemap or structure with reasons tied to the audience's tasks. It keeps existing URLs unless a change is authorized, and it labels the result provisional because only real card sorts or tree tests count as validation.
guide.overview: It reads the current content inventory and navigation before proposing anything, then gives a sitemap or structure with reasons tied to the audience's tasks. It keeps existing URLs unless a change is authorized, and it labels the result provisional because only real card sorts or tree tests count as validation.
guide.value: Organize a site around the tasks readers need to complete. It examines the content and navigation to propose clearer groupings, labels and routes, making information easier to find.

preparation.where: Provide the site's content list, current navigation or sitemap, audience and important tasks. A content inventory can be an export, a list of pages or accessible existing pages; a formal sitemap is not required before beginning.
preparation.missing: If the inventory is incomplete, the proposed structure remains provisional. The skill can propose a sitemap, but card sorts, tree tests and real user results require actual research rather than a generated claim of validation.

reuse.label: General use
reuse.reason: The method accepts the user’s project sources and takes private context as an explicit input.
reuse.basis: Source classification and automated reference scan; cross-environment execution has not been tested.

skills.markdown:
---
name: design-information-architecture
description: "Design or review a website or product's navigation, sitemap, labels, content taxonomy, or URL structure. Use for findability and structural design requests; file cleanup, private source routing, and database schemas are outside this skill."
license: MIT
---


# Design information architecture

Make the product's content findable for the audience's actual tasks. Read the current content inventory and navigation before proposing a structure. Use the supplied product scope; do not reorganize private source folders or change their authority routes.

Read [Structure and validation](references/structure-and-validation.md). Identify the audience's goals, available content, page types, and existing entry points. Keep required content and unknown inventory visible. Group by a supported user need rather than the organization's departments or an arbitrary number of menu items.

Choose a hierarchy, facets, search, or a combination that suits the content. Give labels enough meaning to help a reader predict the destination. Separate primary navigation from page-level or contextual links when their jobs differ. Show representative paths through the proposed structure.

Preserve existing public URLs unless a change is necessary and authorized. If a proposal changes them, provide a current-to-proposed map and identify the redirect and link-update work. A proposed map does not prove that redirects exist or a migration is deployed.

Treat card sorting, tree tests, and first-click studies as participant research. Report validation only when actual observations support it. An agent review can identify ambiguity or inconsistent labels; it cannot stand in for users. Without research, label the structure provisional and give a focused validation plan.

Deliver the requested sitemap or structural recommendations with reasons tied to the audience and inventory. Show content gaps that affect the paths. Preserve confirmed names and labels unless the user requested changing them. Existing brand, source, writing, and completion rules govern any finished artifact.

examples.title: Navigation and sitemap for a community tool library website
examples.markdown:
## Request

Our tool library's website has grown messy and members keep emailing us to ask things they should be able to find themselves. Can you propose a new navigation and sitemap from the inventory and notes I've attached? We'd like to keep our existing URLs if we can.

## Inputs

Run of the built `design-information-architecture` task package. The recording session invented this scenario, the request and the inputs below before running the skill. It had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so.

#### current-site.md

#### Current site: Fernbank Tool Library (example.com/fernbank)

Top navigation today: Home | About Us | Our Stuff | Members | Get Involved | News | Contact

| Page | URL | Current parent | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Home | / | – | Hero photo, latest news |
| About Us | /about | Top | Mission, history |
| Our Team | /about/team | About Us | Staff and volunteers |
| Opening Hours | /about/hours | About Us | Hours for both sites |
| Find Us | /about/find-us | About Us | Maps, parking, step-free access |
| Our Stuff | /catalogue | Top | Searchable catalogue, 1,100 items |
| Tool Categories | /catalogue/categories | Our Stuff | Garden, Wood, Electrical, etc. |
| Workshop Kits | /catalogue/kits | Our Stuff | Bundled loan kits |
| Join | /members/join | Members | Sign-up form, fee table |
| Membership Fees | /members/fees | Members | Duplicate of fee table on Join? (not compared) |
| Borrowing Rules | /members/rules | Members | Loan length, late fees, damage policy |
| My Account | /members/login | Members | Login, renewals, reservations |
| FAQ | /faq | Top (footer only) | 42 questions in one list |
| Skills Workshops | /events/workshops | Get Involved | Booking links |
| Repair Café | /events/repair-cafe | Get Involved | Monthly |
| Volunteer | /get-involved/volunteer | Get Involved | Role list, form |
| Donate Tools | /get-involved/donate-tools | Get Involved | What we accept |
| Donate Money | /get-involved/donate | Get Involved | |
| News | /news | Top | 60 posts, mostly 2022–2024 |
| Contact | /contact | Top | Form only, no phone or email shown |
| Accessibility statement | – | – | Does not exist yet |

#### notes.md

#### Notes from the coordinator

Last quarter's enquiry emails (about 90, hand-tallied):
- 31: "Can I borrow X?" or "do you have X?" (people didn't find the catalogue search)
- 22: opening hours or which site to go to
- 14: how much membership costs / how long I can keep things
- 9: "can I donate my dad's tools?"
- 8: how to book a workshop
- 6: wheelchair access
Rest: miscellaneous.

Audiences: current members (borrow, renew, reserve), prospective members (cost, how it works), donors and volunteers, and a few schools and local groups who ask about group bookings. No analytics available; no user research done.

Constraints:
- Two sites: Fernbank (main) and Lowmoor (open Saturdays only).
- Name "Repair Café" and "Workshop Kits" are established; keep them.
- Volunteers keep the site in a basic CMS; URL changes are painful, and external links from the council website point at /catalogue and /members/join.
- Group bookings (schools) have no page today.

## Output

### Fernbank Tool Library: proposed navigation and sitemap

I propose six top-level groups built around what members and visitors ask you about, and every current URL stays as it is. Only the navigation labels and groupings change, so the council links to `/catalogue` and `/members/join` keep working and no redirects are needed. The structure is provisional. You have no analytics or user research, so it rests on your enquiry tally and the page inventory, and the validation plan at the end covers what to test.

#### What the structure responds to

Your 90 enquiries break down like this:

| Question | Emails | Where it is answered today | Problem |
|---|---|---|---|
| Do you have X / can I borrow X | 31 | `/catalogue`, under "Our Stuff" | The label doesn't say "borrow" or "search" |
| Opening hours, which site | 22 | `/about/hours`, under "About Us" | Visitors don't look for practical visit info under "About" |
| Cost, loan length | 14 | `/members/fees`, `/members/rules` | Under "Members", which reads as a member-only area |
| Donating tools | 9 | `/get-involved/donate-tools` | Two clicks deep, behind a generic label |
| Booking a workshop | 8 | `/events/workshops` | Filed under "Get Involved" |
| Wheelchair access | 6 | `/about/find-us` | Buried in a map page; no accessibility statement |

Prospective members, current members, donors/volunteers and group organisers have different goals, so the groups follow tasks rather than your internal teams.

#### Proposed primary navigation

Header, left to right: **Borrow | Membership | Visit us | Workshops and repairs | Support us | About** — plus utility links on the right: **Search**, **Log in**, **Contact**.

| Group | Purpose | Contents (URL unchanged) |
|---|---|---|
| **Borrow** | Find out whether we have a tool and how to get it | Search the catalogue `/catalogue` · Browse by category `/catalogue/categories` · Workshop Kits `/catalogue/kits` |
| **Membership** | Decide to join, then understand the terms | Join `/members/join` · Fees `/members/fees` · Borrowing rules `/members/rules` · FAQ `/faq` |
| **Visit us** | Plan a trip to Fernbank or Lowmoor | Opening hours `/about/hours` · Find us and step-free access `/about/find-us` · Accessibility statement (new, no URL yet) |
| **Workshops and repairs** | Learn a skill or fix something | Skills Workshops `/events/workshops` · Repair Café `/events/repair-cafe` · Group bookings (new, no URL yet) |
| **Support us** | Give tools, time or money | Donate tools `/get-involved/donate-tools` · Volunteer `/get-involved/volunteer` · Donate money `/get-involved/donate` |
| **About** | Background on the library | About us `/about` · Our team `/about/team` · News `/news` |

Utility links: **Log in** goes to `/members/login` (My Account, covering renewals and reservations), **Contact** to `/contact`, **Search** to the catalogue search.

##### Reasons for the less obvious choices

- **"Borrow" replaces "Our Stuff".** The 31 "do you have X" emails suggest people don't recognise "Our Stuff" as the place to search. "Borrow" names the task. The catalogue keeps its established URL.
- **Fees and rules sit under "Membership", not "Members".** Prospective members ask about cost and loan length before they join, so these pages need to read as public.
- **My Account moves out of the menu into a "Log in" utility link.** Current members use it as an action, not a place to browse. It still has its own URL.
- **Opening hours and access move into "Visit us".** That takes the 22 hours enquiries and 6 access enquiries out of "About". `/about/hours` and `/about/find-us` keep their paths, so the label and the URL will disagree. That is acceptable for now; renaming the URLs later would need the redirect work described below.
- **Workshops and Repair Café are one group.** Both are events a visitor books or attends. The names "Repair Café" and "Workshop Kits" are kept as established. Kits stay under Borrow because they are loaned items, not events. Add a line on the Kits page pointing to workshops that use them, if any do (I have no information on that).
- **"Get Involved" is renamed "Support us" and no longer holds events.** Events are an activity for members and the public, not a way of giving support.
- **News moves under About.** Its 60 posts are mostly 2022–2024, so it doesn't earn a top-level slot. It stays reachable from the home page for recent items.

##### Page-level and contextual links

These do a different job from the menu, so they are not extra menu items:

- Home page: a catalogue search box above the fold, and four quick links — Opening hours, Join, Donate tools, Book a workshop. These cover about 75 of the 90 enquiries.
- Join, Fees and Rules link to each other in a "Membership" side list.
- Each catalogue category and item page shows "How borrowing works" (link to `/members/rules`) and which site holds the item, if the catalogue records that.
- The footer repeats the primary groups and adds Contact, FAQ, Accessibility statement and a Lowmoor/Fernbank hours summary.

#### Representative paths

| Task | Path | Clicks from home |
|---|---|---|
| Check whether you have a mitre saw | Home search box → results (or Borrow → `/catalogue`) | 1–2 |
| Find Saturday opening hours for Lowmoor | Visit us → Opening hours | 2 |
| Learn what membership costs | Membership → Fees | 2 |
| Donate a late relative's tools | Support us → Donate tools | 2 |
| Book a workshop | Workshops and repairs → Skills Workshops | 2 |
| Check step-free access | Visit us → Find us and step-free access, or Accessibility statement once written | 2 |
| Renew a loan | Log in → My Account | 2 |
| A school asks about a group visit | Workshops and repairs → Group bookings (page needed) | 2 |

These are paths in the proposal, not results from users.

#### Current-to-proposed map

No URL changes. Redirects and internal link updates are not required for this proposal. The only link work is editing menu labels and groupings in the CMS, and the home-page quick links.

| Current URL | Current placement | Proposed placement |
|---|---|---|

  • Two sites: Fernbank (main) and Lowmoor (open Saturdays only).

  • Group bookings (schools) have no page today.

Output

Fernbank Tool Library: proposed navigation and sitemap

I propose six top-level groups built around what members and visitors ask you about, and every current URL stays as it is. Only the navigation labels and groupings change, so the council links to /catalogue and /members/join keep working and no redirects are needed. The structure is provisional. You have no analytics or user research, so it rests on your enquiry tally and the page inventory, and the validation plan at the end covers what to test.

---
name: design-process
description: 'Work with a business or operational process in two modes: document it as an SOP, or optimize it. Use Document mode to formalize a process into an SOP with purpose, scope, a RACI matrix, process flow, step detail, exceptions, and metrics for a handoff, audit, onboarding, or to standardize inconsistent work. Use Optimize mode to make a process, workflow, pipeline, or hand-off faster, cheaper, or more reliable. Triggers on write an SOP, document this process, build a RACI, this process is slow, too many steps or approvals, streamline this, remove the bottleneck, cut cycle time, reduce hand-offs. Not for one-off project plans, org charts, product requirements, incident runbooks, or code and query performance tuning.'
---


# Design process

> **Before writing: [`build-card.md`](../_shared/build-card.md) plus
> [`readout-brief.md`](../writing-diagnostics/references/registers/readout-brief.md). Inputs, not a final pass.**

Two modes over one subject. Document a process as a repeatable SOP, or analyze an
existing process and recommend improvements. Pick the mode from the request: a
formalize, standardize, or write-it-down ask is Document; a make-it-faster,
cheaper, or more-reliable ask is Optimize. When both are wanted, document the
current state first, then optimize from it.

## Conventions both modes hold

- Do not invent owners, names, dates, metrics, targets, durations, or cadence. If
  a field is not supplied, write `not captured`. If a section has no content,
  write `none`.
- Surface unresolved decisions rather than papering over them. Where an owner, a
  trigger, or a rule is unsettled, write `open: <the question>` instead of a
  fabricated answer.
- Distinguish the current state you were told from any redesign you propose. Never
  present a recommendation as if it were observed fact.
- Work with whatever tools are connected, and never assume a specific product is
  present. Fall back to the user's description and say so.

---

## Mode: Document (the SOP)

Turn a business process into a complete, repeatable standard operating procedure.

Take whatever the user has: a process name, a rough description, pasted docs, or
meeting notes. If the description is thin, ask targeted questions first, the
trigger, owner, the steps in order, who does each, what each step produces, the
exceptions, and how success is measured. Do not stall on missing detail; capture
what exists and mark the rest.

Two rules carry this mode:

- **The exceptions are the point.** "Usually X, but sometimes Y" is the most
  valuable content in the document. Capture it explicitly, do not smooth it into
  the happy path.
- **RACI integrity: exactly one Accountable per step.** If two names are given as
  accountable, flag it as `open: single accountable owner unresolved`.

Produce the SOP in this structure. Keep placeholder brackets only where the user
supplied a value; otherwise apply the conventions above.

```markdown
## Process Document: [Process Name]
**Owner:** [Person/Team] | **Last Updated:** [Date] | **Review Cadence:** [Quarterly / Annually / not captured]

### Purpose
[Why this process exists and what it accomplishes]

### Scope
[What is included and what is explicitly excluded]

### RACI Matrix
| Step | Responsible | Accountable | Consulted | Informed |
|------|-------------|-------------|-----------|----------|
| [Step] | [Who does the work] | [Single owner] | [Who to ask] | [Who to tell] |

### Process Flow
[Step-by-step sequence, or an ASCII flowchart if branching matters]

### Detailed Steps

#### Step 1: [Name]
- **Who:** [Role]
- **When:** [Trigger or timing]
- **How:** [Instructions specific enough to follow without asking]
- **Output:** [What this step produces]

#### Step 2: [Name]
[Same format]

### Exceptions and Edge Cases
| Scenario | What to Do |
|----------|------------|
| [Exception] | [How to handle it] |

### Metrics
| Metric | Target | How to Measure |
|--------|--------|----------------|
| [Metric] | [Target] | [Method] |

### Related Documents
- [Related process or policy, or `none`]
```

---

## Mode: Optimize

Analyze an existing process and recommend improvements. Lead with the answer: the
biggest constraint and what to change, then the supporting map.

One rule carries this mode: **impact estimates must trace to supplied numbers.**
Step times, volumes, error rates, and costs come only from what the user gives you
or from records they point to. If cycle time or cost is not captured, state the
direction of the change, faster or fewer hand-offs, and mark the magnitude `not
captured` rather than fabricating a percentage. A plausible-looking made-up
duration or cost is a defect.

### 1. Map the current state
- List every step, decision point, and hand-off in order.
- For each step capture owner, trigger, duration, and whether it is manual,
  automated, or an approval. Use `not captured` for anything unknown.
- Mark queue and wait time between steps separately from work time.

### 2. Find the waste
- Waiting: time in queues or waiting for approvals.
- Rework: steps that fail and get redone; note the failure trigger.
- Hand-offs: each one is a delay and failure point; count them.
- Over-processing: steps that add no value to the outcome.
- Manual work: tasks a rule or integration could do instead.

Name the single largest constraint. Everything else is secondary until it is fixed.

### 3. Design the future state
- Eliminate steps that add no value.
- Automate manual steps where a clear rule exists.
- Reduce hand-offs; merge steps under one owner where possible.
- Parallelize independent steps.
- Add checkpoints, not gates: verify without blocking flow.

### 4. Quantify the impact
- Time saved per cycle, from captured durations, else `not captured`.
- Error or rework rate change.
- Cost change and load on the people involved.
- State the assumptions behind each figure in one line.

Return, in chat by default: the headline constraint and top recommendation; a
before/after step comparison with hand-off and step counts for each; prioritized
recommendations, each with expected impact and effort; open questions and figures
marked `not captured`; and an implementation order, quick wins first.

---

## Delivery

Default to returning the result inline in the conversation as Markdown. Only write
a file if the user asks and a writable working directory is available; on a hosted
or read-only surface where a write fails, fall back to inline output without
stopping. Never make the deliverable depend on a file write succeeding.

## If tools are connected

Optional, only when the capability is actually available, never block on it. A
connected knowledge base: search first for an existing version to update rather
than duplicate, then offer to publish. A connected task tracker: link related
work and, if the user wants, open tasks for `open:` items and improvement actions.

## Release gate (required)

Before you deliver, run the gate. This is a required step, not a suggestion. Full
spec in [`release-gate.md`](../_shared/release-gate.md).

1. Apply review-writing to the prose. Use the bundled diagnostic tools to check saved writing. For
   a final artifact it emits a receipt the quality gate requires.
2. Run review-deliverable before you call it final.

Do not present the artifact as finished until both checks have passed.

  • For each step capture owner, trigger, duration, and whether it is manual,

automated, or an approval. Use not captured for anything unknown.

  • Mark queue and wait time between steps separately from work time.

2. Find the waste

  • Waiting: time in queues or waiting for approvals.
  • Rework: steps that fail and get redone; note the failure trigger.
  • Hand-offs: each one is a delay and failure point; count them.
  • Over-processing: steps that add no value to the outcome.
  • Manual work: tasks a rule or integration could do instead.

Name the single largest constraint. Everything else is secondary until it is fixed.

3. Design the future state

  • Eliminate steps that add no value.
  • Automate manual steps where a clear rule exists.
  • Reduce hand-offs; merge steps under one owner where possible.
  • Parallelize independent steps.
  • Add checkpoints, not gates: verify without blocking flow.

4. Quantify the impact

  • Time saved per cycle, from captured durations, else not captured.
  • Error or rework rate change.
  • Cost change and load on the people involved.
  • State the assumptions behind each figure in one line.

Return, in chat by default: the headline constraint and top recommendation; a before/after step comparison with hand-off and step counts for each; prioritized recommendations, each with expected impact and effort; open questions and figures marked not captured; and an implementation order, quick wins first.

---

Delivery

Default to returning the result inline in the conversation as Markdown. Only write a file if the user asks and a writable working directory is available; on a hosted or read-only surface where a write fails, fall back to inline output without stopping. Never make the deliverable depend on a file write succeeding.

If tools are connected

Optional, only when the capability is actually available, never block on it. A connected knowledge base: search first for an existing version to update rather than duplicate, then offer to publish. A connected task tracker: link related work and, if the user wants, open tasks for open: items and improvement actions.

Release gate (required)

Before you deliver, run the gate. This is a required step, not a suggestion. Full spec in release-gate.md (../_shared/release-gate.md).

  1. Apply review-writing to the prose. Use the bundled diagnostic tools to check saved writing. For

a final artifact it emits a receipt the quality gate requires.

  1. Run review-deliverable before you call it final.

Do not present the artifact as finished until both checks have passed.

examples.title: Speeding up a supplier invoice approval process
examples.markdown:
## Request

Our supplier invoice approval process takes far too long and suppliers keep chasing us for payment. I've pasted how it works today plus some timings from last month's invoices; can you work out what to fix first and how the process should look instead?

## Inputs

Run of the built `design-process` task package. The recording session invented this scenario, the request and the inputs below before running the skill. It had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so.

#### current-process.md

#### Supplier invoice approval: how it works today (Finance team notes)

1. Suppliers email invoices to invoices@example.com. A shared inbox is checked by the AP clerk (Dana) each morning.
2. Dana prints or saves each invoice, then keys the supplier, amount, date and PO number into the accounting system by hand.
3. Dana looks for the matching purchase order in a shared spreadsheet kept by Procurement. If she cannot find the PO number, she emails Procurement and waits for a reply.
4. Dana emails the invoice to the budget holder (the manager who raised the PO) for approval. Budget holders reply "approved" by email, or sometimes by chat.
5. Dana chases budget holders who have not replied. There is no fixed chase schedule; she does it when she remembers.
6. Invoices over 5,000 also need sign-off from the Finance Manager (Priya). Dana forwards the approved email to her.
7. Dana records the approval in the accounting system and adds the invoice to the weekly payment run, which the Finance Manager releases on Thursdays.
8. Invoices that miss the Thursday cut-off (approval recorded after Wednesday 5pm) wait for the next week's run.

Known problems from the team: invoices with no PO number on them are common; budget holders on leave leave invoices sitting; nobody is named as backup for approvals; some approvals are given in chat and cannot be found later.

Supplier payment terms: 30 days from invoice date.

#### october-timings.md

#### October timings (from Dana's tracking sheet)

Invoices processed in October: 120
Invoices over 5,000: 18
Invoices with missing or unmatched PO: 31 (of the 120)

Average working time per invoice for data entry (step 2): 6 minutes
Average time to find PO when it matches first time (step 3): 2 minutes
Average calendar days from receipt to data entry complete: 1.0
Average calendar days waiting for Procurement reply on unmatched POs: 3.5
Average calendar days from approval request to budget holder approval: 6.2
Average additional calendar days waiting for Finance Manager sign-off (over-5,000 only): 2.1
Average calendar days from approval recorded to payment run: 3.4
Average calendar days from receipt to payment, all invoices: 13.9

Invoices paid after the 30-day terms: 9 of 120
Invoices where the approval email or chat could not be located during the audit sample: 6 of 25 sampled

Not tracked: how many invoices needed more than one chase; budget-holder time spent per approval; cost of late payment.

## Output

#### Supplier invoice approval: what to fix first

**The biggest constraint is the wait for budget-holder approval.** It averages 6.2 calendar days, about 45% of the 13.9 days from receipt to payment (6.2 ÷ 13.9). Nothing in the process makes that wait end: there is no chase schedule, no named backup when a budget holder is away, and approvals arrive by email or chat. Fix this step first.

**Top recommendation:** send every approval request from one place with a fixed reminder schedule and a named delegate for each budget holder. The second fix is at intake: stop invoices with no PO number entering the process (31 of 120 in October).

Everything below the "Current state" heading is traced to your October timings. Where the timings don't give a figure, I mark it `not captured` instead of estimating it.

##### Current state (as you described it)

| # | Step | Owner | Type | Time (October) |
|---|------|-------|------|----------------|
| 1 | Invoice arrives in the shared inbox | AP clerk (Dana) | Manual | 1.0 day to reach end of step 2 |
| 2 | Key supplier, amount, date, PO into accounting system | Dana | Manual | 6 min per invoice |
| 3 | Match PO in Procurement's spreadsheet | Dana | Manual | 2 min when it matches first time |
| 3a | If no PO found: email Procurement and wait | Dana, Procurement | Manual, wait | 3.5 days average, 31 invoices |
| 4 | Email invoice to budget holder for approval | Dana, budget holder | Approval, wait | 6.2 days average |
| 5 | Chase non-responders | Dana | Manual | Chase count `not captured` |
| 6 | Over 5,000: forward to Finance Manager (Priya) for sign-off | Dana, Priya | Approval, wait | 2.1 days extra, 18 invoices |
| 7 | Record approval, add to weekly payment run | Dana | Manual | Part of the 3.4 days below |
| 8 | Priya releases the run on Thursdays; approvals after Wednesday 5pm wait a week | Priya | Approval, wait | 3.4 days from approval to run |

**Hand-offs:** 4 on every invoice (inbox to Dana, Dana to budget holder, budget holder back to Dana, Dana to the payment run). Procurement adds 2 for unmatched POs and Priya's sign-off adds 2 for invoices over 5,000, so up to 8.

**Work time versus wait time.** Data entry is 6 minutes × 120 invoices = 12 hours in the month. Calendar waits are measured in days. Typing is not what slows payment.

##### Where the 13.9 days go

| Segment | Average | Share of invoices affected | Weighted contribution to the 13.9 days |
|---------|---------|---------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| Receipt to data entry done | 1.0 days | 120 of 120 | 1.0 |
| Budget-holder approval | 6.2 days | 120 of 120 | 6.2 |
| Approval recorded to payment run | 3.4 days | 120 of 120 | 3.4 |
| Waiting for Procurement on unmatched POs | 3.5 days | 31 of 120 | about 0.9 |
| Finance Manager sign-off | 2.1 days | 18 of 120 | about 0.3 |

The segments sum to about 11.8 days. The remaining 2.1 days of the 13.9 average is not explained by your timings. It may be time before the budget-holder request is sent or overlap between segments: `open: where do the other 2.1 days sit?`

*Assumption:* the Procurement and sign-off averages cover only the invoices that needed those steps, so I weighted them by 31/120 and 18/120.

##### Waste found

- **Waiting (largest):** 6.2 days for approval, 3.4 days for the payment run, 3.5 days on unmatched POs.
- **Rework:** 31 of 120 invoices (26%) arrive without a matching PO and loop back through Procurement. The cause on the supplier side is `not captured`.
- **Hand-offs:** every approval goes through Dana as relay. The Finance Manager sign-off is a second relay.
- **Manual work:** keying invoice data by hand and looking up POs in a spreadsheet.
- **Control gap:** in the audit sample, 6 of 25 approvals (24%) could not be found, because some were given in chat.
- **Outcome:** 9 of 120 invoices (7.5%) were paid after the 30-day terms.

##### Recommendations

Impact figures come only from your October data. Effort is my judgment and has no source in your notes.

| Priority | Change | Expected impact | Effort |
|----------|--------|-----------------|--------|
| 1 | **One approval channel with a fixed reminder schedule and a named delegate per budget holder.** Record the approval where the invoice lives, not in email or chat. | Targets the 6.2-day segment (45% of total). Size of reduction `not captured`. Also closes the 6-of-25 missing-approval gap. | Medium |
| 2 | **Require a PO number on every supplier invoice.** Send suppliers a notice, and auto-reply to invoices without one asking for a corrected copy. | Removes the Procurement loop for the 31 invoices (about 0.9 days of the average, 3.5 days on each affected invoice) once suppliers comply. Compliance rate `not captured`. | Low |
| 3 | **Change the payment-run cadence or cut-off.** For example, run twice a week, or release approved invoices on a rolling basis. | Targets the 3.4-day segment (24% of total). Direction is shorter; magnitude `not captured`. | Low to medium |
| 4 | **Request Priya's sign-off at the same time as the budget holder** for invoices over 5,000, instead of after. | Up to 2.1 days on 18 invoices (15% of volume). Only valid if sign-off doesn't depend on seeing the budget holder's decision: `open: does it?` | Low |
| 5 | **Give Procurement a live PO list** that Dana can search, replacing emails for lookups. | Reduces the 2-minute lookups and some of the 3.5-day waits. Magnitude `not captured`. | Medium |
| 6 | **Capture invoice data automatically** from the email or PDF, if the accounting system supports it. | Up to 12 hours of keying per month, minus time spent checking captured data (`not captured`). Cost `not captured`. | Medium to high |

Recommendation 4 changes a control. Treat it as a checkpoint, not a gate: Priya sees the invoice early, and payment still requires both approvals.

##### Future state

1. Invoice arrives at the shared inbox. An automatic reply returns any invoice without a PO number to the supplier.
2. Dana (or automatic capture) enters the invoice; the PO is matched against a searchable PO list.
3. The approval request goes to the budget holder from one system. Reminders go on the agreed schedule, then escalate to the named delegate.
4. For invoices over 5,000, Priya's sign-off request goes out at the same time.
5. Both approvals are recorded against the invoice. The invoice joins the next payment run under the new cadence.

**Steps:** 8 today (plus conditional step 3a) become 5. **Hand-offs:** 4 on every invoice today (up to 8) become 2 on every invoice (inbox to Dana, system to payment run). The budget-holder request and reply happen inside one system, and the Procurement loop is removed once suppliers comply. Priya's sign-off stays a separate approval, but runs in parallel. That count assumes the system's approval step does not count as a hand-off through Dana; if you count it, the figure is 4.

*Assumption:* these counts are a design target. They depend on the accounting system supporting in-system approvals, which your notes don't say (`open`).

##### Open questions and figures not captured

- `open:` What reminder interval and escalation point should apply? Your notes give no current rule to base a number on.
- `open:` Who is the named delegate for each budget holder?
- `open:` Can the accounting system send approval requests and reminders, or will this need a separate tool?
- `open:` Can Priya's sign-off run in parallel, or must it follow the budget holder's decision?
- `open:` What payment-run cadence is acceptable to Priya?
- `open:` Where do the other 2.1 days of the 13.9 average go?
- `not captured:` chase counts, budget-holder time per approval, cost of late payment, supplier compliance rate on PO numbers, and the time saved by any recommendation.

##### Implementation order

1. **Week-one fixes:** agree a named delegate for each budget holder; stop approving in chat; send the PO-number notice to suppliers. Dana's own tracking sheet already holds the baseline.
2. **Next:** set the reminder schedule and escalation rule; decide the payment-run cadence with Priya.
3. **Then:** move approvals into one system; run Priya's sign-off in parallel if she agrees.
4. **Later:** a searchable PO list, then automatic invoice capture.

After a month, repeat the October measurements. The baselines to beat are 6.2 days for approval, 3.4 days to the payment run, 31 of 120 unmatched POs, 9 of 120 late payments, and 6 of 25 approvals missing from the audit sample.

##### Checks run before delivery

The bundled scripts (preflight, writing check, quality gate) can't run here, so I did the checks by hand: I recomputed every percentage and the weighted segments from the October figures, confirmed that every impact claim traces to a supplied number or is marked `not captured`, and read the text for filler. The brand renderer does not apply because there is no styled file. No formal receipt exists.

**Files:** none produced; the analysis above is the deliverable (this file, `out/answer.md`).

skills.title: Design software system
skills.description: Produce a fast, unbranded working design for a new system, service, API, or data architecture, usually inline. Covers requirements, components, data flow, data model, API contracts, storage, caching, queues, scaling, reliability, capacity, and explicit trade-offs. Use when someone asks how to build or structure a new product or service, how it will scale, which database, cache, queue, or API style fits, or wants component boundaries explored before decisions are formalized. Do NOT use for reviewing existing code, capturing one already-made decision as a short ADR. For a formal sourced architecture document, use the formal architecture reference mode and its write-architecture-reference workflow.

guide.what: Explore a system or service design.
guide.when: A working architecture or technical trade-off discussion is needed.
guide.inputs: The problem, requirements, constraints, scale, and existing system context.
guide.outputs: A working design covering components, data, interfaces, and trade-offs.
guide.example: Explore a working design for this service, including its data flow and trade-offs.
guide.expect: It states its assumptions, then walks requirements, components, data model, APIs, scaling and trade-offs, leading with a recommended design. It marks assumed scale or latency figures as assumed instead of inventing them, and points you to the formal architecture mode if you need a sourced reference.
guide.overview: It states its assumptions, then walks requirements, components, data model, APIs, scaling and trade-offs, leading with a recommended design. It marks assumed scale or latency figures as assumed instead of inventing them, and points you to the formal architecture mode if you need a sourced reference.
guide.value: Work through how a service or system could meet its requirements, including components, data, APIs, scale and trade-offs. It gives a recommended working design for discussion before a formal architecture reference is needed.

preparation.where: Describe the problem, users, requirements and constraints. For an existing system, provide the relevant code or diagrams. Scale and latency targets are supplied requirements or explicitly stated assumptions, not hidden defaults.
preparation.missing: No existing architecture document is required to explore a new design. Unknown requirements remain assumptions or decisions. Use the formal architecture-reference mode when you need a sourced record of settled design rather than an exploratory recommendation.

preparationSkills.reason: Produces a formal sourced reference once the design has sufficient decisions and evidence.

reuse.label: General use
reuse.reason: The method accepts the user’s project sources and takes private context as an explicit input.
reuse.basis: Source classification and automated reference scan; cross-environment execution has not been tested.

> [`readout-brief.md`](../writing-diagnostics/references/registers/readout-brief.md). Inputs, not a final pass.**

Design systems and evaluate architectural choices. Lead with a recommended design, then show the reasoning and the trade-offs behind it.

## Ground rules

- When extending an existing system, inspect the supplied implementation, contracts and operating evidence first. State what was inspected and what remains unavailable; proposed extensions must respect confirmed behavior. This design inspection does not imply a completed code review.
- State assumptions before you design on them. If scale, latency, budget, or team constraints were not given, say what you are assuming and mark it. Do not invent load figures, SLAs, or user counts and present them as fact.
- Every choice has a cost. Name the trade-off you accept with each decision, not just the benefit.
- Simplest design that meets the stated requirements wins. Add mechanism only when a requirement forces it.

## When NOT to use

- Reviewing or debugging code that already exists.
- Recording one decision that is already made. That is an ADR, not a design.

For a formal sourced reference, select the formal architecture reference mode
and read [write-architecture-reference](../write-architecture-reference/SKILL.md). It preserves source
locators, the selected project profile, complementary architecture and engineering
views, and artifact review. The portable System Design package embeds that workflow.
The framework below covers exploratory working design; it does not replace the
formal mode or its acceptance checks.

## Framework

Walk these in order. Skip a section only when it plainly does not apply, and say so.

### 1. Requirements
- Functional: what it must do.
- Non-functional: scale, latency, availability, durability, cost.
- Constraints: team size, timeline, existing stack, compliance.
- If any of these are unknown, ask or assume-and-mark before proceeding.

### 2. High-level design
- Components and their responsibilities.
- Data flow between them.
- API contracts, data ownership and state changes at the boundaries.
- Identity and authorization: principals, relevant tenant or isolation key, allowed actions, enforcement location, and denial behavior. Tenant isolation does not establish permission to act on a record. Require every applicable identity, tenant, ownership or explicit grant check; deny when a required check fails or the governing policy is unavailable. Do not claim a tenant filter compensates for a missing permission check.
- Storage choices per component.

### 3. Deep dive
- Data model: entities, keys, relationships, access patterns.
- API endpoints: shape, method, idempotency (REST, GraphQL, or gRPC as fits).
- Caching: what, where, invalidation, staleness tolerance.
- Async: queues, events, ordering, delivery guarantees.
- Failure handling: timeouts, retries with backoff, idempotency keys, dead-letter paths. A read of completed state followed by a write does not prevent concurrent duplicate work. Specify the atomic claim or uniqueness constraint, idempotent state change, and treatment of external side effects before claiming a redelivery is safe. State any remaining failure window; do not promise exactly-once effects without supporting evidence. A failed claim does not prove work is complete. Distinguish completed, busy and expired claims; do not acknowledge unfinished work unless a separate durable recovery trigger has accepted responsibility. Otherwise defer or retry delivery under the queue contract. State what restarts work if the current owner dies.

### 4. Scale and reliability
- Load estimate: request rate, data volume, growth. Show the arithmetic.
- Scaling approach: horizontal vs vertical, statefulness, partitioning.
- Redundancy and failover: single points of failure and how they are removed.
- Observability: the metrics, logs, and alerts that would catch a problem first.

### 5. Trade-off analysis
- List the decisions that could reasonably have gone another way.
- For each: the alternative, why it lost, and the condition under which it would win.
- Weigh complexity, cost, team familiarity, time to market, maintainability.

## Output

Produce a structured design: recommendation first, then components, data model, APIs, scaling, and trade-offs. Include a diagram (ASCII, or described in words if ASCII is too coarse). State assumptions explicitly and flag them. Close with what you would revisit as the system grows, and the earliest signal that would trigger each revisit.

Write the design to a file when a working filesystem is available and the user wants an artifact. In an ephemeral or hosted environment where writes will not persist, deliver the full design inline in the reply instead.

## Release gate (required)

Before you deliver, run the gate. This is a required step, not a suggestion. Full
spec in [`release-gate.md`](../_shared/release-gate.md).

1. Apply review-writing to the prose. Use the bundled diagnostic tools to check saved writing. For
   a final artifact it emits a receipt the quality gate requires.
2. Run review-deliverable before you call it final.

Do not present the artifact as finished until both checks have passed.

examples.title: Design for an SMS appointment reminder and reply service
examples.markdown:
## Request

We want to replace our nightly appointment-reminder script with a proper service that sends SMS reminders and lets patients confirm or cancel by replying. My notes and the current setup are in the inputs folder; can you design it and tell me what you'd recommend and what the trade-offs are?

## Inputs

Run of the built `design-software-system` task package. The recording session invented this scenario, the request and the inputs below before running the skill. It had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so.

#### current-script.txt

Current setup (written by Tomas Ibarra, from memory of the script; the script itself is not attached)

- A Python script runs from cron at 17:00 each weekday on VM-1.
- It reads tomorrow's appointments from the SchedBook read-only reporting view (columns: appt_id, patient_id, clinic_id, start_time, mobile, status).
- For each row it calls the Northgate send API one at a time and writes a line to a log file. No database record is kept of what was sent.
- Twice last year the script was re-run by hand after a crash partway through; some patients received two texts. Nobody counted how many.
- Replies arrive in a Northgate inbox. A front-desk person reads them and updates SchedBook by hand.
- SchedBook exposes a REST endpoint to cancel an appointment (POST /appointments/{id}/cancel, requires an API key). We have not tested it. Whether repeating the call is harmless is unknown.
- STOP replies are not tracked anywhere except Northgate's own opt-out list.

#### requirements-notes.md

#### Reminder service: notes from planning meeting (Priya Raman, ops lead)

Harbourline Community Health runs 6 clinics. Appointments live in the scheduling system (vendor product "SchedBook"), which we cannot modify.

##### What we want
- SMS reminder 48 hours and 4 hours before each appointment.
- Patient replies C to confirm, X to cancel. A cancel must free the slot in SchedBook so the front desk can rebook it.
- Front-desk staff see reminder status (sent, delivered, confirmed, cancelled, failed) on a per-clinic screen. Staff should see only their own clinic's patients.
- Patients who reply STOP must never be texted again.

##### Numbers we have
- About 1,400 appointments per weekday across all clinics; clinics closed weekends.
- Last quarter, no-show rate was 14%. Goal is under 10%. (Target is ours, not a promise.)
- SMS provider is Northgate Messaging (example.com account). Their API returns a message ID and sends delivery receipts by webhook. Rate limit: 20 messages per second.

##### Constraints
- One developer (Tomas Ibarra) plus part-time help from IT. Go-live target is the end of January.
- Existing stack is a single Postgres 15 database and two small VMs on a cloud provider. Team knows Postgres and Python; no one has run a message broker.
- Message text must not include diagnosis or clinic service type, only date, time, clinic name and a call-back number. Compliance has asked for this.
- Budget: no figure given.

##### Not decided
- Whether reminders go out in the patient's language (we hold a language field, about 70% filled).

## Output

#### Recommendation

Build one small Python service on your existing Postgres 15 database, with no message broker. Run two processes from the same code: a **web** process (Northgate webhooks and the staff screen) and a **worker** process (sync from SchedBook, send, cancel). Both can run on VM-1 and VM-2 because workers claim rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.

The duplicate texts came from the old script keeping no record of what it sent. A unique reminder row per appointment and kind, written before each send, fixes that. Volume is small (about 0.14 webhook calls per second), nobody on the team has run a broker, and Tomas Ibarra can build this with skills already in the team.

**What I inspected:** Priya Raman's planning notes and Tomas's description of the current script. **Not available:** the script itself, SchedBook and Northgate API documentation, and any count of past duplicates. The design marks what depends on those.

#### Design

```
 SchedBook view ──poll 5 min──▶ worker (sync, send, cancel) ──▶ Northgate send API
 SchedBook cancel API ◀──────── worker
                                   │ claim / update
 Northgate webhooks ─▶ web ─────▶ Postgres 15 ◀───── web ◀── staff browser
```

- **Sync:** every 5 minutes, upsert appointments from the reporting view and create a 48h and a 4h reminder row each. A cancelled or rescheduled appointment cancels unsent reminders.
- **Sender:** claims a due row, re-checks appointment status and the opt-out list, sends, stores the Northgate message ID.
- **Webhook:** verifies the signature, stores the event in `inbound_event` (unique on provider event ID), then answers 200. That stored row is the durable hand-off; Northgate redelivers if it gets no 200.
- **Replies:** STOP writes to a local `opt_out` table and skips pending reminders. C marks the reminder confirmed. X creates one `cancel_request` per appointment; the cancel worker reads the appointment status from SchedBook first, calls the cancel endpoint, retries four times, then shows the failure to staff for a manual cancel.

**Tables:** `appointment`, `reminder` (UNIQUE on appointment and kind; state, claim owner, claim expiry, provider message ID, attempts), `inbound_event`, `cancel_request`, `opt_out`, `staff_clinic_grant`.

**Authorization:**

| Principal | Allowed | Denied when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Northgate | Post events | Signature invalid |
| Patient | Confirm or cancel an appointment whose mobile on file matches the sender | Number does not match |
| Front-desk staff | View reminders for clinics in their grant | No grant, or grant lookup unavailable |

A clinic filter alone does not give permission; staff need a login and a grant row. The staff screen is read-only in version 1.

#### Failure handling

A worker that dies after Northgate accepted a message but before the ID was stored leaves the row `sending` with an expired claim. The service cannot tell whether the text went out. If Northgate can look up a message by client reference (unknown), the sweeper checks. If not, it marks the row `unknown`, does not resend, and shows it on the staff screen. That accepts a missed reminder in a rare crash instead of a duplicate. An unexpired claim means another worker owns the row, so the sweeper leaves it. Every worker runs the sweeper, so the surviving worker restarts the dead one's work.

Timeouts and 5xx responses retry at 30 s, 2 min and 10 min, then `failed`. A 429 waits and is not counted as an attempt.

#### Scale

- Outbound: 1,400 × 2 = 2,800 messages per weekday. One burst at 20 per second takes 2,800 / 20 = 140 seconds; in practice they spread across the day.
- Inbound (assumed 40% reply rate): 0.4 × 2,800 = 1,120 replies, plus 2,800 delivery receipts, about 3,920 webhook calls per day.
- Storage: 2,800 × 260 weekdays = 728,000 reminder rows a year.

One Postgres instance carries this. Add workers to scale. Postgres is the single point of failure; no backup arrangements were supplied, so confirm a nightly backup before go-live.

**First alerts:** pending reminders more than 10 minutes overdue; any `unknown` or `failed` reminder; sync lag over 15 minutes; cancel requests not done after 15 minutes; webhook errors and signature failures.

#### Trade-offs

| Decision | Alternative | Why it lost | When it wins |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Postgres as the queue | RabbitMQ or SQS | Nobody has run one; volume is low | Other services need the events, or volume grows about 100× |
| No resend on `unknown` | Resend | Avoids repeating the duplicate problem | Northgate lookup exists, or missed reminders cost more than duplicates |
| Poll SchedBook | SchedBook notifications | Vendor product cannot be changed | SchedBook adds change notifications |
| Cancel on one X | Second confirming reply | Fewer steps for patients | A family sharing a number causes a wrong cancellation |
| Read-only staff screen | Staff can resend or cancel | Smaller permission surface | Front desk asks and an audit trail exists |

#### Assumptions to confirm

- **A1/A2:** Sends fall between 08:00 and 20:00 clinic time, which puts the 48-hour reminder for a Monday appointment on Saturday morning. Please confirm weekend texts are acceptable.
- **A3:** 40% reply rate is a sizing guess; your notes give none.
- **A4:** SchedBook's reporting view is current within a few minutes.
- **A5:** Northgate supports a client reference and lookup.
- **Budget:** none given; the design adds no paid component.
- **Language:** version 1 sends English only, since the language field is about 70% filled. This was undecided in your notes.

#### Test before building

1. Is SchedBook's cancel call safe to repeat, and is the reporting view's status current? Test in a non-production account. The retry logic reads status first until this is known.
2. Does Northgate support client references and lookup?

#### Revisit as it grows

| Revisit | Earliest signal |
| --- | --- |
| Add a broker | Webhook backlog or lock waits in the slow-query log |
| Two-step cancel | First wrongly cancelled appointment on a shared number |
| Translated templates | Front desk reports patients unable to read English text |
| Postgres failover | Any outage delaying reminders by more than an hour |
| Staff actions on screen | Repeated requests for manual resend |

The 14% to under 10% no-show goal is yours; this design does not predict that outcome. Measure it after go-live.

#### Release check

I could not run the bundled prose checker, receipt tool or review-deliverable scripts here. I checked the wording by hand and recomputed every figure above. There is no scanner result or receipt, so a scripted quality record would show the prose and receipt checks as blocked. This is a working design in Markdown, so the brand check does not apply. Nothing has been built, sent or tested against SchedBook or Northgate.

#### File

- `out/reminder-service-design.md` — the full design: requirements, authorization table, data model, interfaces, claim query, failure handling, scale arithmetic, observability and trade-offs.

### File: reminder-service-design.md

#### Appointment reminder service: design

##### Recommendation

Build one small Python service on the existing Postgres 15 database, with no message broker. Postgres holds the appointments, the reminder queue, the inbound replies and the opt-out list. Two processes run from the same code: a web process (Northgate webhooks and the staff screen) and a worker process (sync, send, cancel). Both can run on VM-1 and VM-2 at the same time because workers claim rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`.

The main reason for this shape is the duplicate texts from the old script. They happened because nothing recorded what had been sent. A unique row per appointment and reminder kind, written before the send, fixes that without new infrastructure. Nobody on the team has run a broker, and the volume does not need one.

##### Inspected and not available

Inspected: the planning notes and Tomas Ibarra's description of the current script. Not available: the script itself, the SchedBook API documentation, the Northgate API documentation, and any count of past duplicates. Everything below that depends on those is marked as an assumption or an open question.

##### 1. Requirements

Functional (from the notes):
- Send an SMS 48 hours and 4 hours before each appointment.
- Reply C confirms; reply X cancels the appointment in SchedBook.
- Reply STOP permanently stops texts to that number.
- A per-clinic screen shows sent, delivered, confirmed, cancelled and failed. Staff see only their own clinic.
- Message text contains only date, time, clinic name and a call-back number.

Non-functional:
- About 1,400 weekday appointments (given). Target no-show rate under 10% against 14% last quarter (the clinic's goal; this design does not predict it will be reached).
- Northgate allows 20 messages per second (given).
- One developer, go-live end of January, Postgres and Python skills only (given).

Assumptions (marked A):
- A1: Reminders send between 08:00 and 20:00 clinic time. A reminder due outside that window goes out at 20:00 the previous evening or 08:00, whichever is nearer inside the window. Confirm with Priya Raman.
- A2: Weekend appointments do not exist, but 48-hour reminders for Monday morning fall on Saturday. A1 moves them to Saturday 08:00. Confirm whether weekend texts are acceptable.
- A3: About 40% of patients reply. The notes give no reply rate; this is a sizing guess.
- A4: SchedBook's reporting view is refreshed within a few minutes. Unknown.
- A5: Northgate can attach a client reference to a send, and can look a message up by it. Unknown; the design works without it.
- A6: Budget is unstated, so cost is judged only as "no new paid components".

##### 2. High-level design

```
 SchedBook reporting view ──poll 5 min──▶ ┌──────────────┐
                                          │  worker      │──send──▶ Northgate API
 SchedBook cancel API ◀──cancel───────────│  (sync, send,│
                                          │   cancel)    │
                                          └──────┬───────┘
                                                 │ claim / update
                                          ┌──────▼───────┐
 Northgate webhooks ──▶ ┌──────────┐      │  Postgres 15 │
 (delivery, inbound)    │  web     │─────▶│              │
 Staff browser ────────▶│  process │◀─────│              │
                        └──────────┘      └──────────────┘
```

Components:
- **Sync (worker):** every 5 minutes reads appointments from the reporting view and upserts them. New rows create two reminder rows. A cancelled or rescheduled appointment cancels unsent reminders and creates new ones.
- **Sender (worker):** claims due reminders, re-checks the appointment and opt-out status, sends through Northgate, records the message ID.
- **Webhook handler (web):** verifies the Northgate signature, writes the event to `inbound_event`, then answers 200. It does no other work.
- **Inbound processor (worker):** reads `inbound_event` rows, applies STOP, C and X.
- **Staff screen (web):** read-only list of reminders for the user's clinic.

###### Identity and authorization

| Principal | Allowed | Enforced | Denial |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Northgate (webhook) | Post delivery and inbound events | Signature check in the web process | 401, event not stored |
| Patient (SMS reply) | Confirm or cancel an appointment whose number on file matches the sender | Inbound processor | Reply ignored and logged |
| Front-desk staff | View reminders for clinics they are granted | Web process, per request | 403 |
| Worker | Call the SchedBook cancel API with the service key | Key held only on worker hosts | Task goes to failed state |

Clinic filtering alone does not give permission to act. Staff access needs both a valid login and a row in `staff_clinic_grant`. If the grant lookup or the login provider is unavailable, the screen denies. The service never lets staff cancel or edit through the screen in this version, so no write permission is needed there.

A reply cancels only when the sender number equals the mobile on the appointment and the appointment has at least one reminder sent to that number. A number shared by a family could cancel another member's appointment; the reply text names the date and time and allows a "reply Y to confirm cancellation" step (see trade-offs).

##### 3. Deep dive

###### Data model

| Table | Key columns | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `appointment` | `appt_id` (PK), `patient_id`, `clinic_id`, `start_time`, `mobile`, `status`, `synced_at` | Mirror of the view |
| `reminder` | `id`, `appt_id`, `kind` (48h/4h), `due_at`, `state`, `claim_owner`, `claim_expires_at`, `provider_msg_id`, `attempts`; UNIQUE (`appt_id`, `kind`) | The queue and the audit record |
| `inbound_event` | `provider_event_id` (UNIQUE), `kind` (reply/delivery), `payload`, `received_at`, `processed_at` | Webhook landing table |
| `cancel_request` | `id`, `appt_id` (UNIQUE), `state`, `claim_owner`, `claim_expires_at`, `attempts` | One cancel per appointment |
| `opt_out` | `mobile` (PK), `at` | Checked before every send |
| `staff_clinic_grant` | `staff_id`, `clinic_id` | Staff screen authorization |

Reminder states: `pending → sending → sent → delivered`, plus `confirmed`, `failed`, `skipped` (opted out, cancelled or past), and `unknown` (see failure handling). Access patterns: due reminders by `due_at` where state is `pending`, reminders by clinic and date for the screen, events by `processed_at IS NULL`.

###### Interfaces

- `POST /hooks/northgate` — Northgate calls it. Idempotent through `provider_event_id`.
- `GET /clinics/{clinic_id}/reminders?date=` — staff screen data. Checks the grant.
- Outbound: Northgate send, SchedBook `POST /appointments/{id}/cancel`.

No other endpoints. A cancel in SchedBook is not known to be safe to repeat (open question 1).

###### Sending and failure handling

1. The sender claims a row: `UPDATE reminder SET state='sending', claim_owner=:w, claim_expires_at=now()+2 min WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM reminder WHERE state='pending' AND due_at<=now() FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1)`. The unique key on (`appt_id`, `kind`) means a re-run of the sync cannot create a second row.
2. It re-reads the appointment and the opt-out list. If the appointment is cancelled, in the past or opted out, state becomes `skipped`.
3. It calls Northgate, with a client reference of the reminder id if A5 holds, then stores `provider_msg_id` and sets `sent`.
4. Timeouts and 5xx responses set the row back to `pending` with a backoff of 30 s, 2 min, 10 min; after 4 attempts the state is `failed`. A 429 waits for the 20 per second limit and does not count as an attempt.

  • Twice last year the script was re-run by hand after a crash partway through; some patients received two texts. Nobody counted how many.
  • Replies arrive in a Northgate inbox. A front-desk person reads them and updates SchedBook by hand.
  • SchedBook exposes a REST endpoint to cancel an appointment (POST /appointments/{id}/cancel, requires an API key). We have not tested it. Whether repeating the call is harmless is unknown.
  • STOP replies are not tracked anywhere except Northgate's own opt-out list.
requirements-notes.md
Reminder service: notes from planning meeting (Priya Raman, ops lead)

Harbourline Community Health runs 6 clinics. Appointments live in the scheduling system (vendor product "SchedBook"), which we cannot modify.

What we want
  • SMS reminder 48 hours and 4 hours before each appointment.
  • Patient replies C to confirm, X to cancel. A cancel must free the slot in SchedBook so the front desk can rebook it.
  • Front-desk staff see reminder status (sent, delivered, confirmed, cancelled, failed) on a per-clinic screen. Staff should see only their own clinic's patients.
  • Patients who reply STOP must never be texted again.
Numbers we have
  • About 1,400 appointments per weekday across all clinics; clinics closed weekends.
  • Last quarter, no-show rate was 14%. Goal is under 10%. (Target is ours, not a promise.)
  • SMS provider is Northgate Messaging (example.com account). Their API returns a message ID and sends delivery receipts by webhook. Rate limit: 20 messages per second.
Constraints
  • One developer (Tomas Ibarra) plus part-time help from IT. Go-live target is the end of January.
  • Existing stack is a single Postgres 15 database and two small VMs on a cloud provider. Team knows Postgres and Python; no one has run a message broker.
  • Message text must not include diagnosis or clinic service type, only date, time, clinic name and a call-back number. Compliance has asked for this.
  • Budget: no figure given.
Not decided
  • Whether reminders go out in the patient's language (we hold a language field, about 70% filled).

Output

Recommendation

Build one small Python service on your existing Postgres 15 database, with no message broker. Run two processes from the same code: a web process (Northgate webhooks and the staff screen) and a worker process (sync from SchedBook, send, cancel). Both can run on VM-1 and VM-2 because workers claim rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.

The duplicate texts came from the old script keeping no record of what it sent. A unique reminder row per appointment and kind, written before each send, fixes that. Volume is small (about 0.14 webhook calls per second), nobody on the team has run a broker, and Tomas Ibarra can build this with skills already in the team.

What I inspected: Priya Raman's planning notes and Tomas's description of the current script. Not available: the script itself, SchedBook and Northgate API documentation, and any count of past duplicates. The design marks what depends on those.

Design
 SchedBook view ──poll 5 min──▶ worker (sync, send, cancel) ──▶ Northgate send API
 SchedBook cancel API ◀──────── worker
                                   │ claim / update
 Northgate webhooks ─▶ web ─────▶ Postgres 15 ◀───── web ◀── staff browser
  • Sync: every 5 minutes, upsert appointments from the reporting view and create a 48h and a 4h reminder row each. A cancelled or rescheduled appointment cancels unsent reminders.
  • Sender: claims a due row, re-checks appointment status and the opt-out list, sends, stores the Northgate message ID.
  • Webhook: verifies the signature, stores the event in inbound_event (unique on provider event ID), then answers 200. That stored row is the durable hand-off; Northgate redelivers if it gets no 200.
  • Replies: STOP writes to a local opt_out table and skips pending reminders. C marks the reminder confirmed. X creates one cancel_request per appointment; the cancel worker reads the appointment status from SchedBook first, calls the cancel endpoint, retries four times, then shows the failure to staff for a manual cancel.

Tables: appointment, reminder (UNIQUE on appointment and kind; state, claim owner, claim expiry, provider message ID, attempts), inbound_event, cancel_request, opt_out, staff_clinic_grant.

Authorization:

PrincipalAllowedDenied when
NorthgatePost eventsSignature invalid
PatientConfirm or cancel an appointment whose mobile on file matches the senderNumber does not match
Front-desk staffView reminders for clinics in their grantNo grant, or grant lookup unavailable

A clinic filter alone does not give permission; staff need a login and a grant row. The staff screen is read-only in version 1.

Failure handling

A worker that dies after Northgate accepted a message but before the ID was stored leaves the row sending with an expired claim. The service cannot tell whether the text went out. If Northgate can look up a message by client reference (unknown), the sweeper checks. If not, it marks the row unknown, does not resend, and shows it on the staff screen. That accepts a missed reminder in a rare crash instead of a duplicate. An unexpired claim means another worker owns the row, so the sweeper leaves it. Every worker runs the sweeper, so the surviving worker restarts the dead one's work.

Timeouts and 5xx responses retry at 30 s, 2 min and 10 min, then failed. A 429 waits and is not counted as an attempt.

Scale
  • Outbound: 1,400 × 2 = 2,800 messages per weekday. One burst at 20 per second takes 2,800 / 20 = 140 seconds; in practice they spread across the day.
  • Inbound (assumed 40% reply rate): 0.4 × 2,800 = 1,120 replies, plus 2,800 delivery receipts, about 3,920 webhook calls per day.
  • Storage: 2,800 × 260 weekdays = 728,000 reminder rows a year.

One Postgres instance carries this. Add workers to scale. Postgres is the single point of failure; no backup arrangements were supplied, so confirm a nightly backup before go-live.

First alerts: pending reminders more than 10 minutes overdue; any unknown or failed reminder; sync lag over 15 minutes; cancel requests not done after 15 minutes; webhook errors and signature failures.

Trade-offs
DecisionAlternativeWhy it lostWhen it wins
Postgres as the queueRabbitMQ or SQSNobody has run one; volume is lowOther services need the events, or volume grows about 100×
No resend on unknownResendAvoids repeating the duplicate problemNorthgate lookup exists, or missed reminders cost more than duplicates
Poll SchedBookSchedBook notificationsVendor product cannot be changedSchedBook adds change notifications
Cancel on one XSecond confirming replyFewer steps for patientsA family sharing a number causes a wrong cancellation
Read-only staff screenStaff can resend or cancelSmaller permission surfaceFront desk asks and an audit trail exists
Assumptions to confirm
  • A1/A2: Sends fall between 08:00 and 20:00 clinic time, which puts the 48-hour reminder for a Monday appointment on Saturday morning. Please confirm weekend texts are acceptable.
  • A3: 40% reply rate is a sizing guess; your notes give none.
  • A4: SchedBook's reporting view is current within a few minutes.
  • A5: Northgate supports a client reference and lookup.
  • Budget: none given; the design adds no paid component.
  • Language: version 1 sends English only, since the language field is about 70% filled. This was undecided in your notes.
Test before building
  1. Is SchedBook's cancel call safe to repeat, and is the reporting view's status current? Test in a non-production account. The retry logic reads status first until this is known.
  2. Does Northgate support client references and lookup?
Revisit as it grows
RevisitEarliest signal
Add a brokerWebhook backlog or lock waits in the slow-query log
Two-step cancelFirst wrongly cancelled appointment on a shared number
Translated templatesFront desk reports patients unable to read English text
Postgres failoverAny outage delaying reminders by more than an hour
Staff actions on screenRepeated requests for manual resend

The 14% to under 10% no-show goal is yours; this design does not predict that outcome. Measure it after go-live.

Release check

I could not run the bundled prose checker, receipt tool or review-deliverable scripts here. I checked the wording by hand and recomputed every figure above. There is no scanner result or receipt, so a scripted quality record would show the prose and receipt checks as blocked. This is a working design in Markdown, so the brand check does not apply. Nothing has been built, sent or tested against SchedBook or Northgate.

File
  • out/reminder-service-design.md — the full design: requirements, authorization table, data model, interfaces, claim query, failure handling, scale arithmetic, observability and trade-offs.

File: reminder-service-design.md

Appointment reminder service: design
Recommendation

Build one small Python service on the existing Postgres 15 database, with no message broker. Postgres holds the appointments, the reminder queue, the inbound replies and the opt-out list. Two processes run from the same code: a web process (Northgate webhooks and the staff screen) and a worker process (sync, send, cancel). Both can run on VM-1 and VM-2 at the same time because workers claim rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.

The main reason for this shape is the duplicate texts from the old script. They happened because nothing recorded what had been sent. A unique row per appointment and reminder kind, written before the send, fixes that without new infrastructure. Nobody on the team has run a broker, and the volume does not need one.

Inspected and not available

Inspected: the planning notes and Tomas Ibarra's description of the current script. Not available: the script itself, the SchedBook API documentation, the Northgate API documentation, and any count of past duplicates. Everything below that depends on those is marked as an assumption or an open question.

1. Requirements

Functional (from the notes):

  • Send an SMS 48 hours and 4 hours before each appointment.
  • Reply C confirms; reply X cancels the appointment in SchedBook.
  • Reply STOP permanently stops texts to that number.
  • A per-clinic screen shows sent, delivered, confirmed, cancelled and failed. Staff see only their own clinic.
  • Message text contains only date, time, clinic name and a call-back number.

Non-functional:

  • About 1,400 weekday appointments (given). Target no-show rate under 10% against 14% last quarter (the clinic's goal; this design does not predict it will be reached).
  • Northgate allows 20 messages per second (given).
  • One developer, go-live end of January, Postgres and Python skills only (given).

Assumptions (marked A):

  • A1: Reminders send between 08:00 and 20:00 clinic time. A reminder due outside that window goes out at 20:00 the previous evening or 08:00, whichever is nearer inside the window. Confirm with Priya Raman.
  • A2: Weekend appointments do not exist, but 48-hour reminders for Monday morning fall on Saturday. A1 moves them to Saturday 08:00. Confirm whether weekend texts are acceptable.
  • A3: About 40% of patients reply. The notes give no reply rate; this is a sizing guess.
  • A4: SchedBook's reporting view is refreshed within a few minutes. Unknown.
  • A5: Northgate can attach a client reference to a send, and can look a message up by it. Unknown; the design works without it.
  • A6: Budget is unstated, so cost is judged only as "no new paid components".
2. High-level design
 SchedBook reporting view ──poll 5 min──▶ ┌──────────────┐
                                          │  worker      │──send──▶ Northgate API
 SchedBook cancel API ◀──cancel───────────│  (sync, send,│
                                          │   cancel)    │
                                          └──────┬───────┘
                                                 │ claim / update
                                          ┌──────▼───────┐
 Northgate webhooks ──▶ ┌──────────┐      │  Postgres 15 │
 (delivery, inbound)    │  web     │─────▶│              │
 Staff browser ────────▶│  process │◀─────│              │
                        └──────────┘      └──────────────┘

Components:

  • Sync (worker): every 5 minutes reads appointments from the reporting view and upserts them. New rows create two reminder rows. A cancelled or rescheduled appointment cancels unsent reminders and creates new ones.
  • Sender (worker): claims due reminders, re-checks the appointment and opt-out status, sends through Northgate, records the message ID.
  • Webhook handler (web): verifies the Northgate signature, writes the event to inbound_event, then answers 200. It does no other work.
  • Inbound processor (worker): reads inbound_event rows, applies STOP, C and X.
  • Staff screen (web): read-only list of reminders for the user's clinic.
Identity and authorization
PrincipalAllowedEnforcedDenial
Northgate (webhook)Post delivery and inbound eventsSignature check in the web process401, event not stored
Patient (SMS reply)Confirm or cancel an appointment whose number on file matches the senderInbound processorReply ignored and logged
Front-desk staffView reminders for clinics they are grantedWeb process, per request403
WorkerCall the SchedBook cancel API with the service keyKey held only on worker hostsTask goes to failed state

Clinic filtering alone does not give permission to act. Staff access needs both a valid login and a row in staff_clinic_grant. If the grant lookup or the login provider is unavailable, the screen denies. The service never lets staff cancel or edit through the screen in this version, so no write permission is needed there.

A reply cancels only when the sender number equals the mobile on the appointment and the appointment has at least one reminder sent to that number. A number shared by a family could cancel another member's appointment; the reply text names the date and time and allows a "reply Y to confirm cancellation" step (see trade-offs).

3. Deep dive
Data model
TableKey columnsNotes
appointmentappt_id (PK), patient_id, clinic_id, start_time, mobile, status, synced_atMirror of the view
reminderid, appt_id, kind (48h/4h), due_at, state, claim_owner, claim_expires_at, provider_msg_id, attempts; UNIQUE (appt_id, kind)The queue and the audit record
inbound_eventprovider_event_id (UNIQUE), kind (reply/delivery), payload, received_at, processed_atWebhook landing table
cancel_requestid, appt_id (UNIQUE), state, claim_owner, claim_expires_at, attemptsOne cancel per appointment
opt_outmobile (PK), atChecked before every send
staff_clinic_grantstaff_id, clinic_idStaff screen authorization

Reminder states: pending → sending → sent → delivered, plus confirmed, failed, skipped (opted out, cancelled or past), and unknown (see failure handling). Access patterns: due reminders by due_at where state is pending, reminders by clinic and date for the screen, events by processed_at IS NULL.

Interfaces
  • POST /hooks/northgate — Northgate calls it. Idempotent through provider_event_id.
  • GET /clinics/{clinic_id}/reminders?date= — staff screen data. Checks the grant.
  • Outbound: Northgate send, SchedBook POST /appointments/{id}/cancel.

No other endpoints. A cancel in SchedBook is not known to be safe to repeat (open question 1).

Sending and failure handling
  1. The sender claims a row: UPDATE reminder SET state='sending', claim_owner=:w, claim_expires_at=now()+2 min WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM reminder WHERE state='pending' AND due_at<=now() FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1). The unique key on (appt_id, kind) means a re-run of the sync cannot create a second row.
  2. It re-reads the appointment and the opt-out list. If the appointment is cancelled, in the past or opted out, state becomes skipped.
  3. It calls Northgate, with a client reference of the reminder id if A5 holds, then stores provider_msg_id and sets sent.
  4. Timeouts and 5xx responses set the row back to pending with a backoff of 30 s, 2 min, 10 min; after 4 attempts the state is failed. A 429 waits for the 20 per second limit and does not count as an attempt.
