skills.markdown:
---
name: design-sticker
description: Develop and critique typography-led stickers through visual references, distinct compositions, type auditions, optical refinement, and print-scale proofing.
---


# Design sticker

Use for sticker concepts, typography refinement, collection direction, and visual critique. For imposing existing PNGs onto cutting sheets, use the project's production workflow. If a sheet-layout skill is unavailable, inspect the existing generator and machine profile; do not redesign the approved images or guess cut settings. This skill does not select a political stance, invent a brand identity, or authorize publication.

Read [shared workflow](references/estate/workflow.md) and [brand policy](references/estate/brand.md). Resolve the current project brief and decisions from its `AGENTS.md` or index. Keep project identities, private phrases, fonts, and licensed artwork in the project. If no brief exists, infer a small working brief from the request and label the assumptions; do not require an intake interview. For unbranded artwork, propose an artifact-scoped type and color treatment from the request; identify it as a proposal. The neutral reporting style is not a requirement to use system fonts in expressive artwork.

## Decide the visual idea

Preserve supplied copy and meaningful informality. Treat a substantive rewrite or punctuation change as a visible alternative. Identify the phrase's function and intended reading order. Direct statements need not become jokes.

Use documented references for a specific mechanism, such as a line break, density, rhythm, or relationship between text and object. Cite the actual artifact or designer source. Study more than one source before delivering a developed new visual direction. An early brief may name reference questions to investigate without pretending that research has already occurred; a narrow correction may need no new research. Do not reproduce a recognizable composition, lettering asset, or trade dress from a reference.

When alternatives would help, make them structurally distinct: change reading order, alignment, typographic voice, density, or silhouette for a reason. Font and color swaps on one layout are auditions, not different concepts. Match the number of alternatives to the decision; a narrow correction may need only one.

## Set and refine the type

Read [typography and critique](references/typography.md). Audition the actual words in real, available font files. Assess individual letterforms, width, weight, contrast, and behavior at the intended output size. Do not infer font rights from installation or embedding flags.

Preserve font shaping and kerning as the starting point. Avoid independently scaling every line to a common width, synthetic stretching, and automatic optical kerning across scripts or monospace text. Apply changes only to demonstrated problems. Let the outer shape and composition develop together.

Use a renderer that can preserve the selected fonts, shaping, editable copy, and intended geometry. Programmatic typesetting is acceptable when its output is visually reviewed. An image generator may support illustration or exploratory imagery when requested; exact final text needs a reliable lettering workflow.

## Critique before expanding

Inspect the rendered proof closely and at the proposed physical size or a clearly labeled scale preview. Check reading order, meaning, tone, optical spacing, composition, and reproduction separately. Numerical fit checks do not establish visual quality. Critique with concrete observations and recommend a route; do not automatically praise every option.

Develop a representative approved direction before extending it across a collection. Approval of one proof does not freeze every design choice into a brand rule. Record decisions with the artifact, version, and scope.

## Deliver and hand off

Read [production and sources](references/production.md) when exporting or preparing print work. Deliver inspectable proofs, editable wording and layout source, exact font records, and an outlined or otherwise stable viewing export when appropriate. Do not bundle commercial font files without redistribution rights.

Keep source, screen proof, print-tested artwork, and approved production files distinct. Use the current project folder and index. Explain the meaningful design choice and exact next action; leave internal checks off the artwork. Publication, sales claims, font purchases, and cloud uploads follow the user's specific authorization.

examples.title: Two type directions for a volunteer tool library bucket sticker
examples.markdown:
## Request

We're a volunteer tool library and I need a sticker for the lids of our loan buckets that says "Return it better than you found it." Can you give me a couple of distinct directions and tell me which one to print? Brief, fonts we have and our cutter details are attached.

## Inputs

**Dry run.** This skill normally works on live systems or its owner's own setup. Here the system state is invented in the inputs below, and nothing was changed anywhere. Run of the built `design-sticker` task package. The recording session invented this scenario, the request and the inputs below before running the skill. It had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so. Other files it produced, not shown here: `directions-source.svg`.

#### brief.md

#### Loan bucket sticker brief

Organisation: Alder Row Tool Library (volunteer-run, lends hand tools in grey 10-litre buckets).

Copy (supplied, keep as written): Return it better than you found it.

Use: one sticker per bucket lid, read at arm's length when someone is dropping a bucket off. Borrowers are neighbours, ages 16 to 80. Tone: warm, direct, a little dry. It is a house rule, not a joke.

Colours: no brand guide. Lid is mid-grey plastic. Prefer two inks plus the sticker paper white.

No logo on this sticker. Do not change the wording.

Open questions from the committee: someone suggested all caps "BETTER" as the loud word. Someone else thinks that sounds like a scolding.

Size: 3 in wide, round or rounded rectangle, either is fine.

#### fonts-and-cutter.txt

Fonts installed on the library laptop (font manager export, 4 Nov 2026)
Fraunces  v1.000 variable (opsz, wght, SOFT, WONK)   licence file: OFL.txt present
Archivo   v2.001 variable (wdth 62-125, wght 100-900)  licence file: OFL.txt present
Space Mono Regular/Bold v1.100                         licence file: OFL.txt present
Inter     v4.0 variable                                licence file: OFL.txt present
Gill Sans MT  (came with Office)                       no licence file; rights unknown

Production
Cutter: Cricut Explore 3 (Design Space, version not recorded)
Material: printable white sticker paper, matte, 8.5 x 11 in
Printer: office inkjet, colour (model not recorded)
Method: Print Then Cut
Previous sticker: cut ran about 1 mm off to the left on the first test sheet
No proof printed yet for this design.

## Output

### Bucket lid sticker: two directions, and which to print

**Recommendation: print Direction A (the stacked version) as the first proof.** It reads at arm's length, keeps "better" as the one emphasised word without shouting it, and the line breaks follow how people say the sentence. Direction B is the warmer fallback if the committee prefers a badge feel, but its smallest words are too small for lid-at-arm's-length reading.

Neither direction has been rendered or looked at yet. I could only write the editable source, not run a renderer, so everything below about how they look is intent plus size arithmetic. The first job is to open the file, see whether the fonts loaded, and judge it by eye.

#### Working brief (from your notes)

- Copy kept exactly: "Return it better than you found it."
- Function: a house rule, warm and dry, not a joke and not a scolding.
- Read at arm's length on a mid-grey lid, by borrowers aged 16 to 80.
- No brand guide, so the type and colour below are a **proposal for this sticker only**: ink green #1F3A2E and amber #B25E09 on white paper. Both pass 4.5:1 against white by a wide margin (the green is very dark; I estimated the amber at roughly 5:1 and it should be checked in a contrast tool).

#### The caps question

I'd keep sentence case. In "Return it better than you found it", the stress falls on "better", and the committee's worry is right: capitals on that word would make the rule read as a telling-off. A is built so "better" wins on size and weight alone, which is firmer than B's italic but still polite.

#### Direction A: stacked house rule

- **Structure:** left-aligned, four lines: *Return it / **better** / than you / found it.* Reading order is top to bottom with the eye landing on "better", then falling to "found it."
- **Type:** Archivo (installed v2.001, OFL), medium weight for the plain lines at 40 units (about 29 pt on a 3 in sticker), extra bold at 60 units for "better" in amber. One family, so hierarchy comes from weight, size and colour only.
- **Shape:** 3 x 3 in rounded square, 0.30 in corner radius.
- **Why:** plain and sturdy, like a label on a tool you trust. Breaking at "than you / found it." keeps the comparison in one breath.
- **Risk to check:** "better" at 60 units is estimated to be about 2.1 in wide against about 2.3 in of usable width, which is tight. If it crowds the right edge in the proof, drop it to 56 rather than stretching or condensing the letters.

#### Direction B: one even sentence in a badge

- **Structure:** centred, two lines: *Return it **better** / than you found it.* No size change; the only emphasis is amber italic on "better".
- **Type:** Fraunces (installed v1.000, OFL), medium weight, 24 units (about 17 pt).
- **Shape:** 3 in circle with a thin inner ring.
- **Why:** reads as a single friendly sentence, closer to a shop-door plaque. It's the softer tone.

examples.title: Turning an employer-era dock audit into a fixed-price consulting offer
examples.markdown:
## Request

I'm going independent and want to turn the dock dwell audit I built at my last job into a fixed-price consulting offer I can put on my site. The source notes and my rights/claims ledger are in inputs/. Please build the offer page copy and a synthetic worked example, and tell me what I still have to decide before I publish.

## Inputs

Run of the built `develop-independent-product` task package. The recording session invented this scenario, the request and the inputs below before running the skill. It had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so.

#### rights-and-claims-ledger.md

#### Rights and claims ledger (Priya Nandakumar, updated 2026-10-28)

##### Rights
- Separation letter, 2026-09-12, clause 7: I may reuse "general methods, templates and know-how" I developed. Brightwell data, names, systems access and confidential figures stay with Brightwell.
- No written clearance exists for naming Brightwell or Calloway as a reference.
- The workbook DwellAudit_v7.xlsx was built on company time; I am rebuilding the logic, not copying the file.

##### Claims
| Claim | State |
|---|---|
| Method splits dwell into four segments | Mine to describe |
| Median dwell fell 94 to 71 minutes at one DC | True at Brightwell; not cleared for public use; no independent replication |
| $212,000 detention figure | Confidential. Do not use |
| "Typically finds the biggest wait is not unloading" | Seen at one site only |

##### Offer I'm planning
- Name: Dock Dwell Audit
- Fixed price: $6,500, two weeks, one site
- Client supplies 4 weeks of yard and door timestamps
- Deliverable: findings report plus a door-assignment rule proposal
- I have not run it for any paying client yet.

#### source-notes.md

#### Dock dwell audit: working notes (Brightwell Grocery Distribution, Calloway DC)

Author: Priya Nandakumar, operations analyst, 2024–2026.

##### What it does
Measures how long trucks sit at the dock from gate check-in to gate release, and splits the time into four waits: yard queue, door assignment, unload/load, paperwork release. The finding is usually that the biggest wait is not unloading.

##### Method
1. Pull 4 weeks of gate and door-scan timestamps (we used the YMS export `calloway_gate_log.csv` and the WMS door scan table).
2. Match each visit by trailer ID. Drop visits with a missing timestamp and report how many were dropped.
3. Compute the four segments per visit and the median and 90th percentile for each, by hour of day.
4. Mark "idle door" minutes: a door empty while a truck waits in the yard.
5. Review the top three hours with the dock supervisor and propose door-assignment rules.

##### Calloway results
- 1,840 visits in the sample, 6% dropped for missing scans.
- Median dwell 94 minutes; door-assignment wait was the largest segment (31 min median).
- After a rule change (reserve doors 4–6 for frozen, assign by appointment time), median dwell fell to 71 minutes over 12 weeks.
- Carrier detention charges at Calloway: about $212,000 a year. Do not quote.

##### Dependencies
- Workbook `DwellAudit_v7.xlsx` lives on the Brightwell SharePoint (contains Calloway data, carrier names such as Tristate Haulage, and Brightwell's login for the YMS API: do not copy).
- Needs any yard system export with check-in, door-in, door-out and gate-out times.

##### Next
Rebuild the calculation from scratch in a clean workbook or Python script.

## Output

I've written the Dock Dwell Audit offer page and a worked example built on made-up data. Neither is published. Three decisions are still open, listed at the end.

#### What I relied on

Clause 7 of your separation letter lets you reuse general methods, templates and know-how. I treated the four-segment dwell method as covered. I did not reuse Brightwell's data, names, systems access or confidential figures, and I did not copy the workbook. I rebuilt the example from the method description alone.

#### Migration map

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Useful mechanism | Split gate-to-gate time into yard queue, door assignment, unload and paperwork. Report median and 90th percentile by hour, count idle-door minutes, then review the worst hours with the dock supervisor. |
| Original dependencies | `DwellAudit_v7.xlsx` on the former employer's SharePoint, their yard and warehouse exports, their API login, and their carrier names. |
| Independent form | A two-week, $6,500, one-site audit. The client sends a CSV, so no system access is needed. |
| Next build step | Write a clean script or workbook from the five method steps and run it on the example data. |

#### The offer page

The page covers what the client receives, what you need from them (four weeks of timestamps with a trailer ID on each visit), a day-by-day schedule, and a link to the example. Its "About" line says the offer is new and has not yet been delivered as a paid engagement, because your ledger says that is the case.

#### The worked example

The example uses eight invented visits at a fictional site. I computed the medians by hand:

| Wait | Median (min) |
|---|---|
| Yard queue | 11.0 |
| Door assignment | 30.5 |
| Unload | 41.0 |
| Paperwork | 10.5 |
| Total visit | 93.0 |

In this sample, unloading is the longest wait and door assignment comes second. That is deliberate. Your ledger records "biggest wait is not unloading" as seen at one site only, so I didn't build the example to prove it. The example omits the 90th percentile because eight visits are too few for it to mean anything.

#### What I left out, and why

- **Brightwell and Calloway names, the carrier name, file names, the API login.** These are employer details and no reference clearance exists.
- **94 to 71 minute improvement.** The ledger says it is true at Brightwell but not cleared for public use, and no one has replicated it.
- **$212,000 detention figure.** Confidential.
- **"Typically finds the biggest wait is not unloading."** This rests on one site, so the page doesn't claim it.

The page makes no claim about results, customers or deployment.

#### What I checked, and what I couldn't

- I compared every number and claim on the page and the example against the ledger. Nothing on them comes from Brightwell.
- I recomputed the medians from the eight rows by hand. Each row's four waits add up to its total.
- I couldn't run `writing_check.py` here. I read each file through for filler, repeated sentence shapes and unsupported claims instead. That is a reading pass, not a scanner result.
- The page has not been rendered or put on a site. It exists only as local Markdown.
- I invented the contact address `priya@example.com` as a placeholder. Replace it with your real one.

#### Decisions for you

1. **Your "About" line.** I wrote "two years on dock scheduling at a grocery distribution centre". Decide whether that wording is acceptable or whether you want to say less about the previous employer. The ledger gives no clearance for naming Brightwell, so I left the name out.
2. **The 94 to 71 minute result.** Decide whether to ask Brightwell for written clearance before using it. Until you have clearance, the page stays as written.
3. **When to publish.** Publishing is a separate step. I'd rebuild and test the calculation first, so the example reflects code you have actually run.

#### Files

- `out/offer-page.md`: the public page copy, with the price, schedule, client inputs and about line described above.
- `out/worked-example.md`: the made-up eight-visit tables, medians, an idle-door illustration and an illustrative rule proposal.
- `out/migration-map-private.md`: the map above plus the source links and the list of omitted items. Keep it out of the public site.

### File: migration-map-private.md

#### Migration map (private record, keep out of the public site)

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Useful mechanism | Four-segment split of gate-to-gate time per visit; median and P90 by hour; idle-door minutes; supervisor review of worst hours |
| Original dependencies | DwellAudit_v7.xlsx on the former employer's SharePoint; employer YMS/WMS exports; employer YMS API login; employer carrier names |
| Independent form | Fixed-price two-week audit, client supplies a CSV; calculation rebuilt from the method description |
| Next build step | Write a clean script or workbook from the five method steps and test it on the synthetic data (eight-visit example hand-computed here) |

##### Source links used
- inputs/source-notes.md: method, dependencies, next step
- inputs/rights-and-claims-ledger.md: separation letter clause 7, claims table, offer terms

##### Left out on purpose
- Employer and site names, the carrier name, file names, the API login: not copied.
- 94 to 71 minute result: ledger says not cleared for public use.
- $212,000 detention figure: confidential.
- "Biggest wait is not unloading": one site only. The worked example shows unloading as the longest wait.
- Workbook file: not copied; rebuilt.

### File: offer-page.md

#### Dock Dwell Audit

Find out where your trucks wait between the gate and the door, and which door-assignment rules would shorten it.

**$6,500 fixed price. Two weeks. One distribution site.**

##### What you get

A report that splits each truck visit into four waits: yard queue, door assignment, loading or unloading, and paperwork release. It gives the median and 90th-percentile time for each wait by hour of day, and it flags the hours when a door sat empty while a truck waited in the yard.

I then review the three worst hours with your dock supervisor and propose door-assignment rules for them. The rule proposal is a recommendation. You decide what to change and when.

##### What I need from you

Four weeks of yard and door timestamps for one site: check-in, door-in, door-out and gate-out, with a trailer ID on each. A CSV export from your yard or warehouse system is enough. I do not need login access to either system.

##### How it runs

1. Days 1–2: you send the export. I match visits by trailer ID, drop any with a missing timestamp, and tell you how many that was.
2. Days 3–7: I calculate the four waits and the idle-door minutes.
3. Days 8–10: I review the worst hours with your dock supervisor.
4. Days 11–14: you receive the report and the rule proposal, and we walk through it together.

##### Example

[A worked example with made-up data](worked-example.md) shows the tables you would receive.

##### About

I am an operations analyst who spent two years on dock scheduling at a grocery distribution centre. This offer is new, and I have not yet delivered it as a paid engagement.

Contact: priya@example.com

### File: worked-example.md

#### Worked example: made-up data

This example uses eight invented truck visits at a fictional site. The data, carriers and numbers are synthetic. A real audit uses four weeks of your visits, often well over a thousand.

##### Time per visit, in minutes

| Visit | Yard queue | Door assignment | Unload | Paperwork | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| V1 | 12 | 35 | 40 | 10 | 97 |
| V2 | 8 | 10 | 45 | 12 | 75 |
| V3 | 20 | 42 | 38 | 9 | 109 |
| V4 | 5 | 6 | 50 | 15 | 76 |
| V5 | 15 | 28 | 35 | 11 | 89 |
| V6 | 10 | 38 | 42 | 8 | 98 |
| V7 | 9 | 12 | 30 | 10 | 61 |
| V8 | 14 | 33 | 44 | 13 | 104 |

##### Median per wait

| Wait | Median (min) |
|---|---|
| Yard queue | 11.0 |
| Door assignment | 30.5 |
| Unload | 41.0 |
| Paperwork | 10.5 |
| Total visit | 93.0 |

In this sample unloading is still the longest single wait. Door assignment is second at 30.5 minutes, and it ranges from 6 to 42 minutes across visits, which is the spread a rule change would target. With eight visits the 90th percentile is not meaningful, so the example omits it.

##### Idle doors

In the invented 06:00–09:00 window, door 5 was empty for 55 minutes while V1, V3 and V6 were in the yard. The audit would list each such stretch with the door, the trucks waiting and the minutes lost.

##### Rule proposal (illustration)

Assign the next truck to the first free door that suits its load type, instead of holding it for the door it was originally booked to. Check this against the three worst hours with the dock supervisor before recommending it, since door equipment and temperature zones may limit which doors can take a given load.

Request

I'm going independent and want to turn the dock dwell audit I built at my last job into a fixed-price consulting offer I can put on my site. The source notes and my rights/claims ledger are in inputs/. Please build the offer page copy and a synthetic worked example, and tell me what I still have to decide before I publish.

Inputs

Run of the built develop-independent-product task package. The recording session invented this scenario, the request and the inputs below before running the skill. It had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so.

source-notes.md
Dock dwell audit: working notes (Brightwell Grocery Distribution, Calloway DC)

Author: Priya Nandakumar, operations analyst, 2024–2026.

What it does

Measures how long trucks sit at the dock from gate check-in to gate release, and splits the time into four waits: yard queue, door assignment, unload/load, paperwork release. The finding is usually that the biggest wait is not unloading.

Method
  1. Pull 4 weeks of gate and door-scan timestamps (we used the YMS export calloway_gate_log.csv and the WMS door scan table).
  2. Match each visit by trailer ID. Drop visits with a missing timestamp and report how many were dropped.
  3. Compute the four segments per visit and the median and 90th percentile for each, by hour of day.
  4. Mark "idle door" minutes: a door empty while a truck waits in the yard.
  5. Review the top three hours with the dock supervisor and propose door-assignment rules.
Calloway results
  • 1,840 visits in the sample, 6% dropped for missing scans.
  • Median dwell 94 minutes; door-assignment wait was the largest segment (31 min median).
  • After a rule change (reserve doors 4–6 for frozen, assign by appointment time), median dwell fell to 71 minutes over 12 weeks.
  • Carrier detention charges at Calloway: about $212,000 a year. Do not quote.
Dependencies
  • Workbook DwellAudit_v7.xlsx lives on the Brightwell SharePoint (contains Calloway data, carrier names such as Tristate Haulage, and Brightwell's login for the YMS API: do not copy).
  • Needs any yard system export with check-in, door-in, door-out and gate-out times.
Next

Rebuild the calculation from scratch in a clean workbook or Python script.

Output

I've written the Dock Dwell Audit offer page and a worked example built on made-up data. Neither is published. Three decisions are still open, listed at the end.

What I relied on

Clause 7 of your separation letter lets you reuse general methods, templates and know-how. I treated the four-segment dwell method as covered. I did not reuse Brightwell's data, names, systems access or confidential figures, and I did not copy the workbook. I rebuilt the example from the method description alone.

Migration map
ItemDetail
Useful mechanismSplit gate-to-gate time into yard queue, door assignment, unload and paperwork. Report median and 90th percentile by hour, count idle-door minutes, then review the worst hours with the dock supervisor.
Original dependenciesDwellAudit_v7.xlsx on the former employer's SharePoint, their yard and warehouse exports, their API login, and their carrier names.
Independent formA two-week, $6,500, one-site audit. The client sends a CSV, so no system access is needed.
Next build stepWrite a clean script or workbook from the five method steps and run it on the example data.
The offer page

The page covers what the client receives, what you need from them (four weeks of timestamps with a trailer ID on each visit), a day-by-day schedule, and a link to the example. Its "About" line says the offer is new and has not yet been delivered as a paid engagement, because your ledger says that is the case.

The worked example

The example uses eight invented visits at a fictional site. I computed the medians by hand:

WaitMedian (min)
Yard queue11.0
Door assignment30.5
Unload41.0
Paperwork10.5
Total visit93.0

In this sample, unloading is the longest wait and door assignment comes second. That is deliberate. Your ledger records "biggest wait is not unloading" as seen at one site only, so I didn't build the example to prove it. The example omits the 90th percentile because eight visits are too few for it to mean anything.

What I left out, and why
  • Brightwell and Calloway names, the carrier name, file names, the API login. These are employer details and no reference clearance exists.
  • 94 to 71 minute improvement. The ledger says it is true at Brightwell but not cleared for public use, and no one has replicated it.
  • $212,000 detention figure. Confidential.
  • "Typically finds the biggest wait is not unloading." This rests on one site, so the page doesn't claim it.

The page makes no claim about results, customers or deployment.

What I checked, and what I couldn't
  • I compared every number and claim on the page and the example against the ledger. Nothing on them comes from Brightwell.
  • I recomputed the medians from the eight rows by hand. Each row's four waits add up to its total.
  • I couldn't run writing_check.py here. I read each file through for filler, repeated sentence shapes and unsupported claims instead. That is a reading pass, not a scanner result.
  • The page has not been rendered or put on a site. It exists only as local Markdown.
  • I invented the contact address priya@example.com as a placeholder. Replace it with your real one.
Decisions for you
  1. Your "About" line. I wrote "two years on dock scheduling at a grocery distribution centre". Decide whether that wording is acceptable or whether you want to say less about the previous employer. The ledger gives no clearance for naming Brightwell, so I left the name out.
  2. The 94 to 71 minute result. Decide whether to ask Brightwell for written clearance before using it. Until you have clearance, the page stays as written.
  3. When to publish. Publishing is a separate step. I'd rebuild and test the calculation first, so the example reflects code you have actually run.
Files
  • out/offer-page.md: the public page copy, with the price, schedule, client inputs and about line described above.
  • out/worked-example.md: the made-up eight-visit tables, medians, an idle-door illustration and an illustrative rule proposal.
  • out/migration-map-private.md: the map above plus the source links and the list of omitted items. Keep it out of the public site.

File: offer-page.md

Dock Dwell Audit

Find out where your trucks wait between the gate and the door, and which door-assignment rules would shorten it.

$6,500 fixed price. Two weeks. One distribution site.

What you get

A report that splits each truck visit into four waits: yard queue, door assignment, loading or unloading, and paperwork release. It gives the median and 90th-percentile time for each wait by hour of day, and it flags the hours when a door sat empty while a truck waited in the yard.

I then review the three worst hours with your dock supervisor and propose door-assignment rules for them. The rule proposal is a recommendation. You decide what to change and when.

What I need from you

Four weeks of yard and door timestamps for one site: check-in, door-in, door-out and gate-out, with a trailer ID on each. A CSV export from your yard or warehouse system is enough. I do not need login access to either system.

How it runs
  1. Days 1–2: you send the export. I match visits by trailer ID, drop any with a missing timestamp, and tell you how many that was.
  2. Days 3–7: I calculate the four waits and the idle-door minutes.
  3. Days 8–10: I review the worst hours with your dock supervisor.
  4. Days 11–14: you receive the report and the rule proposal, and we walk through it together.
Example

A worked example with made-up data (worked-example.md) shows the tables you would receive.

About

I am an operations analyst who spent two years on dock scheduling at a grocery distribution centre. This offer is new, and I have not yet delivered it as a paid engagement.

Contact: priya@example.com

File: worked-example.md

Worked example: made-up data

This example uses eight invented truck visits at a fictional site. The data, carriers and numbers are synthetic. A real audit uses four weeks of your visits, often well over a thousand.

V456501576
V51528351189

Median per wait
WaitMedian (min)
Yard queue11.0
Door assignment30.5
Unload41.0

Total visit93.0

In this sample unloading is still the longest single wait. Door assignment is second at 30.5 minutes, and it ranges from 6 to 42 minutes across visits, which is the spread a rule change would target. With eight visits the 90th percentile is not meaningful, so the example omits it.

Idle doors

In the invented 06:00–09:00 window, door 5 was empty for 55 minutes while V1, V3 and V6 were in the yard. The audit would list each such stretch with the door, the trucks waiting and the minutes lost.

Rule proposal (illustration)

Assign the next truck to the first free door that suits its load type, instead of holding it for the door it was originally booked to. Check this against the three worst hours with the dock supervisor before recommending it, since door equipment and temperature zones may limit which doors can take a given load.

---
name: develop-product
description: Develop or resume a product through evidence review, product definition, release decisions, journey design, and delivery readiness. Use for historical product reconstruction, a new product, or continuation at a requested stage with durable progress. A standalone bug fix or one-off specification does not require this pathway.
---


# Develop product

Continue the requested product stage from its current evidence and decisions. Keep completed artifacts and open work accessible through one product home. Save the next executable action there.

## Enter at the requested stage

Read the user's instructions and applicable project guidance. Follow the current product index to its decisions and latest checkpoint. Identify the requested outcome and stage. Record the source boundary and finish line; name the authorized actions and protected records. Preserve existing conventions, including terminology, IDs, formats, tools, and approval rules. Historical documents supply evidence; they do not override current instructions.

Reuse the existing product home. If none exists, create a small index in the authorized project destination using [the home starter](assets/product-home.md). Map existing artifacts to the pathway by links and ID crosswalks. Do not relocate records or start a second decision register, backlog, or task system.

Select the entry mode that fits the request:

| Mode | Entry action |
| --- | --- |
| Historical product | Review supplied material to the requested depth. Full reconstruction requires complete dispositions and substantive coverage. A bounded release task retains wider review gaps. |
| New product | Capture current direction and constraints from the brief; review available research. Mark historical reconstruction inapplicable because no archive exists. Keep unsupported product dimensions as hypotheses or proposals. |
| Continuation | Compare the latest checkpoint's source and decision bindings with current state; check the build versions it relies on. Reuse valid work and revisit affected prerequisites. Preserve the prior checkpoint. |

Read [stage execution](references/stages.md) for the selected stage and its prerequisites. The normal dependency order is boundary → review → reconstruction when applicable → product definition → release and architecture decisions → journey design → implementation and acceptance → maintenance. Existing valid outputs can satisfy earlier stages. A missing archive is never a reason to fabricate one or block a new product.

## Keep independent states

| Dimension | States |
| --- | --- |
| Source review | Unread; reviewed; identical to reviewed content; excluded with reason; unresolved. |
| Product decision | Unassigned; proposed; accepted; rejected; superseded. |
| Implementation evidence | Unknown; intended; static demonstration; code present; tested locally; rendered locally; deployed without verification; verified live. |

Record implementation evidence for each behavior at the layer exercised.

For each capability, distinguish **should do** (desired outcome and decision), **can do** (demonstrated behavior and limits), and **will do** (accepted commitment for a named release). Keep commitments for different releases as separate records. A reviewed source cannot accept a feature; an accepted feature cannot prove implementation; a test cannot establish demand or adoption.

Use stable IDs and exact source locators or current user decisions. Read [capture structures](references/records.md) when adding records; adapt the [record template bank](assets/record-templates.json) to existing project formats. Create only applicable records. Mark unknown information as unknown and inapplicable dimensions with a reason. Do not fill gaps with invented dates, owners, budgets, scores, or metrics.

## Choose the next action from readiness evidence

For the requested stage, record each applicable gate as `satisfied`, `blocked`, `not_assessed`, or `not_applicable`, with supporting record IDs and revisions. State separately whether the output is ready for review, ready for an authorized build, accepted for a release, or verified at a destination. A populated template or passing structural check cannot satisfy a substantive gate.

Resolve the next action in this order:

1. Reassess changed evidence that the requested result depends on.
2. Complete the nearest missing prerequisite for the requested stage; do not restart unrelated stages.
3. If a material decision blocks that work, state the exact choice and affected output. Identify the authorized decider. Continue independent supported work within scope.
4. Otherwise execute the smallest action that produces the requested output or its acceptance evidence. Name its target and required authorization. Record the expected receipt and stop condition.

Keep full product coverage separate from release readiness. A release can exclude deferred capabilities without deleting them from the catalogue. A scoped journey can be ready while wider historical review remains incomplete, unless the user made full reconstruction a prerequisite.

## Maintain the home at each work boundary

Read [continuation and change impact](references/continuity.md) when resuming, changing a baseline, or closing a work boundary. Save completed artifacts with their evidence, retain unresolved work with its dependencies, and append a checkpoint after a meaningful review, decision, design, build, or failed check. Record the exact next action in the home before ending the session. Revalidate stale claims and dependent acceptance evidence before presenting them as current.

Knowledge Hub integration is optional. Use [the hub adapter](references/knowledge-hub.md) only when the product has an authorized destination and the request includes that action. Local progress must remain usable without a hub connection. No particular hub, account, folder, or sharing boundary is part of this skill.

## Use related workflows only when needed

This skill owns stage selection, traceability, readiness, and durable product progress. If available and applicable, use `write-feature-spec` for detailed specifications, `plan-usability-study` for participant research, `design-analytics-plan` for measurement design, `design-information-architecture` for navigation, and `verify-work-state` for destination verification. A product map does not require those specialized workflows automatically.

Use the project's reconciliation workflow for authorized file cleanup and its task adapter for work-item state. Use `develop-independent-product` only for an authorized develop-independent-product migration, and `prepare-session-handoff` for a requested session handoff. Preserve their boundaries; pathway work does not authorize cleanup, migration, outreach, deployment, or task closure. If a companion skill is absent, perform the bounded task with the evidence rules here and name any review you could not complete.

At handoff, state what changed, where it exists, who can use it, what verifies it, what remains unchanged, and the exact next action. Link the product home and latest checkpoint. Do not report proposed, local, installed, released, or live work as a later state.

examples.title: Turning a volunteer scheduling prototype into a first release
examples.markdown:
## Request

We built a volunteer shift-scheduling prototype for our food pantry network last year and want to turn it into something the three pantries can actually use by spring. I've put the prototype README, notes from our September meeting and the coordinator's wish list in inputs/. Can you work out what the product is, what a first release should and shouldn't include, and what we do next?

## Inputs

Run of the built `develop-product` task package. The recording session invented this scenario, the request and the inputs below before running the skill. It had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so.

#### coordinator-wishlist.txt

Dana's wish list (Oct 2026), in her order

1. Text reminders the day before a shift
2. Everyone's data in one place, not on my laptop
3. Tell me when someone cancels, and let me find a replacement fast
4. See which drivers are cleared
5. One view across pantries
6. Volunteer hours report for the funder (they ask every June)
7. A rota for the holiday food drive
8. Paper print-out of the week for volunteers without phones
9. Let volunteers swap shifts themselves
10. Photos on volunteer profiles

#### meeting-notes-sept.md

#### Network meeting, 18 Sept 2026

Present: Dana (Eastfield coordinator), Ravi (Northgate coordinator), Imogen (Millbrook coordinator), Tom (board treasurer).

- Eastfield trial: Dana says no-shows fell "noticeably" but nobody counted. She still phones people the night before.
- Ravi: Northgate uses a shared spreadsheet and a WhatsApp group; 70 active volunteers. Wants one view across all three pantries because people volunteer at more than one site.
- Imogen: Millbrook volunteers are mostly over 65; many have no smartphone. Some would need a phone call or a paper sheet.
- Tom: budget for this is £6,000 total, one-off, and no ongoing hosting spend above about £40 a month. Board must approve any spend over £1,000.
- Drivers must have licence and insurance checked before first delivery shift. Dana does it; Ravi says Northgate relies on honesty.
- Agreed: Dana will own product decisions for the pilot; Tom approves money. Target: live at Eastfield and Northgate by 1 April 2027, Millbrook later.
- Open: whether volunteers under 18 may sign up (no policy yet).

#### prototype-readme.md

#### ShiftBasket prototype (v0.3, built Oct 2025)

Single-page web app used in a two-week trial at Eastfield Pantry only.

##### What it does
- Coordinator creates shifts (date, start, end, role, headcount needed).
- Volunteers open a link, pick a name from a dropdown and sign up for a shift. No password.
- Shift page shows "3 of 5 filled".
- Coordinator can export the week as CSV.

##### Roles in the data
Sorter, Driver, Front desk. Drivers have a "licence checked" flag set by hand in the database.

##### Known limits
- Data lives in one browser's local storage per device; the Eastfield laptop was the source of truth.
- No reminders. The SMS reminder screen is a mock-up only (buttons do nothing).
- Cancelling a signup deletes it; nobody is told.
- Not tested with more than 24 volunteers.

## Output

I've written a product home for ShiftBasket with a proposed first release. It's ready for you to review, and nothing in it is accepted yet.

#### What the product is

ShiftBasket helps pantry coordinators fill volunteer shifts and keeps volunteers turning up. The coordinators are Dana, Ravi and Imogen. The volunteers include many people over 65, and some at Millbrook have no smartphone. Tom's board approves money.

Today Dana phones people the night before. Northgate uses a spreadsheet and a WhatsApp group for about 70 volunteers. The prototype keeps its data in one laptop's browser.

**What the prototype can do, from its README:**
- Create shifts and let volunteers sign up.
- Export a week as CSV.
- Hold a hand-set "licence checked" flag for drivers.

**What it can't do:**
- The SMS reminder screen is a mock-up, and its buttons do nothing.
- Cancelling deletes the signup and tells nobody.
- It has no shared storage and no cross-pantry view.

I could only read the README. I haven't seen the code, the database or the trial data, so every "can do" is the README's claim, not something I checked.

#### Proposed first release

**Target and constraints:** live at Eastfield and Northgate by 1 April 2027, which is about 21 weeks away. The budget is £6,000 one-off and about £40 a month to run. Tom approves anything over £1,000. Dana owns product decisions for the pilot.

| Priority | Items |
| --- | --- |
| Must | Shared data store; shifts and signup; day-before text reminders; cancellation notice to the coordinator; driver clearance before a delivery shift |
| Should | Replacement search; cross-pantry view; paper print-out of the week |
| Could | CSV export; hours report for the funder |
| Won't this horizon | Holiday-drive rota; volunteer shift swaps; photos; Millbrook rollout |

**Why these placements:**
- **Shared data** is first because two sites can't run from one laptop.
- **Reminders** are Dana's first priority and the reason for the pilot.
- **The hours report** is only Could because the funder asks in June, after launch. The CSV export plus a spreadsheet covers it until then.
- **Millbrook** comes later, as the September notes say.
- **Everything deferred** stays in the catalogue, each with a reason and a point to revisit.

These placements are my proposal. Nothing becomes a commitment until Dana accepts it.

#### Decisions needed

1. **Dana:** accept or change the priorities above.
2. **Dana, with Ravi:** how are driver licence and insurance checked at Northgate, and can a driver sign up before being cleared? Dana checks today. Ravi says Northgate relies on honesty.
3. **Dana:** how does a volunteer prove who they are? The name dropdown lets anyone book as anyone.
4. **Not assigned in the notes:** can volunteers under 18 sign up? There's no policy yet. This blocks signup design only.
5. **Dana:** you described three pantries by spring, but the September notes say Eastfield and Northgate by 1 April and Millbrook later. Which is the commitment?

#### Gaps and risks

- **SMS cost is unknown.** I can't tell whether reminders for about 70 volunteers fit inside £40 a month. If they don't, reminders drop to Should.
- **There's no no-show baseline.** Dana's "noticeably fewer" wasn't counted, so the benefit of reminders is a hypothesis.
- **Scale is untested.** The trial had 24 volunteers or fewer, and Northgate has about 70.
- **Nobody has compared this against existing scheduling tools.** I make no claim that it's unique, and I picked no technology stack.

#### Next step

I haven't contacted anyone or spent anything. Two things can run alongside the decisions:
- Get a written SMS price for roughly 70 volunteers at about two reminders a week.
- Have the coordinators count no-shows for four weeks.

Once the priorities are accepted, the next stage is designing the journey from creating a shift through reminders, cancellation and replacement. An architecture comparison inside the £40 limit comes with it.

I couldn't compute content hashes for the three input files, so they're identified by path and a full read.

#### File

`out/product-home.md` is the one place to start. It holds:
- Source records for the three inputs.
- The product definition.
- The 13-capability catalogue, with what the README says each can do.
- The 14 proposed release items.
- Decisions D1–D5.
- Risks and contradictions X1–X6.
- Stage gates, which show the decision gate blocked and architecture not yet assessed.
- A "Continue here" section with the next action.

- **Finish line:** a product definition and a proposed release scope that the decider can accept or change. This is "ready for review". Nothing is accepted, built or deployed.

| 3 Reconstruction | applicable as a subset | Behavior is taken from the README only (source_reported). No code or runtime was exercised. |

| 5 Release and architecture | scope proposal ready for review; architecture `not_assessed` | G4. No decision is accepted. No stack was compared or chosen. |
| 6–8 | not_assessed | Design, build and maintenance wait on accepted scope. |

##### Source records

| ID | Location | Family and date | Authority role | Review state |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| S2 | `inputs/meeting-notes-sept.md` | Network meeting, 18 Sept 2026 | Holds the only recorded decisions (owner, budget, target date) | reviewed |
| S3 | `inputs/coordinator-wishlist.txt` | Dana's list, Oct 2026 | Priorities of one coordinator; a wish list, not a decision | reviewed |

##### Product definition (proposed, ready for review)

**Audience.** Pantry coordinators (Dana at Eastfield, Ravi at Northgate, Imogen at Millbrook) fill shifts. Volunteers, many of them over 65 and some without smartphones at Millbrook (S2), sign up and show up. The board treasurer (Tom) approves spend (S2). Coordinators and volunteers are the daily users. The board approves money.

**Problem and workaround.** Eastfield coordinator phones people the night before; Northgate runs a spreadsheet and a WhatsApp group for about 70 volunteers (S2). The trial prototype held data in one laptop's browser (S1).

**Jobs.**

- J2 Volunteer finds a shift and commits. Constraint: no password, possibly no smartphone.
- J3 Coordinator learns of a cancellation early enough to find a replacement.

| C12 | Volunteer-initiated shift swap | No | intended | S3 #9 |

##### Proposed release R1 (every item `proposed`, none accepted)

**Horizon and outcome.** Live at Eastfield and Northgate by 1 April 2027 (S2, agreed in the meeting; roughly 21 weeks from 4 Nov 2026). Outcome: both coordinators run their weekly rota in ShiftBasket instead of phone calls, spreadsheet and WhatsApp. Constraints: £6,000 one-off, about £40 a month running, board approval above £1,000 (S2). The decider for product scope is Dana; Tom decides money (S2).

| R1-02 | C1, C2 shifts and signup | Must | The core job. Identity without passwords needs a decision (D3). | — |
| R1-03 | C4 reminders | Must | Dana's first priority and the stated reason for the pilot. Depends on an SMS cost check (X1) staying inside £40 a month. | If SMS fits no budget: Should, with coordinator phone list printed from C11. |
| R1-04 | C5 cancellation notice (coordinator told) | Must | Silent deletion defeats J3. | — |
| R1-05 | C5 replacement search | Should | Coordinator can use the shift list as a workaround. | Reconsider after one month of cancellation data. |
| R1-06 | C6 driver clearance | Must | S2 requires checks before the first delivery shift; Northgate has no process today. Needs D2. | — |

| R1-09 | C9 CSV export | Could | Exists in the prototype; keep if cheap. | — |

| R1-11 | C10 holiday rota | Won't this horizon | Drive falls after the April launch. | Reconsider in September 2027. |
| R1-12 | C12 shift swap | Won't this horizon | Needs identity and rules not yet decided. | After D3 and one quarter of use. |
| R1-13 | C13 photos | Won't this horizon | No stated outcome; adds a privacy question. | Only on a stated need. |

skills.markdown:
---
name: draft-application-materials
description: "Draft the pieces around the candidate's tailored resume (cover letter, form answers, outreach, LinkedIn sections, reference packets) from the role work record and current evidence, in the candidate’s voice, as drafts only."
---


# Draft application materials

Use only the candidate identity, career records, thresholds, author profile and destinations explicitly supplied or authorized for this task. Record names below describe a suggested source map; resolve them under the confirmed career root or accept equivalent supplied records. None is a bundled personal default. Missing optional context does not block a bounded draft from supplied facts.

Runs beside `prepare-job-application` once a role has a work record with a completed narrative translation table; if the table is empty, run `prepare-job-application tailor` first. Select evidence for each piece’s question, audience and purpose. Keep facts consistent across materials without requiring the same examples or repeating the résumé.

Before drafting, load `00_Master/Career_Application_Operating_Context.md`, the role's `Role_Work_Record.md` (including its Estimate basis section), the tailored resume copy, the live posting, `00_Master/Professional_Profile.md`. Claim authority starts with the candidate’s corrections and confirmed facts, then original evidence and the claim ledger, then detailed program records. The professional profile is a summary for navigation; Portfolio case studies are public copies, not a source of figures. LinkedIn work starts from `00_Master/LinkedIn_Profile_Draft.md` and `00_Master/LinkedIn_Profile_Positioning_Brief.md`. Behavioral answers draw on `05_Reference/Story_Bank/Success_Stories.md` and the anchor stories in `04_Interview/Interview_Preparation.md`. References use `02_Templates/References_Template_One_Page.docx`.

the candidate is the author. Before drafting, state audience, purpose, reader action and consequence level; hiring material gets deep review. Write under `apply-author-style` with an explicitly supplied confirmed profile and `review-writing`; run the bundled writing diagnostics on each finished file where installed, fix structure rather than swapping words, and say plainly when no scan ran.

## Bounded drafts from supplied facts

When the user supplies the relevant role facts inline and asks for a short draft, deliver the requested prose using those facts. Keep its provisional state separate from submission readiness. Missing posting details limit role-specific claims; they do not require replacing a requested short letter with a paragraph outline. Omit an unsupported requirement, mechanism or recipient detail rather than filling a placeholder as though it were known. The user's requested length governs that bounded draft; the normal full-letter format applies when a complete application letter is requested.

## Rules for every piece

- Open with the point. Each sentence carries a name, number, system, decision or date.
- Use posting language where it describes real work; do not repeat terms to meet a frequency target.
- Preserve who did what and what was observed. Leading work does not establish personal design or implementation ownership. A named property such as retry-safe does not prove zero failures, a particular mechanism, or a production guarantee. Keep the source's trial, time and outcome qualifiers; an observed reduction does not mean elimination. Omit a missing mechanism rather than inventing one to complete a paragraph.
- State only supported people-leadership responsibilities and counts. Use the candidate’s supplied disclosure preferences; no headcount is implied by a title.
- Figures are locked or stated figures from the sources above, or estimates already in the record's Estimate basis. Years-per-skill for a form field count as an estimate: compute from role dates, record in Estimate basis, then use.
- Determine current employment from the supplied dated record. Preserve exact official dates and titles; do not infer current employment from an old resume. Keep exit history out unless it answers the request.
- Nothing employer-owned: no former-employer branding, client-sensitive facts, internal identifiers or repositories.
- Caveats stay in the ledger. Reader-facing copy states what is true and leaves out what is not; no "not verified", "directional" or "I don't claim" sentences.
- People stories: never invent a hiring, performance, termination or team-conflict case. If a prompt needs one and the sources hold none, mark the gap and ask the candidate for a real event.
- Alignment flag in the record's Current decision (for example, an industry the candidate has identified as a concern) with the candidate choosing to pursue: "why us" copy names the role's mandate and platform problem in the candidate’s words and ties it to the candidate’s stated reason for the move. Never a mission or values endorsement the candidate has not said. If the candidate’s reason line is missing, ask for it before drafting.

## Cover letter

250–350 words, four paragraphs, to a named person when WebSearch finds one, otherwise no salutation line.

1. The specific reason this role fits, tied to one program from the translation table.
2. Two or three posting requirements, each answered with one program, its mechanism and its result.
3. Use another relevant example or address a material question with supported adjacent evidence when that helps the hiring reader. No career category is a default differentiator.
4. What the candidate would want to discuss first.

No "I am excited to apply", no trait statements, no closing moral. Deliver one letter as a Codex doc; when a file is required, a DOCX beside the resume as `Candidate_Name_<Company>_<Role>_Cover_Letter.docx`.

## Application-form answers

Answer the question asked, then stop; plain text ready to paste.

- Experience questions: skill, years, one sentence of where the candidate used it; years match the resume.
- "Why this company or role": specific to the company, connected to the candidate’s real work, under 150 words unless the field allows more; under an alignment flag, the rule above.
- Work samples: the most relevant publish-cleared case studies, one line each with link and one proof point.
- Behavioral prompts: 100–200 words from the anchor stories, ending on the result, under the people-story rule.
- Ratings and dropdowns: the accurate level.
- Pause with no draft: salary expectations, work authorization and sponsorship, demographic and self-identification questions, attestations and signatures.

Present answers as a table of field, answer, character count, field limit. Entering fields and submitting belong to `prepare-job-application fill` and its authorization boundaries.

## Outreach to a hiring manager or connection

Subject under eight words, specific to their team or the role. Body under 150 words: one specific about their work, one result of the candidate’s that bears on it, one ask (a twenty-minute conversation or a referral path). Link one case study. Cut any sentence that could go to another company. Draft only; a Gmail draft when the candidate asks; sending and recruiter contact are separate approval boundaries.

## LinkedIn sections

Headline under 220 characters, selected for the current brief and supported work. A prior headline or positioning correction does not establish a permanent professional identity. About: first person, three to five short paragraphs, opening with what the candidate led and built, two or three named results, a closing line on what the candidate wants only if the candidate wants open-to-work visible. Experience entries carry the resume's titles, dates and figures exactly and may add context the resume cut. Skills: top three pinned to the lane the candidate is prioritizing. Output is a section-by-section diff against the staged draft. Publication is the candidate's action and a separate approval boundary.

## References

the candidate names the references. For each: name, current title and company, relationship and the period they saw the candidate’s work, the lane and claims they can speak to, contact details as the candidate supplies them. Produce a permission request, a briefing note (the role, three things worth emphasizing, the evidence behind each) and a thank-you note, in the candidate’s voice. The list lives in the role folder on the one-page template and is private.

## Recording

Write each piece's path and state into the role work record under Resume and materials; keep `03_Tracker/applications.md` current. States: `prepared locally` for a file; `filled and awaiting submission` only after `prepare-job-application fill`; `submitted` only with employer confirmation. End with changed, verified, unchanged and the exact next action.

examples.title: Cover letter and form answers for a director of customer onboarding role
examples.markdown:
## Request

I'm applying for the Director of Customer Onboarding role at Harbourline Software and my role work record and the posting are in the inputs folder. Can you write the cover letter, and draft answers for the application form fields listed at the bottom of the record?

## Inputs

Run of the built `prepare-job-application` task package in its "supporting application materials" mode. The recording session invented this scenario, the request and the inputs below before running the skill. It had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so.

#### Role_Work_Record.md

#### Role work record — Harbourline Software, Director, Customer Onboarding

Candidate: Marisol Teague. Date of record: 2026-11-03. State: researching → tailored resume prepared locally.

##### Current decision
Pursue. No alignment flag. Reason for the move, in Marisol's words: "I have fixed onboarding for one product. I want to own it across a whole portfolio, where the handoff problems are bigger."

##### Employment (exact)
- Senior Manager, Implementation Programs, Brightwater Freight Systems, March 2022 to present.
- Implementation Lead, Oakmere Software, June 2018 to February 2022.

##### Narrative translation table
| Posting mandate | Program | Mechanism | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Signed order to first live feed | Enterprise onboarding redesign | Staged plan with a fixed integration checklist per carrier | Median onboarding time for enterprise accounts fell from 74 to 41 days across 38 accounts, 2024–2025 |
| Standard Sales-to-Implementation handoff | Intake form | Replaced free-text handoff notes with a required form (integration list, go-live date, data owners) plus a 12-item checklist | Used in 3 regions; Marisol wrote both |
| Lead managers, contractor budget | Team and budget | Leads 6 implementation managers; manages contractor budget of $420k a year | 2025 spend $409k against $420k |
| Time-to-value reporting | Weekly report | SQL reports from the implementation tracker, reviewed monthly with the VP of Customer Success | Basis for the 74-to-41 figure |

##### Gaps
- No P&L ownership of services revenue. Closest: the contractor budget above.
- Has worked only on one product line.

##### Estimate basis
- Onboarding/implementation years: June 2018 to November 2026 = 8 years.
- SQL years: first used for tracker reports in March 2022 = 4 years.

##### Rules
- Hiring manager name not known. Do not name anyone at Harbourline.
- Do not mention Marisol's reason for leaving Oakmere.

#### posting.md

#### Director, Customer Onboarding — Harbourline Software (remote, US)

Posted 27 October 2026 at careers.example.com/harbourline/director-onboarding

Harbourline sells freight-visibility software in three product lines: Track, Dock and Route. Onboarding differs by product and by region, and customers wait too long for their first live shipment feed.

You will:
- Own onboarding from signed order to first live shipment feed across all three product lines.
- Define one standard handoff between Sales and Implementation.
- Lead a team of implementation managers and manage the contractor budget.
- Report time-to-value to the executive team each month.
- Hold P&L responsibility for onboarding services revenue.

You have: 6+ years in software implementation or onboarding, 3+ years leading managers, working SQL for reporting, and experience with enterprise logistics or supply-chain customers.

Application form fields: (1) Years of experience in software onboarding or implementation. (2) Years of SQL. (3) Why Harbourline? (150 words max) (4) Salary expectations.

## Output

I've drafted the cover letter and three of the four form answers for the Harbourline Director of Customer Onboarding role. I left salary expectations blank because that is your decision. Nothing has been entered into the form or submitted.

**Framing:** The reader is a Harbourline hiring manager, and I couldn't find a name for them, so the letter has no salutation. The purpose is to get you a first conversation. This is hiring material, so I gave it the deepest review. Every figure comes from your work record.

#### Cover letter (about 310 words)

> Harbourline's Director of Customer Onboarding owns the path from signed order to first live shipment feed across Track, Dock and Route. I have worked on that path at Brightwater Freight Systems since March 2022, where I redesigned enterprise onboarding around a staged plan and a fixed integration checklist per carrier. Median onboarding time fell from 74 to 41 days across 38 accounts between 2024 and 2025. I have fixed onboarding for one product, and I want to own it across a portfolio, where the handoff problems are bigger.
>
> Your posting asks for one standard handoff between Sales and Implementation. I wrote Brightwater's: a required intake form covering the integration list, go-live date and data owners, which replaced free-text notes, plus a 12-item checklist. Three regions use it. You also ask for monthly time-to-value reporting to the executive team. I build those reports in SQL from the implementation tracker and review them monthly with our VP of Customer Success; they are the source of the 74-to-41-day figure. I lead six implementation managers and manage a $420,000 annual contractor budget, which closed 2025 at $409,000.
>
> The posting includes P&L responsibility for onboarding services revenue, and I have not held one. The contractor budget is the closest I have, and I have managed it against a fixed annual figure. My onboarding work has also been on a single product line, so Dock and Route would be new to me. I would start with their handoff failures, since that is where I know how to look.
>
> I would like to begin by discussing how onboarding is split across Track, Dock and Route today, and which handoff between Sales and Implementation fails most often.
>
> Marisol Teague

How the letter follows your record:
- **Paragraph 1** opens on the enterprise onboarding redesign and uses your own reason for the move.
- **Paragraph 2** answers three posting requirements: the standard handoff, time-to-value reporting, and the team and budget.
- **Paragraph 3** covers the largest gap, P&L ownership, using the contractor budget as the nearest evidence. It also names the single-product limit.
- **Paragraph 4** says what you want to discuss first.
- I left out your reason for leaving Oakmere, as your record says.

#### Application form answers

| Field | Answer | Characters (approx.) | Field limit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Years of experience in software onboarding or implementation | 8. Implementation Lead at Oakmere Software (June 2018 to February 2022), then Senior Manager, Implementation Programs at Brightwater Freight Systems (March 2022 to present). | about 170 | none stated |
| Years of SQL | 4. I have used it since March 2022 to build time-to-value reports from our implementation tracker. | about 100 | none stated |
| Why Harbourline? | See below | about 690 | 150 words (about 115 used) |
| Salary expectations | No draft. This is your decision. | – | – |

**Why Harbourline?**

> Harbourline's posting describes a problem I recognise: onboarding differs by product and region, and customers wait too long for their first live shipment feed. At Brightwater Freight Systems I cut median enterprise onboarding time from 74 to 41 days across 38 accounts (2024–2025) by building a fixed integration checklist per carrier and a required Sales-to-Implementation intake form, now used in three regions. I have fixed onboarding for one product and want to own it across a portfolio, where the handoff problems are bigger. skills.markdown:
---
name: estimate-project
description: Rough-estimate method within scope-project. Build a sourced effort or cost range from a supplied scope, comparables or quote, and preserve its basis and reopening conditions.
---


# Estimate project

> **Before writing: [`build-card.md`](../_shared/build-card.md) plus the writing-diagnostics register
> for briefs. Inputs, not a final pass.**

The ROM answers one question: what will this roughly cost and take, and what is that estimate
standing on? It is a range and a basis, never a quote. It gives the buyer a decision-grade
investment frame before deep scoping, and it surfaces the dimensions driving the estimate so
both sides know what to confirm. The moment a ROM implies precision the underlying data does
not support, it becomes a liability at the table. An honest wide range beats a false-precise
tight one.

Two audiences, one substrate. Buyer-facing: the range, the basis of estimate, what moves the
number. Deal-desk-facing: the same plus the reconciliation print and the confidence
composition. Pin the audience before building; it sets what renders, not what gets verified.

## The money rule is absolute

Use the supplied scope and current rate card or relevant comparables as the
basis. Preserve each source revision and state how effort was derived. An
existing quote supplies confirmed commercial values when one is available;
it is not a prerequisite for a rough estimate. Never invent a rate or silently
turn a modeled range into a commitment.

## Orient on the available source

Read the brief and existing work breakdown. Use a local export when supplied.
A configured pricing connector can retrieve a quote, but its absence does not
block local scoping. Separate a fixed fee from time-and-materials assumptions.
Use phases from the project source; identify proposed phases as proposals.

Read the primary scope-project workflow for the local calculator. From that
package root, `python3 scripts/estimate.py scope.json --output attempt/estimate.json`
creates a sourced working estimate and readable explanation. Its capacity
calculation is a lower bound, not a committed schedule.

Pin the audience and the requested level of detail before rendering the range.
For effort-only work without rates, deliver the hours and its basis. Identify
the missing pricing input rather than refusing the request.

## Evidence first

Run **evidence-core** before drafting. The registry entry for `estimate-project` requires these
load-bearing domains: scope basis, workstream effort, role assumptions, rates or cost basis,
confidence, range reopeners, commercial posture. If a domain lacks support, retain the supported scope or effort work and name
the input needed for the missing calculation. Do not invent a full cost range.
Generated examples cannot supply evidence for a real engagement.

Every figure the ROM shows is a ledger entry: figure, source, confidence, as-of. Confidence
uses the evidence-core register, nothing else:

- **Confirmed**: stated in the quote and cross-checked by computation, traceable to a scope
  input.
- **Inferred**: derived from a comparable engagement or current-knowledge scoping, with its
  derivation stated. Keep derived effort labeled as estimated.
- **Unknown**: depends on a footprint dimension the client has not confirmed. These are
  flagged assumptions. They live in the basis-of-estimate table, each with a confirmation
  action (and the source-named phase in which it gets confirmed, when the source timeline has
  one), and each appears in the assumptions register with an owner and the gate it blocks.

Map confidence to presentation: Confirmed renders as fact, Inferred renders with its
derivation, Unknown renders as a flagged assumption, never as a settled figure. Conflicts
between sources render as both values with a recommendation, never a silent pick.

## The sections

Derive the set from the ledger, not from an example. Read
`references/basis-of-estimate.md` before writing the BOE table and
`references/range-discipline.md` before stating the range.

| Section | What it answers | The bar |
|---|---|---|
| Header | What engagement, which tier or option, what pricing model, which source revision or quote | A reader knows in five seconds what governs the page |
| Metric strip | The range, hours, duration, and the model-specific card | Every figure traces to its estimate input or quote field; fixed-price and T&M cards never coexist |
| Phase distribution | Hours across the source-stated phases | Phases come from the quote timeline; a heavy phase has a named reason |
| Basis of estimate | The footprint dimensions the estimate rests on | Every row is countable and specific to this client; Unknowns are flagged with a confirmation action, and a confirming phase when the source timeline evidences one |
| What moves the number | The range reopeners: scope conditions that would require a revised estimating basis. Contractual consequences come from the actual agreement | Read from this deal's scope, never a generic list |
| Reconciliation (review-deal-economics view) | The printed tie-out | Present verbatim from the gate output |
| Footer | Confidentiality and status | Clear whether this is an internal draft or a client-ready range |

## The reasoning tests

1. **The math holds.** For T&M, hours times the sourced billing rate reconciles to
   the quoted fee within the gate's retained 0.5 percent diagnostic tolerance. A
   fixed fee instead requires its authoritative `fee_source` and `fixed_fee_basis`;
   it may differ from hours times rate. Never substitute hourly billings for an
   independently agreed fixed fee. Surface discrepancies without changing the quote.
2. **The three-way tie holds.** Phase hour totals equal role hour totals equal work-package
   hour totals equal the quote grand total, or the variance is flagged with per-line deltas.
   This reconciliation is the artifact's spine.
3. **Phase distribution tells a story.** If one phase carries 40 percent of hours, that phase
   is doing something specific. Name it, from the source.
4. **BOE dimensions are real and specific.** "Custom objects" is not a BOE dimension.
   "Custom objects in CPQ requiring migration of pricing rules" is. The specificity bar is in
   `references/basis-of-estimate.md`.
5. **The model-specific card is correct.** Fixed fee: the fixed price and milestone basis.
   T&M: sourced rates and planned effort. Include a ceiling, upfront payment or
   milestone condition only when the selected agreement supplies it. Never infer
   payment terms from the model name.
6. **Range reopeners are this deal's reopeners.** "Additional integrations beyond the scoped
   four" is real. "Scope changes" is not.
7. **The range is honest about its precision.** A ROM standing on Unknown dimensions is wider
   than one standing on Confirmed ones, and the BOE table makes that visible.

## Verify by computation, then print it

Never assert a total you did not recompute. For a quote-anchored range using the
figures-block schema in `references/reconciliation-format.md`, run this module's gate from its own directory:

```bash
python3 scripts/rom_gate.py figures.json
```

The gate recomputes the three-way tie, checks T&M hours times rate against the fee
(or requires a separately sourced fixed fee and its basis), checks that
the range bounds bracket the quote total, and checks the model card matches the pricing
model. It prints the full reconciliation and exits nonzero on any failure. The printed
reconciliation goes on the review-deal-economics view verbatim; for the buyer view it stays in the build
notes. Report the gate's counts, never an adjective. "Clean" is not a finding; "PASS, 0
failures" is.

**Discrepancy handling.** If a quoted figure fails to reconcile, preserve the quoted
discrepancy, label it, and request a corrected authoritative source. Do not present it as an
approved quote. A separately labeled calculated scenario may support the decision; it cannot
replace the source value, and a derived figure never silently substitutes for a quoted one in
a client-facing deliverable. Never silently smooth, and never silently override the quote. Cascade: if any figure changes, regenerate from the
figures block so numbers cannot drift between the model and the markup.

## Rendering and voice

Hand rendering to **brand-renderer**: it owns the palette, type, logo, layout
tokens, and the parity, visual, and brand release gates. Do not inline hex values here or in
the artifact build notes. Brand applies during the build, not after.

Run the **writing-diagnostics** checker on every prose surface of the artifact and on this skill's own
output. Apply review-writing and the confirmed author profile. Preserve material
uncertainty in the claim. Review the rendered result after the diagnostic checks.

Fallback: if a governor is not installed on the current surface, state the check it would
have run, perform the best manual substitute, and say that is what you did. Never silently
skip.

## Boundaries

- Does not scope and does not create or edit quotes. That is the primary **scope-project** workflow.
- Does not build the SOW. That is **sow**.
- Does not build the firm proposal. That is **build-interactive-proposal**.
- Derives prospective effort or cost only from the supplied basis. Commercial approval remains a separate project decision; an estimate cannot overwrite an accepted quote.
- Supports standalone effort ranges when their scope and estimating basis are supplied. An unavailable rate leaves pricing unresolved.

## State discipline

Stamp the artifact with actual available source identifiers, revision, timeline
snapshot when supplied, and as-of date. For a quote-anchored estimate include its
Q-number and quoted total; never invent these for local estimates. Where a playbook
is involved, live-read its 00-STATE file at open; truth hierarchy: live quote, then
definition file, then state file, then memory, then chat context. Never hand-patch the
rendered output; fix the figures block and regenerate.

## Degradation ladder

When time is short, cut in this order and say what you cut:

1. The review-deal-economics confidence-composition view (keep the buyer view).
2. Phase-distribution commentary (keep the distribution itself).
3. Comparable-engagement derivation notes on Inferred figures (keep the Inferred label).

Never cut the evidence review, verified calculations, the BOE table with its
flagged Unknowns, or the assumptions register. Quote-anchored figures require the
ROM gate and printed reconciliation. Local or effort-only estimates instead use
the primary calculator and its incomplete-estimate contract: preserve missing
rates and unestimated scope without inventing quote-schema fields.

## Files

- `scripts/rom_gate.py`: the deterministic figure gate. `--selftest` runs the fixtures.
- `scripts/rom_selftest.py`: standalone selftest wrapper for estate sync.
- `scripts/fixtures/`: one passing and one failing figures block.
- `references/basis-of-estimate.md`: BOE row spec, specificity bar, confidence mapping.
- `references/range-discipline.md`: how the range is stated, band width, model handling.
- `references/reconciliation-format.md`: the figures-block schema and the printed tie-out
  format.

## Release gate (required)

Before you deliver, run the gate. This is a required step, not a suggestion, and
not something a reviewer does later. Full spec in
[`release-gate.md`](../_shared/release-gate.md).

1. Apply review-writing to the prose. Use the bundled diagnostic tools to check saved writing. For
   a final artifact it emits a receipt the quality gate requires.
2. Run brand-renderer on the branded artifact: palette, borders, radii, logo,
   footer.
3. Run review-deliverable before you call it final.

Do not present the artifact as finished until every check that applies has passed.
