  11. Immediate next steps: each with an owner and timing.
  12. Decisions needed: what the team must decide and who decides it.
  13. A last-updated provenance line: Last updated: YYYY-MM-DD by <who or what run>, from <sources>.

Record genuinely unknown content under Important unknowns. An unresolved placeholder (TBD, TKTK, {{ }}) fails the brief.

The brief is a living artifact

Repeated runs update it idempotently: re-running on the same facts changes nothing, and new facts update the sections they belong to rather than appending duplicates.

Human-authored material is protected with HTML comment markers:

<!-- human -->
The CFO told me directly he will not fund this before Q3. Do not push timeline.
<!-- /human -->

Updates must NEVER rewrite, trim, or reflow anything between ` and . Content moves around them, not through them. The checker enforces this: run check_pursuit_brief.py --before old.md --after new.md` before replacing the file, and abort the update if it fails.

Where it lives

The Pursuit Brief draws its durable client facts from client.profile and client.relationships, then points to the active opportunity.front_door. Update only the records this skill owns, idempotently, under the Hub contract. The full brief remains a durable Markdown artifact per _shared/output-contract.md, named <client>-pursuit-brief.md.

Gate it

python3 scripts/check_pursuit_brief.py <client>-pursuit-brief.md
python3 scripts/check_pursuit_brief.py --before old.md --after new.md   # on updates

Exit 0 passes. Correct every reported brief defect.

Mode B: the Upcoming Call Brief

Prepares ONE specific call. Start from the calendar event: when the call is, who is on the invite, who organized it. The attendee list is the stakeholder map and drives the audience partition below. If no event exists, ask who is in the room before researching.

Required content

  1. Call objective: the one or two things the call must produce.
  2. Desired decisions or outcomes.
  3. Attendees and roles, both sides.
  4. Known context: what the record already establishes, sourced.
  5. Run of show: a concise sequence of moves.
  6. Agenda with time allocation.
  7. Questions: tailored and ranked. When a discovery ledger exists (built by maintain-discovery-record), pull the ranked Column B questions from it rather than inventing a parallel list; add call-specific questions only where the ledger is silent, and say which are which.
  8. Risks and sensitivities.
  9. Facts vs assumptions vs unknowns, explicitly separated.
  10. Follow-up plan.
  11. Relationship to the Pursuit Brief: name the pursuit brief file, which of its recommended calls this one is, and what it should feed back.

Gate it with python3 scripts/check_pursuit_brief.py --mode call <file>.md.

Evidence disciplines the call brief inherits

These four behaviors are load-bearing, not optional polish:

Sections are earned by evidence, never required by a template. A talk track requires a verbatim ask from a transcript. A Q&A bank requires questions the counterpart actually raised. A figure ledger requires reconciled figures. A section whose evidence is absent is omitted, and the gap is reported in chat. Four sections built entirely from the record beat ten where six were inferred.

No figure without reconciliation. Every number is written into an evidence ledger (assets/evidence.schema.json) and checked against every other source that mentions it:

python3 scripts/reconcile.py evidence.json

It fails on unsourced figures, unreconciled conflicts, and leaks of never-tagged material. Conflicts are surfaced, never silently resolved by picking the better-reading number: both values go in the brief with the disagreement named, and the presenter decides.

No voice without a recording. Spoken lines in a talk track are assembled from the presenter's own recorded phrasing: their analogies, their framings, their register, mined from transcripts where they speak. Absent such a transcript, produce intents only, say so in chat, and never simulate a voice from a job title.

Every retrieved statement carries an audience tag. public may appear anywhere; internal appears in the brief only, usually as a landmine or Q&A answer; never (a person assessing a named individual, for instance) is excluded from every artifact and may appear only as an explicit do-not-repeat instruction with no detail. The counterpart's statements about their own organization are internal: reflectable back to them, not portable to their colleagues.

Gaps go in chat, never in the artifact. After building, report: sections omitted and why, figures that could not be reconciled, stale evidence, and any decision the presenter must make before the call. The artifact stays clean; the user gets the honest picture.

The research machinery, supporting both modes

Depth is set by the clock. Two hours means parallel research agents and the full pack. Twenty minutes means one research pass and a tight brief; say what you are cutting rather than half-building more.

Harvest internal knowledge first. Public research is commodity work any competitor can do. Search the authorized project sources and connected account relevant to this task, such as Slack, Drive, CRM and calendar. Do not broaden to other personal or employer accounts. A zero-result Salesforce search is itself a finding. Read transcripts verbatim, never summaries: a summary may omit the actor, mechanism or qualification that changes the decision. Preserve those details from the authorized source rather than inventing an example.

Then public research, in parallel, with citation discipline. Spawn two subagents in the same turn: Agent A on the business (how they make money, who pays them, financial condition, priorities), Agent B on the people and the field (attendees, absent deciders, competitors, platform landscape). Prompt templates are in references/research-prompts.md; the two demands worth preserving in any edit are the inline source URL next to every claim and the [ASSUMPTION] label with confidence on unverified reasoning. Write agent output to disk and read it there.

Make the money flow a first-class object. Who pays, through what instrument, how pricing moves over a deal's life, where revenue leaks. Then reconcile that against the client's operational pain; the collision between what their filings say and what their transcript says is where differentiated insight lives. The client's own filings usually describe the consequence of the operational problem they are about to describe to you.

Find what nobody else has. Vendor changes since the client last evaluated, whether a competitor's product literally applies, the org-chart diff since a past initiative died, numbers that moved since the client formed their opinion. Each must survive a hostile read as a plain fact with a source, or it goes to the assumptions register instead.

Write the atomic knowledge base when depth allows: topic-per-file Markdown, each independently footnoted, per references/knowledge-base-spec.md. Footnote types: [^S1] filings and company sources, [^W1] web, [^I1] internal, [^A1] assumptions. Flag conflicts rather than resolving them silently, and keep the assumptions register as its own file with a client-safety verdict column.

Build the interactive HTML brief when the call warrants it: assets/brief-template.html is the working shell (footnote popovers, assumption highlighting, money-flow explorer, drill mode); you fill in content, not mechanics, per references/html-brief-spec.md. Build and verify with:

python3 scripts/build_brief.py draft.html -o out.html --verify

It resolves the explicitly selected project brand profile (or neutral default), embeds declared assets, and verifies the result only in permitted browser infrastructure. Missing assets or unavailable rendering remain acceptance gaps. The file must stay fully self-contained, no CDN dependencies: these get opened on planes and in client parking lots. The HTML is secondary; the Markdown brief is the canonical record per _shared/output-contract.md.

Landing the work

Deliver the artifact, register its location, update client.profile and client.relationships with supported changes, and write session memory pointing at the records rather than restating them.

Close with the top three facts, then the landmines. Then flag your biggest judgment call and argue the other side of it honestly. A brief presented as settled when it contains a real fork is the failure mode.

Quality gates

  • scripts/check_pursuit_brief.py for each Pursuit Brief and Call Brief, plus

--before/--after when revising an existing Pursuit Brief.

  • scripts/reconcile.py on the evidence ledger whenever a Mode B brief carries figures.
  • review-writing owns writing review: run its bundled diagnostics on the prose. No em dashes, no buzzwords, no AI-construction patterns. Report the counts it prints.
  • brand-renderer and _shared/build-card.md own any branded surface. Use --profile for an explicitly supplied profile; the renderer otherwise stays neutral and never discovers an employer brand from personal folders.

Boundaries

  • maintain-discovery-record owns post-call transcript ingestion, question closure,

decision logging, and its two-column ledger. Mode B reads that record and carries supported post-call updates into the Pursuit Brief.

  • NOT scope item creation, quote editing, or pricing. That is scope-project and the Pricing System.
  • NOT post-sale delivery work, project status, or requirements sessions.
  • Never invents stakeholder names, availability, commitments, or facts. Roles, not guessed people.

What to skip when time is short

Cut in this order and say what you cut: drill-mode content, the full knowledge base (keep index, current-state, stakeholders, deal-strategy, assumptions), Agent A's deep financial history. Never cut: the internal harvest, the assumptions register, the landmines, citations, or the checkers.

Files

  • scripts/check_pursuit_brief.py · the gate for both brief modes and the human-marker idempotency check. Stdlib only; exits nonzero on failure.
  • scripts/check_pursuit_brief_selftest.py · runs the gate against scripts/fixtures/.
  • scripts/reconcile.py · the figure and evidence gate for Mode B ledgers.
  • scripts/reconcile_selftest.py · its selftest.
  • scripts/build_brief.py · inlines brand assets into the HTML brief and render-verifies it.
  • assets/evidence.schema.json · the Mode B evidence ledger structure.
  • assets/brief-template.html · the working interactive shell.
  • references/research-prompts.md · prompt templates for the two research subagents.
  • references/knowledge-base-spec.md · atomic file list, footnote conventions, assumptions register format.
  • references/html-brief-spec.md · HTML section structure, content schemas, brand constraints.

Release gate (required)

Before delivery, run the required gate. Complete it during production. Full spec in release-gate.md (../_shared/release-gate.md).

  1. Apply review-writing to the prose. Use the bundled diagnostic tools to check saved writing. For

a final artifact it emits a receipt the quality gate requires.

  1. Run brand-renderer on the branded artifact: palette, borders, radii, logo,

footer.

  1. Run review-deliverable before you call it final.

Do not present the artifact as finished until every check that applies has passed.

examples.title: First discovery call with a regional freight carrier
examples.markdown:
## Request

Prep me for Thursday's 45-minute first discovery call with Tidewater Freight Co. Dana Whitfield (VP Customer Experience) is the lead and Marcus Oyelaran (IT) joins for the second half. Everything I have is in ./inputs/.

## Inputs

Run of the built `prepare-sales-pursuit` task package. All inputs below are invented. The run had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so. Files it also produced, not shown here: `tidewater-freight-evidence.json`, `tidewater-freight-pursuit-brief.md`.

#### account-notes.md

#### Tidewater Freight Co. — account notes (fictional)

- Regional less-than-truckload (LTL) carrier, 14 terminals across Virginia, the Carolinas and Georgia. About 1,900 employees, 1,100 tractors.
- Revenue about $410M (FY2025, company-reported in a trade-press interview).
- Customer service runs from one contact center in Norfolk: 62 agents, three shifts. Today they use a 2014-era on-premise ticketing tool ("ServiceDesk Pro") plus shared Outlook inboxes for claims.
- Transportation management system (TMS): "RouteLine 9", hosted by the vendor, REST API available for shipment status and proof-of-delivery images.
- Pain points raised by the inbound lead form: customers can't self-serve shipment status; freight-claims cycle averages 41 days; no single view of a shipper account across terminals.
- Inbound lead came from the VP of Customer Experience after a webinar on Service Cloud for logistics.


#### contacts.md

#### Contacts (fictional)

| Name | Title | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Dana Whitfield | VP, Customer Experience | Lead source. Owns the contact center and claims. Joined 8 months ago from a parcel carrier. |
| Marcus Oyelaran | Director, IT Applications | Owns RouteLine integration. Skeptical of "another platform." |
| Priya Raman | Claims Manager | Runs a team of 9 claims adjusters. |
| Tom Becker | CFO | Not on the first call; signs anything over $250K. |


#### email-thread.md

From: Dana Whitfield
To: (our account executive)
Subject: Re: Intro call Thursday

Thanks for reaching out. Thursday at 10 works. Marcus from IT will join for the second half. Our big question is whether we can get customers tracking shipments and filing claims online by peak season next fall, and what that would roughly cost. We've been burned by a long implementation before, so we care a lot about phasing.

## Output

### Tidewater Freight Co.: prep for Thursday 2026-11-05, 10:00

I built a call brief for Thursday and seeded a Pursuit Brief, since neither existed. Everything below comes from your three input files. None of them is dated, so treat every fact as "as of an unknown date."

#### Top three facts

1. **Dana's ask is specific and time-boxed.** She wants customers tracking shipments and filing claims online by peak season next fall, wants a rough cost, and cares about phasing because a past implementation ran long (her email).
2. **The pain is operational.** One Norfolk contact center (62 agents), a 2014-era on-premise ticketing tool, claims in shared Outlook inboxes, a 41-day average claims cycle, and no cross-terminal account view (account notes, from their inbound form).
2. **Marcus holds the feasibility answer.** He owns the RouteLine 9 integration, and RouteLine has a REST API for shipment status and proof-of-delivery images (contacts, account notes). Whether it covers what a claims portal needs is unknown.

#### Landmines

- **Cost.** Dana asked for a rough cost in writing. You gave me no pricing, and pricing belongs to scope-project. The brief sets the intent: name the cost drivers, promise a ranged estimate after scoping, give no number.
- **Marcus.** Your contacts sheet has a note characterizing him. Don't repeat it to anyone. The brief builds his half around the thing the sheet supports: he owns the integration.
- **Tom Becker's $250K signing level** is internal. Ask Dana about approvals in general terms.
- **Dana's background** (8 months in role, from a parcel carrier) is internal. Don't assume she lived through the past implementation, and don't compare Tidewater to her old employer.
- **Who started this?** The account notes say an inbound form after a webinar; Dana's reply says "Thanks for reaching out." Don't say which.
- **Service Cloud** was the webinar topic. That shows interest, not a product choice. Don't pitch before she defines "online tracking and claims."

#### The call plan

Objective: learn what phase 1 means in Dana's words and what the RouteLine and ServiceDesk Pro environment allows. Not a price, a date, or a solution commitment.

| Minutes | Segment | Lead |
|---|---|---|
| 0-3 | Introductions, confirm time box, Marcus joins at about minute 22 | You |
| 3-12 | Why now, what "online tracking and claims" means, the peak-season date | Dana |
| 12-22 | Claims journey, account view, the earlier implementation | Dana |
| 22-25 | Marcus joins; one-minute recap | You |
| 25-36 | RouteLine API, ServiceDesk Pro, Outlook inboxes, constraints, security review | Marcus |
| 36-43 | React to a phased shape; cost question | Both |
| 43-45 | Next steps and owners | You |

Highest-ranked questions (13 in the full brief):

1. What does "filing claims online" include: submitting with documents, tracking status, or both? What would a customer see on day one?
2. When does peak season start, and what must be live before it? What is the smallest thing that would help?
3. What made the earlier implementation long, and what would a phase need to deliver to count as a win?
4. How does a claim travel from first email to payment, and how is the 41 days measured?
5. What is your approval process for a project like this, and who else decides?
6. For Marcus: what does the RouteLine API expose, what are the access limits, and what must stay in ServiceDesk Pro and the Outlook inboxes?
7. For Marcus: what does your security and architecture review involve, and how long does it take?

#### Assumptions I made (none is safe to state as fact)

| ID | Assumption | Confidence | Safe to say to client |
|---|---|---|---|
| A-01 | "Online tracking and claims" means a customer portal for status and claim submission | Medium | Yes, as a question |
| A-02 | Shipment status is the cheapest first phase because the RouteLine API exists | Medium | Yes, as a hypothesis |
| A-03 | Claims filing needs a new intake and workflow because claims sit in Outlook | Medium | Yes, as a question |
| A-04 | The project may exceed $250K and need CFO approval | Low | No |
| A-05 | The past implementation predates Dana | Low | No |
| A-06 | IT will want proof the integration work is bounded | Medium | Yes, as a question |
| A-07 | "Peak season next fall" means fall 2027 | Low | Yes, as a question |
| A-08 | The webinar signals a platform category, not a chosen product | Medium | Yes, as a question |

#### Figures

All single-source, so there were no conflicts to reconcile, but none is independently confirmed.

| Figure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Claims cycle | 41 days average | Account notes (inbound form) |
| Agents | 62 | Account notes |
| Terminals | 14 | Account notes |
| Revenue | about $410M, FY2025 | Account notes (trade-press interview, not seen) |
| CFO signing threshold | over $250K | Contacts (internal, not for the client) |

#### Follow-up

- Same day: send Dana her goals and phasing criteria in her words. Propose a claims-workflow session with Priya Raman (Claims Manager) and a technical session with Marcus.
- Within one day: hand the transcript or notes to maintain-discovery-record.
- Within two days: update the Pursuit Brief.
- Before any cost conversation: pass confirmed scope to scope-project.

Recommended sequence in the Pursuit Brief: Call 1 discovery (Thursday), Call 2 claims workflow with Priya, Call 3 RouteLine technical session with Marcus, Call 4 scope and cost review with Dana.

#### Gaps and what I cut

- **Sections omitted:** talk track (no recording of your voice, so the brief gives intents only), Q&A bank (no questions from Tidewater beyond Dana's two asks), and the HTML brief and atomic knowledge base (not enough evidence to earn them).
- **Public research not done.** The run was limited to your inputs, so there are no filings, trade-press, competitor, or RouteLine vendor findings. The $410M figure is second-hand.
- **No CRM, calendar, or discovery ledger available.** A zero-result CRM search is a finding when run; here it was not run. Call length, time zone, and our side's attendees are unconfirmed beyond "Thursday at 10" in Dana's email. I read "Thursday" as 2026-11-05 from today's date.
- **Staleness:** every source is undated.
- **Scripts not run.** I could not run scripts in this session, so I applied their documented rules by hand:
  - `check_pursuit_brief.py` (both modes): I confirmed each required section heading, `Assumption` labels on every assumptions bullet, the last-updated line, the Purpose, Desired outcome and Prerequisites lines on each call, the link to the Pursuit Brief, no placeholders, and no em dashes. I read these off the text rather than executing the checker.
  - `reconcile.py`: every figure has a source and a stated meaning, and no figure appears with two values. It would warn that no source carries a date.
  - **Writing review:** I did not run review-writing or the quality gate, and the brand-renderer step did not apply because no styled artifact was produced. I read the prose by hand against the writing standard. I have no counts to report.

#### Biggest judgment call: no number on Thursday

I recommend giving Dana no cost figure on this call. The case against: she asked in writing, a first call that dodges the one question she raised can read as evasive, and a defensible order-of-magnitude range (for example, by phase) could build trust with a buyer who has been burned. The case for holding: I have no pricing basis, and the scope is undefined (portal only, or claims workflow and account view too?). Whatever you say first becomes her anchor, and she will carry it to the CFO. If you decide to give a range, get it from scope-project beforehand and tie it to a named phase, not to the whole ask.

A second fork: I put shipment status first as the likely phase 1 (A-02). If Dana says claims filing is the real pain, that ordering flips, and the claims-workflow call with Priya moves ahead of the technical call.

#### Files (in `./out/`)

- `tidewater-freight-call-brief-2026-11-05.md`: the call brief. Full content is summarized above, including the agenda, ranked questions, risks, and the assumptions register.
- `tidewater-freight-pursuit-brief.md`: the seeded Pursuit Brief, with context, situation, outcomes, confirmed facts, assumptions, unknowns, stakeholders and missing roles, risks, qualification, four recommended calls, next steps, and decisions needed.
- `tidewater-freight-evidence.json`: the figure and sensitivity ledger.

### File: tidewater-freight-call-brief-2026-11-05.md

#### Tidewater Freight Co. call brief: first discovery call, Thursday 2026-11-05, 10:00

All people and figures come from the fictional files in `inputs/`. Source tags: [AN] account-notes.md, [CT] contacts.md, [ET] email-thread.md. None of the three files carries a date, so every fact is as of the file's last edit, which is unknown.

This is Call 1 in `tidewater-freight-pursuit-brief.md` (the Pursuit Brief). What it should feed back: confirmed scope language, the phasing answer, the integration facts, and who else must be in the room.

##### Call objective

1. Learn what "customers tracking shipments and filing claims online by peak season next fall" means to Dana in practice, and what a phased version she would accept looks like.
2. Learn from Marcus in the second half what the RouteLine 9 and ServiceDesk Pro environment allows, so the next call can be scoped.

##### Desired decisions or outcomes

- Dana's own words for the phase 1 target and the date it must be live.
- Agreement on a claims-workflow session with Priya Raman and the person who owns the Outlook claims inboxes.
- Marcus's agreement to a technical follow-up on the RouteLine API.
- Agreement on how the cost conversation will proceed (see Risks, item 1).
- Not an outcome of this call: a price, a solution commitment, or a date commitment.

##### Attendees and roles

| Person | Role | In the room | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dana Whitfield | VP, Customer Experience; owns contact center and claims; call lead on their side | Whole call | [CT], [ET] |
| Marcus Oyelaran | Director, IT Applications; owns RouteLine integration | Second half | [CT], [ET] |
| Our account executive (you) | Runs the call | Whole call | [ET] |

Not on the call: Priya Raman (Claims Manager, 9 adjusters) and Tom Becker (CFO, signs anything over $250K) [CT]. Our side's other attendees are unknown; add a note-taker if one is available.

##### Known context

- Tidewater is a regional LTL carrier: 14 terminals in Virginia, the Carolinas and Georgia, about 1,900 employees, 1,100 tractors [AN].
- Revenue is about $410M for FY2025, company-reported in a trade-press interview [AN]. We have not seen the interview.
- One Norfolk contact center, 62 agents, three shifts. Tools are ServiceDesk Pro (2014-era, on-premise) plus shared Outlook inboxes for claims [AN].
- TMS is RouteLine 9, vendor-hosted, with a REST API for shipment status and proof-of-delivery images [AN].
- Pain points from the inbound form: no customer self-service for shipment status, claims cycle averages 41 days, no single view of a shipper account across terminals [AN].
- Dana's email: Thursday at 10 works, Marcus joins for the second half. Her big question is whether customers can track shipments and file claims online by peak season next fall, and roughly what it costs. They have been burned by a long implementation before and care about phasing [ET].
- Lead source was Dana after a webinar on Service Cloud for logistics [AN, CT].

Figures (single source each; no conflicts found, but none is independently confirmed):

| Figure | Value | Source | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claims cycle | 41 days average | [AN], from the lead form | Dana's team's number. Ask how it is measured (filing to payment? first notice to close?) |
| Agents | 62, three shifts | [AN] | |
| Terminals | 14 | [AN] | |
| Revenue | about $410M, FY2025 | [AN] | Trade-press, company-reported, not seen |
| Approval threshold | over $250K needs CFO | [CT] | Internal. Do not cite to the client |

##### Run of show

1. Open neutrally and confirm the time box and that Marcus joins at about minute 22.
2. Let Dana define success in her own terms before anything is proposed.

5. When Marcus joins, recap in one minute and hand him the floor on integration.
6. Test a phased shape as a hypothesis, not a proposal.
7. Handle the cost question (intent below), agree next steps, stop on time.

| 22-25 | Marcus joins; one-minute recap | You |
| 25-36 | Marcus: RouteLine API, ServiceDesk Pro, Outlook inboxes, constraints, security review | Marcus |
| 36-43 | React to a phased shape; cost question | Both |
| 43-45 | Next steps and owners | You |

##### Questions

No discovery ledger exists for this pursuit, so every question below is call-specific, written from the three inputs. Ranked by effect on the next step.

For Dana (minutes 3-22):

1. What does "customers filing claims online" include for you: submitting a claim with documents, tracking its status, or both? What would a customer see on day one? (Resolves A-01.)
2. When does peak season start, and what has to be live before it? What happens to the business if only part is ready? (Resolves A-07.)
3. You mentioned a long implementation that hurt. What made it long, and what would a phase need to deliver to count as a win? (Phasing criteria. Do not ask who was at fault.)
4. How does a claim travel today, from the customer's first email to payment? Where does it wait? How is the 41 days measured?
5. Which customers or shippers matter most for self-service, and what do they ask your agents most often?
6. Who besides you decides on this, and what does your approval process look like for a project of this kind? (Opens the money and sign-off path without citing the CFO threshold. Resolves A-04.)
7. How are you measuring contact-center performance today, and which number would you want to move first?

For Marcus (minutes 25-36):

8. What does RouteLine's API expose today for shipment status and proof of delivery, and who at the vendor controls changes to it? (Resolves A-02.)
9. What are the limits: authentication, call volumes, who can approve new API consumers, any contract terms with the vendor?
10. Which parts of ServiceDesk Pro and the Outlook claims inboxes would have to stay, and which could be retired? (Resolves A-03.)

2. **Do not repeat the contacts-sheet note about Marcus.** It characterizes an individual. Plan the second half around his ownership of the RouteLine integration, which is the fact the sheet supports.
3. **Dana's tenure and background.** The contacts sheet says she joined 8 months ago from a parcel carrier [CT]. Do not assume she owned or witnessed the earlier implementation (A-05), and do not compare Tidewater to her previous employer unless she does.

5. **CFO threshold.** Tom Becker's $250K signing level [CT] is internal. Do not cite it. Ask about approvals in general terms (Question 6).

skills.title: Prepare session handoff
skills.description: Produce a structured end-of-session handoff so a fresh agent can resume without re-explanation. Use when the user says session handoff, wrap up session, hand off, or summarize before I clear, or signals a /clear or new chat. Also use proactively under context pressure: an auto-compact warning, running low on context, or a long session about to be interrupted. Covers provenance, decisions, shipped changes, rejected approaches, user corrections, key files, running state, and open questions. Do not use for status reports written for humans, retrospectives, PR descriptions, commit messages, or memory consolidation.

guide.what: Prepare another session to resume the same work.
guide.when: The current session is ending or needs a handoff.
guide.inputs: The session’s decisions, files, running state, and completed checks.
guide.outputs: A handoff with the current state, verification, open questions, and exact next action.
guide.example: Prepare a handoff with the current files, decisions, verification, and exact next action.
guide.expect: It stamps the time, directory and git state once, then writes a fixed-template handoff from what happened in the session, with absolute paths and 'none' for empty sections. It prints the handoff in chat and saves a file only where a handoffs directory already exists, and it does not audit the filesystem or update memory.
guide.overview: It stamps the time, directory and git state once, then writes a fixed-template handoff from what happened in the session, with absolute paths and 'none' for empty sections. It prints the handoff in chat and saves a file only where a handoffs directory already exists, and it does not audit the filesystem or update memory.
guide.value: Give a fresh session the decisions, current files, verification state and next action it needs to resume. It helps preserve working context without requiring the next agent to reconstruct the entire conversation.

preparation.where: Use it in the session that did the work, or supply a reliable session record. File paths, Git state, commands and unresolved questions come from that work; no separate handoff document is required beforehand.
preparation.missing: It cannot reconstruct missing history by assumption. It prints the handoff in chat and saves only to an existing handoffs directory. This workflow does not perform an unrelated filesystem audit or update memory.

name: prepare-session-handoff
description: 'Produce a structured end-of-session handoff so a fresh agent can resume without re-explanation. Use when the user says session handoff, wrap up session, hand off, or summarize before I clear, or signals a /clear or new chat. Also use proactively under context pressure: an auto-compact warning, running low on context, or a long session about to be interrupted. Covers provenance, decisions, shipped changes, rejected approaches, user corrections, key files, running state, and open questions. Do not use for status reports written for humans, retrospectives, PR descriptions, commit messages, or memory consolidation.'
---


# Prepare session handoff

> **Before writing: [`build-card.md`](../_shared/build-card.md) plus
> [`email-slack.md`](../writing-diagnostics/references/registers/email-slack.md). Inputs, not a final pass.**

Produce a handoff so the user can clear context and start a fresh agent without losing continuity. The next agent should be able to resume by reading this alone.

This is a **context-handoff artifact**, not a status report. The audience is a future instance of you, not a stakeholder. Write it the way a competent engineer hands off at end of shift: paths, commands, decisions, and the things that will otherwise be rediscovered the hard way.

## Two forms

**Full form.** End of session, before `/clear`, or when context is nearly exhausted. Use the complete template below. This is the default.

**Short form.** A mid-session pivot, where the user is moving to unrelated work in the same chat and just needs something pasteable. Five to eight lines: what was done, where it lives, what's left, pick up here. No file written unless asked. Offer this rather than the full template when the session is being *redirected* rather than *ended*.

If it isn't obvious which is wanted, produce the full form. It's cheaper to have too much handoff than too little.

## Step 1. Stamp the provenance

Run this once, first. It is the only filesystem lookup this skill performs:

```bash
date -u '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M UTC'; pwd; git branch --show-current 2>/dev/null; git rev-parse --short HEAD 2>/dev/null; git status --porcelain 2>/dev/null | wc -l
```

Why this matters more than it looks: a handoff is a **snapshot**, and multi-session or parallel-agent work is common. Without a timestamp and commit, the next agent has no way to tell whether your "deferred work" list is still true or whether another session already shipped half of it. Trusting a stale list means duplicated work or a clobbered tree. The stamp converts "trust me" into "diff me."

This is a narrow exception to the no-auditing rule below. Capture HEAD; do not go reading logs or diffing.

## Step 2. Gather from the session, not the disk

Pull state from these, in order:

- **Plan or spec files** referenced this session. Name the path the user or you actually used. Do not guess at a conventional location; if no plan file drove the session, say so.
- **Task/todo list state**, whatever the harness calls it. Any in-progress or pending items.
- **Background processes** you started. Their IDs are load-bearing and the next agent cannot recover them.
- **Files created or modified** this session. You know what you touched; don't grep to rediscover.
- **Memory files** written or updated, at whatever memory directory this environment provides.
- **Corrections the user made to you.** The most expensive thing to lose, because a fresh agent will cheerfully repeat the mistake.
- **Approaches tried and abandoned**, and why.
- **Unresolved questions.** Things you asked that never got a clear answer, or things the user asked that got deflected.

**Do not audit the filesystem.** Beyond the provenance stamp: no `git log`, no broad `Glob` sweeps, no re-reading files to check your work. This is synthesis of what happened in THIS session. If you didn't touch it this session, it doesn't belong here.

## Step 3. Output template

Use this structure, every time:

```
# Session Handoff: <one-line title of what this session was about>

Written: <UTC timestamp> | <branch> @ <short SHA> | tree <clean|N files dirty> | cwd <absolute path>

## Where it started
<2-3 sentences: what the user asked for, key framing or constraints that emerged>

## Decisions locked + what shipped
- <decision or change>. <why, and where it lives (absolute path if a file)>
- Tried and rejected: <approach>. <why it failed, so it isn't retried>
- Corrected by user: <what you had wrong>. <what's actually true>

## Key files for next session
- `<absolute path>`. <why the next agent should read this first>
- Plan/spec file: `<path>` (if one drove the session). List this first
- Memory files touched: `<paths>`

## Running state
- Background processes: <IDs + what they are + how to kill>, or "none"
- Dev servers / ports: <url + port>, or "none"
- Worktrees / branches: <absolute path>, <live | merged | abandoned>, or "none"
- Uncommitted work in the tree: <what, and whether it's yours>, or "none"

## Verification: how to confirm things still work
- `<command>`. <expected outcome>

## Deferred + open questions
- Deferred: <item>. <why pushed>. Touches: `<paths>`
- Open: <question needing the user's input>. <context>

## Pick up here
<1-2 sentences: the single most likely next action for a fresh agent>
<If any deferred item touches files, add: "Re-verify the deferred list against HEAD before acting. It was true at the stamp above, not necessarily now.">
```

## Step 4. Deliver it

**Always print the full handoff in chat.** That is the primary channel and it is never skipped.

**Also write it to a file, by default.** The filename is always:

```
handoff-<YYYY-MM-DD-HHMM>-<short-kebab-topic>.md
```

The directory is whichever of these the environment actually provides, in order. Resolve it, do
not assume it:

1. A handoffs directory the user or the project has already named. If one exists, it wins.
2. A persistent handoffs location explicitly supplied by the current harness or its configuration. Do not derive one from a host name, a conventional home directory, or another account's previous session.
3. No persistent location. Then write nothing and say so in one line.

Create the directory if it does not exist. Say the resolved path in one line after the chat
output. Do not narrate the write.

Skip the file if the user says "chat only", if this is the short form, or if the filesystem is absent or ephemeral. Ephemeral matters: some hosted environments give you a writable sandbox that disappears when the session ends, so a file written there is worse than no file, because it looks saved and is not. If you can't tell whether the path persists, say so in one line and rely on the chat output, which is the channel that always works.

Never write the handoff anywhere other than the handoffs directory, and never update memory from this skill; memory is a separate concern with its own rules.

## Hard rules

1. **Never invent state.** If a section has nothing to report, write "none". Do not omit the section. Structure stability is the whole point: the next agent learns where to look and can trust that a missing item means nothing happened, not that you forgot.
2. **Absolute paths always.** The next agent may have a different working directory.
3. **If a plan or spec file drove the session, name it first** in Key files, so it gets read before anything else.
4. **Background process IDs are critical.** Without them in Running state, with the kill command, the next agent cannot find those processes at all.
5. **No emojis, no hype, no "great progress today".** Terse and concrete: paths, commands, IDs, decisions.
6. **The handoff is a snapshot and should say so.** Deferred work especially. Never write the deferred list as if it were current truth.

## Anti-patterns

- Summarizing the last three turns and calling it a handoff. Review the whole session.
- Relative paths.
- Skipping "Running state" because nothing is running. Write "none".
- Writing the file anywhere other than the handoffs directory, or quietly updating memory.
- A retrospective. "What went well / what went poorly" is not wanted. **This is different from "Tried and rejected".** Recording a failed approach so it isn't repeated is essential; grading the session's vibe is noise. Keep the former, drop the latter.
- Recommending next steps beyond the single "Pick up here" line. The next agent decides.
- Padding thin sections to look thorough. A short honest handoff beats a long speculative one.

examples.markdown:
## Request

I'm about to /clear, context is nearly full. Session handoff please, the session notes and the terminal state are in the inputs.

## Inputs

**Dry run.** This skill normally works on live systems or its owner's own setup. Here the system state is invented in the inputs below, and nothing was changed anywhere. Run of the built `prepare-session-handoff` task package. The recording session invented this scenario, the request and the inputs below before running the skill. It had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so.

#### session-notes.md

#### Session notes (chronological, this chat)

- User asked: move the HTTP retry logic in `parcelsync` (a CLI that syncs shipment data) out of `client.py` into its own module with exponential backoff and jitter. Plan is in `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/docs/plans/retry-refactor.md`.
- I created `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/parcelsync/retry.py` (`RetryPolicy`, `with_retry`) and edited `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/parcelsync/client.py` to call it. Added `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/tests/test_retry.py` (6 tests, all pass).
- First attempt: wrapped retries with the `tenacity` library. Dropped it: the user does not want a new runtime dependency, and tenacity's jitter option couldn't be seeded for tests.
- User correction: I assumed 429 responses should be retried like 5xx. User said 429 must honour the `Retry-After` header and must not count against the max-attempts budget. Implemented in `retry.py`, but the `Retry-After` HTTP-date form (not just seconds) is not parsed yet.
- User correction: I wrote tests against `time.sleep` patching. User wants an injected `sleep` callable instead; tests now use that. `client.py` still passes the real `time.sleep` by default.
- Started a mock server for manual checks: `python tools/mock_api.py --port 8099` as a background process, shell job id `bash_3`.
- `tests/test_client.py` has 2 failing tests (`test_sync_retries_on_503`, `test_sync_gives_up_after_max`). Not yet looked at; likely they still patch `time.sleep`.
- Open question I asked, no answer yet: should max attempts be configurable from `parcelsync.toml` or stay a constant (5)?
- Todo list: [done] retry module, [done] retry tests, [in progress] fix test_client.py, [pending] Retry-After HTTP-date parsing, [pending] update README retry section.
- No memory files written this session.

#### terminal-state.txt

$ date -u '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M UTC'; pwd; git branch --show-current; git rev-parse --short HEAD; git status --porcelain | wc -l
2026-11-04 16:42 UTC
/Users/dev/work/parcelsync
feature/retry-module
a3f91c2
4

$ git status --porcelain
 M parcelsync/client.py
?? parcelsync/retry.py
?? tests/test_retry.py
 M tests/test_client.py

$ ls /Users/dev/work/parcelsync/docs/handoffs
handoff-2026-10-28-1015-config-loader.md

$ python -m pytest -q
2 failed, 31 passed

#### CONTRIBUTING.md excerpt
Session handoffs live in docs/handoffs/ (committed to the repo).

## Output

### Session Handoff: Extract parcelsync HTTP retry logic into its own module

Written: 2026-11-04 16:42 UTC | feature/retry-module @ a3f91c2 | tree 4 files dirty | cwd /Users/dev/work/parcelsync

#### Where it started
The user asked to move the HTTP retry logic out of `client.py` into a separate module with exponential backoff and jitter. The plan file drove the session. Constraints that emerged: no new runtime dependency, 429 handled differently from 5xx, and `sleep` injected rather than patched.

#### Decisions locked + what shipped
- New module `RetryPolicy` and `with_retry` in `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/parcelsync/retry.py` (uncommitted, new file).
- `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/parcelsync/client.py` now calls `with_retry`, passing the real `time.sleep` by default (uncommitted edit).
- `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/tests/test_retry.py`: 6 tests, all pass, using an injected `sleep` callable (uncommitted, new file).
- 429 responses honour `Retry-After` and do not count against the max-attempts budget. Implemented for the seconds form only.
- Tried and rejected: wrapping retries with `tenacity`. The user does not want a new runtime dependency, and its jitter could not be seeded for tests.
- Corrected by user: I treated 429 like 5xx. Actually 429 follows `Retry-After` and is outside the attempts budget.
- Corrected by user: I patched `time.sleep` in tests. Actually the user wants an injected `sleep` callable.

#### Key files for next session
- Plan/spec file: `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/docs/plans/retry-refactor.md`
- `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/parcelsync/retry.py`. The new module; `Retry-After` parsing lives here.
- `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/tests/test_client.py`. Two failing tests, `test_sync_retries_on_503` and `test_sync_gives_up_after_max`. Not yet inspected; likely still patching `time.sleep`.
- `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/parcelsync/client.py`. Call site of the new module.
- Memory files touched: none

#### Running state
- Background processes: shell job `bash_3`, mock API started with `python tools/mock_api.py --port 8099`. Stop it with the harness's kill for `bash_3`, or `lsof -ti :8099 | xargs kill`.
- Dev servers / ports: mock API at http://localhost:8099 (the `bash_3` process above)
- Worktrees / branches: `feature/retry-module` in /Users/dev/work/parcelsync, live, not merged
- Uncommitted work in the tree: 4 files, all from this session: modified `parcelsync/client.py` and `tests/test_client.py`; new `parcelsync/retry.py` and `tests/test_retry.py`

#### Verification: how to confirm things still work
- `cd /Users/dev/work/parcelsync && python -m pytest -q tests/test_retry.py`. 6 passed.
- `cd /Users/dev/work/parcelsync && python -m pytest -q`. At the stamp: 2 failed, 31 passed; both failures in `tests/test_client.py`.
- `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://localhost:8099/`. Any HTTP status means `bash_3` is still serving; connection refused means it died with the session.

#### Deferred + open questions
- Deferred: fix the two failing tests in `tests/test_client.py` (in progress when the session ended). Touches: `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/tests/test_client.py`
- Deferred: parse the HTTP-date form of `Retry-After`. Not started. Touches: `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/parcelsync/retry.py`, `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/tests/test_retry.py`
- Deferred: update the retry section of the README. Not started. Touches: `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/README.md`
- Open: should max attempts be configurable from `parcelsync.toml` or stay a constant (5)? Asked, no answer.

#### Pick up here
Open `tests/test_client.py`, change the two failing tests to pass an injected `sleep` instead of patching `time.sleep`, and rerun the full suite.
This list was true at the stamp above, not necessarily now. Re-verify the deferred list against HEAD before acting.

---

Handoff file: `/Users/dev/work/parcelsync/docs/handoffs/handoff-2026-11-04-1642-retry-module-refactor.md` (the directory CONTRIBUTING.md names). A copy is at `out/handoff-2026-11-04-1642-retry-module-refactor.md`.

Notes on how this was built:
- The provenance stamp (UTC time, branch, SHA, dirty count) comes from the terminal output you supplied. I did not run the command myself.
- The README path in the third deferred item is assumed from the repo layout. No README location was stated in your notes, so check it.
- `bash_3` is a shell job ID from your notes. If your harness numbers jobs differently, use the `lsof` fallback.
- The handoff file is not committed, and `docs/handoffs/` is committed to the repo per CONTRIBUTING.md, so commit it with the rest of the branch when you are ready.

skills.title: Prioritize work
skills.description: Rank problems, jobs, roadmap candidates or backlog items with a named framework (ODI, Opportunity Score, RICE, ICE, WSJF, weighted matrix) and check the evidence behind every score, so the ranking is a sourced proposal for the person who decides. Use for "prioritize these", "RICE score", "rank the backlog", "what should we build next", "which outcomes are under-served", "WSJF", or choosing a framework. Do NOT use for MoSCoW values on captured requirements (capture-requirements), job-led debate without scoring (frame-jobs-to-be-done), roadmap layout (build-roadmap), or sprint commitment (plan-sprint).

guide.what: Rank candidates with a named framework and check the evidence behind each score.
guide.when: A team must choose between problems, outcomes, roadmap candidates or backlog items.
guide.inputs: Candidates with their scoring inputs and the source for each input.
guide.outputs: A ranked proposal with each item's formula, flagged unsourced inputs and ties, and the decision owner named.
guide.example: RICE-score these eight roadmap candidates and flag any score that rests on a guess.
guide.expect: It names what is being ranked and picks one framework with a stated reason, then collects each score input with a source and runs a scoring script. The output is a ranked proposal with formulas, flags and a named decision owner, and the flags are carried forward, not cleared by raising a number.
guide.requires: Needs a candidate list with sourced inputs for the chosen framework and Python 3 for the scoring script.
guide.overview: It names what is being ranked and picks one framework with a stated reason, then collects each score input with a source and runs a scoring script. The output is a ranked proposal with formulas, flags and a named decision owner, and the flags are carried forward, not cleared by raising a number.
guide.value: Make a ranking inspectable instead of presenting an unexplained score. It shows the formula, source inputs, ties and uncertainties behind candidate priorities so the decision owner can challenge the trade-offs.

preparation.where: Provide the items to rank and evidence for the chosen framework, such as reach, impact, confidence and effort for RICE. These values come from research, analytics and team estimates; the skill supplies the scoring method, not the measurements.
preparation.missing: Missing inputs stay flagged rather than being raised to improve a candidate's rank. The result is a prioritization proposal, not an authorized tracker update. A score cannot resolve a decision whose evidence is still absent.

reuse.reason: The method accepts the user’s project sources and takes private context as an explicit input.
reuse.basis: Source classification and automated reference scan; cross-environment execution has not been tested.

profile.setup: Needs a candidate list with sourced inputs for the chosen framework and Python 3 for the scoring script.
profile.expect: It names what is being ranked and picks one framework with a stated reason, then collects each score input with a source and runs a scoring script. The output is a ranked proposal with formulas, flags and a named decision owner, and the flags are carried forward, not cleared by raising a number.

---
name: prioritize-work
description: 'Rank problems, jobs, roadmap candidates or backlog items with a named framework (ODI, Opportunity Score, RICE, ICE, WSJF, weighted matrix) and check the evidence behind every score, so the ranking is a sourced proposal for the person who decides. Use for "prioritize these", "RICE score", "rank the backlog", "what should we build next", "which outcomes are under-served", "WSJF", or choosing a framework. # Prioritize work

> **Before writing: [`build-card.md`](../_shared/build-card.md) plus
> [the planning chain](../_shared/planning-chain.md). Inputs, not a final pass.**

This skill turns a candidate list into a ranked proposal with the formula and the evidence for each score visible. The person who owns the decision sets the order. A ranking is not a decision until that person makes it, and track-delivery records it as a DEC entry on an engagement.

## Project context required

Use only the caller-confirmed product, engagement or portfolio and the candidates and evidence supplied for it. Score inputs come from named sources: research, analytics, support records, engineering sizing, or the people in the session. An input with no source is labelled an estimate.

## Workflow

1. **Name what is being ranked.** Problems and jobs come before solutions. If the list is features with no problem named, ask which problem each addresses, or apply frame-jobs-to-be-done's prioritization reference first. The tool flags items without a `job` or `problem`.
2. **Choose one framework** with [the framework reference](references/frameworks.md). State the choice and the reason.
3. **Collect inputs with sources.** For each item record the framework fields and a `sources` entry for confidence, effort and customer importance. Effort comes from engineering. Write the candidate file described in [candidate format](references/candidate-format.md).
4. **Score and read the flags.** Run the tool. Resolve each flag or carry it into the proposal; do not raise a number to clear a flag.
5. **Present the proposal.** Show the ranked table, the formula for each item, the flags and any ties. Name the decision owner and the decision needed. Do not change capture-requirements's MoSCoW values or the roadmap; the owner decides and the owning skill records the change.

## Tool

```bash
python3 scripts/priority_score.py candidates.json --framework rice
python3 scripts/priority_score.py outcomes.json --framework odi --format json --output ranking.json
```

Frameworks: `rice`, `ice`, `opportunity`, `odi`, `wsjf`, `weighted`. The tool caps unsourced confidence above 50%, flags unsourced effort and customer ratings, notes ties and uniform impact, and exits 1 when an item is missing a required field or repeats an ID. Report the counts and flags it prints.

`scripts/priority_score_selftest.py` checks the formulas against the upstream demo scores and the evidence rules against failing fixtures. Run it after any change.

## How rankings feed the chain

- Ranked jobs and outcomes give build-roadmap its Now, Next and Later candidates; the owner places them.
- Ranked requirements inform the Product Owner's backlog order, which refine-backlog and plan-sprint follow.
- On an engagement, a re-ordering that moves committed scope is a scope question; route it through track-delivery before anyone acts on it.

## Durable output

Each run leaves the candidate file, the ranking report (Markdown or JSON) and the decision still needed, per `_shared/output-contract.md`. Deliver or link them.

## Boundaries

- Does not decide. The named owner does.
- Does not set or rewrite MoSCoW values; capture-requirements records them after the client or Product Owner confirms.
- Does not run JTBD research or write job statements. That is `frame-jobs-to-be-done`.
- Does not draw the roadmap. That is `build-roadmap`.
- Does not estimate effort. Engineering does.

## Files

- `references/frameworks.md`: framework selection, formulas, scales, evidence rules and common failures.
- `references/candidate-format.md`: the candidate JSON the tool reads.
- `scripts/priority_score.py`: the scorer, which uses the standard library only.
- `scripts/priority_score_selftest.py` and `scripts/fixtures/`: formula parity and evidence-rule cases.
- `UPSTREAM.md` and `LICENSE-UPSTREAM`: the source this skill adapts and its license.

## Release gate (required)

Before you deliver, run the gate. Full spec in [`release-gate.md`](../_shared/release-gate.md).

1. Apply review-writing to the proposal prose.
2. Run review-deliverable before you call it final.

Do not present the ranking as final until both checks have passed.

examples.title: Ranking a SaaS quarter backlog and choosing cuts
examples.markdown:
## Request

Prioritize the Packwise backlog for next quarter with a scoring framework and tell me what to cut. We have 6 engineers for a 12-week quarter. Backlog and context are in ./inputs/.

## Inputs

Run of the built `prioritize-work` task package. All inputs below are invented. The run had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so. Files it also produced, not shown here: `candidates.json`.

#### backlog.md

#### Packwise — candidate features for next quarter (fictional SaaS for small moving companies)

Context: ~420 paying companies; $1.9M ARR; 6 engineers. Quarter goal: reduce churn (currently 3.1% monthly logo churn) and grow seats in existing accounts.

| Feature | Notes from team |
|---|---|
| Online quote form customers can embed | Sales says 60+ prospects asked; mostly helps acquisition. ~5 eng-weeks. |
| Crew mobile app offline mode | Support: 140 tickets last quarter from crews losing signal in basements/elevators; 3 churned accounts cited it. ~8 eng-weeks. |
| QuickBooks Online two-way sync | Today one-way export. 35% of accounts use QBO; CS says it's a top-3 renewal complaint. ~6 eng-weeks. |
| Damage claim photos attached to job | Requested by 22 accounts. ~2 eng-weeks. |
| Multi-branch dashboards | 18 accounts have 2+ branches; these are the biggest accounts (avg 3x seats). ~6 eng-weeks. |
| SMS arrival notifications to end customers | Competitor parity; 50 requests. Twilio costs pass-through. ~3 eng-weeks. |
| Dark mode | 9 requests. ~2 eng-weeks. |

## Output

### Packwise next-quarter backlog: ICE ranking and cut proposal

**Proposal:** build QuickBooks sync, offline mode, multi-branch dashboards, SMS notifications and damage photos (25 eng-weeks). Cut dark mode and the embeddable quote form (7 eng-weeks). This is a proposal; the person who owns next quarter's roadmap decides. The inputs don't name them.

**Capacity doesn't force the cut.** Six engineers over 12 weeks is 72 eng-weeks. The seven items add up to 32 eng-weeks on the team's own numbers, which is 44% of capacity. I cut the two items that don't serve the quarter goal (reduce 3.1% monthly logo churn and grow seats in existing accounts). The inputs don't give maintenance or support load, so I can't say how much of the 72 weeks is really free.

#### Ranking (ICE: impact x confidence x ease)

I used ICE because there are 7 items, which the skill treats as a quick-sort case. Reach is not comparable across the notes: they mix tickets, requests, accounts and prospects. Impact is scored 1 to 10 against the quarter goal. Ease is 10 for trivial work and is mapped from the team's eng-week figures: 2 weeks is 9, 3 is 8, 5 is 6, 6 is 5, 8 is 3.

| Rank | ID | Feature | Impact | Confidence | Ease | Score | Eng-weeks | Proposal |
|---:|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | QBO | QuickBooks Online two-way sync | 8 | 0.5 | 5 | 20 | 6 | Build |
| 2 | OFFLINE | Crew mobile app offline mode | 8 | 0.8 | 3 | 19.2 | 8 | Build |
| 3 | MULTIBR | Multi-branch dashboards | 7 | 0.5 | 5 | 17.5 | 6 | Build |
| 4 | SMS | SMS arrival notifications | 4 | 0.5 | 8 | 16 | 3 | Build |
| 5 | PHOTOS | Damage claim photos | 3 | 0.5 | 9 | 13.5 | 2 | Build |
| 6 | QUOTE | Embeddable quote form | 2 | 0.5 | 6 | 6 | 5 | Cut |
| 7 | DARK | Dark mode | 1 | 0.5 | 9 | 4.5 | 2 | Cut |

Formulas: QBO 8 x 0.5 x 5; OFFLINE 8 x 0.8 x 3; MULTIBR 7 x 0.5 x 5; SMS 4 x 0.5 x 8; PHOTOS 3 x 0.5 x 9; QUOTE 2 x 0.5 x 6; DARK 1 x 0.5 x 9.

#### Why each call

- **Offline mode** has the strongest evidence: 140 support tickets last quarter, and 3 churned accounts cited it. At 3.1% monthly churn on about 420 accounts, roughly 39 logos leave per quarter, so those 3 are about 8% of churn. That is my arithmetic from the inputs, not a figure the team gave. It is the only item whose confidence (0.8) rests on a written source. It is also the largest item, which is why it ranks second.
- **QuickBooks sync** is a top-3 renewal complaint per CS, and 35% of accounts (about 147) use QBO. There is no complaint count, so confidence stays at 0.5. A ticket or renewal-note count could lift it above offline mode.
- **Multi-branch dashboards** serve 18 accounts, but those accounts average 3x seats. By my arithmetic that is about 12% of seats, with seats counted as 402 single-seat accounts plus 18 at 3x. Nothing in the inputs shows these accounts are at risk or asking for it, so confidence is 0.5. This is the best seat-growth bet.
- **SMS and damage photos** are cheap and have demand (50 requests; 22 accounts), but neither is linked to churn or seats. SMS also carries Twilio pass-through cost, which needs a pricing decision before launch.
- **Quote form** helps acquisition, not the quarter goal. Sales reports 60+ prospects asking, so it is a candidate for next quarter if the goal shifts to growth.
- **Dark mode** has 9 requests and no link to the goal.

#### Flags

- **Near-tie at the top:** QBO (20) and offline (19.2) are not separable at this evidence level. Treat them as equal and commit both.
- **Effort is unconfirmed.** Every eng-week figure is a team note ("~"), and no engineer sized them. The skill says effort comes from engineering. Get sign-off before publishing. If the estimates run 2x, the five committed items need 50 eng-weeks.
- **Ease is derived** from those unconfirmed figures through my mapping, so it carries the same caveat.
- **Impact scores are my judgment** against the quarter goal. Only the offline score has behavioural evidence behind it. Two of seven items share the top impact value (29%), under the 30% recalibration threshold.
- **No source supports confidence above 0.5** except offline mode, so the rest are held at 0.5, as the tool would cap them.

#### If estimates slip

Drop in this order: damage photos, SMS, then multi-branch. Protect QBO and offline mode, which are the two items with a stated retention link.

#### Decisions needed

1. The roadmap owner confirms the five-item scope and the two cuts. If it is a scope change to committed work, route it through track-delivery to log a DEC entry.
2. An engineer sizes the five committed items.
3. Someone supplies maintenance and support load, so the real capacity is known.
4. A pricing owner decides how to pass through Twilio cost on SMS.

#### How this was produced

The scoring script was not run in this session. I scored by hand using its documented ICE formula and evidence rules, and I applied the writing review by reading, with no checker run. The candidate file is in the format the script reads.

#### Files

- `out/candidates.json`: candidate file with problems, scores and sources for each item.
- `out/answer.md`: this ranking and proposal.
