> **Before writing: the shared build card (`../_shared/build-card.md`, where the
> estate mounts it) plus the writing-diagnostics register
> `../writing-diagnostics/references/registers/readout-brief.md`. Inputs, not a final pass.**

The business case is the document that gets someone to say yes and fund it. It
lands a recommendation and then earns it: benefits each tied to a pain the
client named, risks each with a severity and a real mitigation, the cost of
doing nothing in arithmetic, and an ask bounded by what is priced and what
still has to be decided.

The governing idea: **the case against is what makes the case for credible.**
A document that only lists upside is a sales pitch, and an approver who has
signed budget before discounts it on sight. An honest case names what the
skeptic in the room would say, then answers it or concedes it. The strongest
line in a business case is often the one that concedes the downside and holds
anyway.

## Phase 0: run the evidence core, and stop if it says stop

This artifact makes load-bearing factual claims, so `evidence-core`
runs first. Build the ledger there, then validate against the `business_case`
contract:

```bash
python3 ../evidence-core/scripts/evidence_core.py ledger.json business_case
```

The contract's required domains are recommendation, current gap, timing,
benefits, case against, cost of waiting, investment, and approval conditions.
If any load-bearing domain comes back Insufficient, produce the investment
readiness gap memo the contract names and stop. A full business case generated
after an Insufficient gate is a hard fail, because the approver funds against
whatever you print. Evidence-core owns provenance, confidence, conflicts,
staleness, and sufficiency; do not restate its rules here or anywhere else.

If evidence-core is not installed on this surface, say so, state the check it
would have run, do the best manual substitute (named source and date on every
claim, conflicts kept visible, gaps named), and report that as what happened.
Never silently skip the gate.

## Phase 1: sort the ledger into the balance view

The business case reads the validated ledger through three headings, because
the recommendation is their net:

- **Benefits.** Each must name the sourced pain it closes. A benefit that does
  not trace to something the client said hurts is a feature, and features do
  not belong in a business case. Cut it.
- **Costs and risks.** The investment, what is explicitly not priced, and the
  honest risks. Each risk carries a severity and a mitigation that is an
  action, not a restatement. Source risks from real friction: budget pushback,
  a capacity constraint, a cheaper competitor. A risk invented to look
  balanced is as bad as a benefit invented to look strong.
- **Timing facts.** The dated events that drive the cost of waiting: a
  cutover, a renewal cliff, a compounding manual cost. These turn "why now"
  from urgency theater into arithmetic.

This is a view over the evidence-core ledger, not a second ledger. Every entry
keeps its claim ID, source, confidence, and as-of date from the ledger. If the
costs-and-risks side is thin, the recommendation is not yet earned; go back to
the sources, because the risks exist whether or not you logged them.

## Phase 2: the money rule

Every number in the case has exactly one legitimate origin, and the case says
which:

- **Engagement cost figures come from the quote.** The Q-number through the
  scoping integration, or an explicit user-supplied pricing source. This skill
  renders those numbers; it never authors them. What the quote explicitly does
  not price is named in the ask, never folded into the headline figure.
- **Client-side value figures come from sourced client financials** (filings,
  investor materials, discovery numbers the client stated) or they are labeled
  inferences carrying an ID, a basis, and a safe-to-say verdict. An
  unquantified benefit is stated qualitatively. A fabricated value number is
  the fastest way to lose the one reader this artifact exists for.
- **Cost-of-delay arithmetic is shown, printed, and computed, never
  asserted.** Write the computation on the page: inputs, operator, result,
  each input sourced. The gate recomputes every shown product and fails on a
  mismatch.

Source tokens make this checkable. Every line carrying a currency figure or a
percentage ends in one of `[src: ...]`, `[quote: Q-...]`, `[inferred: ...]`,
`[gap: ...]`, or `[computed: ...]`. The full grammar, with the case-against
and cost-of-delay specs, is in `references/economics-and-case-against.md`.
Read it before writing sections 04 and 05.

## Phase 3: derive the structure, then write

Derive the section set from the ledger before consulting any worked example.
The catalog, with each section's job, bar, retrieval sources, and the
load-bearing versus flex table, is in `references/section-catalog.md`.

Always present, because the artifact does not exist without them:

- **01 Executive frame.** The recommendation, why it wins on balance, and the
  strongest argument for and against, up front. An approver who reads only
  this section knows what they are funding and that the case has looked its
  own downside in the eye.
- **04 Economics.** Benefits each closing a named pain, and the cost of
  waiting as shown arithmetic tied to a dated event.
- **05 The case against.** The skeptic's argument written straight, including
  the cheaper alternative, then answered or conceded. This section is what
  makes 01 credible.
- **06 Risk.** Sourced risks, each with severity and an action mitigation.
- **08 The ask.** Exactly what is being approved, by when, what is not yet
  priced, and the open decisions with owners and dates. No blank checks.

Contextual, included only when the ledger has the substance: 02 the client and
the gap, 03 why this moment, 07 investment and delivery. Benefit count equals
the benefits in the ledger; risk count equals the risks. Never pad to a round
number, and never manufacture timing pressure where the ledger has none.

Render confidence honestly as you write: Confirmed states plainly, Inferred
states as an inference with its basis, Unknown renders as a named gap,
conflicts show both values and flag the divergence. Concede before you
reframe.

## Phase 4: gate the draft

```bash
python3 scripts/case_gate.py case.md
```

The gate is deliberately light, because this artifact lives on judgment: it
checks that the load-bearing sections exist and have content, that the
case-against section is non-empty, that every currency figure and percentage
carries a source token, that every shown computation actually computes, and
that no em dash appears anywhere. Exit 0 is the only pass. Report the counts
it prints, never an adjective.

The gate cannot judge whether the case against is honest or the benefits trace
to real pains. That is your job, held to `references/depth-tests.md`. Run the
depth tests and the clone test there before calling the draft done. The
cardinal rule from that file: worked examples are depth-and-voice yardsticks
consulted last, never content sources. If find-and-replacing the client name
would turn your case back into an example, you cloned it.

## Phase 5: render and release

Rendering belongs to `brand-renderer`. This skill ships no CSS, no
JS, no palette, and no renderer of its own; a forked stylesheet is a second
source of truth that drifts. Hand the gated draft to the brand renderer and
ask for the devices this artifact earns: the for/against balance split, the
cost-of-delay timeline with compounding stops, the decision tracker with
owners and dates, muted severity tags with no red/green fills. Density is
visual where it earns it; prose carries judgment.

All four of the renderer's release gates (parity, visual, prose, brand) need a
written disposition before delivery. The prose gate runs the house checker:

```bash
python3 ../writing-diagnostics/scripts/prose_check.py case.md --config ../writing-diagnostics/house.json
```

A clean tool run is not a release authorization. Write a one-line disposition
per gate.

## Phase 6: land it and close the loop

Stamp the artifact with its source objects and dates: the Q-number and quote
total as-of, the ledger snapshot date, the driving event date. Record IDs are
not durable anchors, so the stamp is what lets the next session detect drift.
Deliver the file, commit it to the client or project folder, and write session
memory pointing at the files rather than restating them.

Then tell the user the recommendation, the two or three facts that carry it,
and the landmines. Flag your biggest judgment call and argue the other side of
it honestly. Every real case contains at least one fork: whether the timing
argument is strong enough to lead, whether an inferred value number is safe to
print, which alternative the case against takes on first. Presenting the case
as settled when it holds a real fork is the failure mode to avoid.

## When time is short

Cut in this order, and say what you cut: 07 delivery detail down to the single
cost figure and phase list; 02 down to two sentences inside 01; 03 folded into
the cost-of-waiting arithmetic. Never cut: the evidence gate, the case
against, the source tokens, the shown arithmetic, or `case_gate.py`.

## Running unattended

Phases 3 and 6 need a human for the judgment forks. On a scheduled or headless
run: build the ledger, run the evidence gate, draft, run `case_gate.py` and
the prose checker, and stop with the findings and open forks stated plainly.
Never ship a funding document to a client on an unattended run.

## Boundaries

- Does not price. The quote owns every engagement cost figure; this renders
  them.
- Does not build the deal decision deck. That is `build-deck`.
- Does not build the priced interactive proposal. That is
  `compare-scope-options`.
- Does not run the internal margin gate. That is the Deal Desk readout under
  evidence-core's `deal_desk` contract.
- Does not research the prospect. That is `prepare-sales-pursuit`; this consumes
  its outputs as sources.
- Evidence rules belong to `evidence-core`, brand tokens to
  `brand-renderer`, and writing review to `review-writing` using the confirmed author profile.

## Files

- `references/section-catalog.md` · the eight sections, each with its job,
  bar, retrieval sources, and failure mode, plus the load-bearing/flex table.
- `references/economics-and-case-against.md` · the source-token grammar, the
  cost-of-delay arithmetic spec, and the case-against spec.
- `references/depth-tests.md` · the depth tests, the cardinal rule, and the
  clone test.
- `scripts/case_gate.py` · the structural gate. Stdlib only. Exit 0 pass,
  1 fail.
- `scripts/case_gate_selftest.py` · fixtures under `scripts/fixtures/`. Run it
  after any change to the gate.

examples.title: Business case for appointment reminders and online booking across six clinics
examples.markdown:
## Request

Ines Okafor, our finance director, takes the appointment reminder and online booking project to the finance committee on 2026-11-18. Can you write the business case for her using the quote and my discovery notes? She has said she will push on price, so I want the honest version.

## Inputs

Run of the built `write-business-case` task package. The recording session invented this scenario, the request and the inputs below before running the skill. It had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so. Other files it produced, not shown here: `fix.txt`, `ledger.json`.

#### discovery-notes.md

#### Discovery notes, Calder Valley Veterinary Group (as of 2026-11-02)

Sources: call with Dev Marchetti (practice operations manager) 2026-10-20; email
from Ines Okafor (finance director) 2026-10-29; finance committee calendar.

##### What the clinics told us
- Six clinics, about 6,400 appointments a month across the group (Dev, 2026-10-20).
- Two agency part-timers make reminder calls all day. Agency cost is $2,600 a
  month. They do nothing else (Dev; Ines confirmed the cost, 2026-10-29).

  • 2027-01-27: go-live if approved on 2026-11-18 (10 weeks from approval).
  • 2027-02-14: last day for written notice ending the agency agreement.
  • 2027-02-17: next finance committee meeting.
  • 2027-02-28: agency agreement auto-renews for 12 months.
  • 2027-04-28: go-live if approved on 2027-02-17.

A February approval therefore goes live two months after the renewal has already locked.

04 Economics

*Bar: each benefit closes a pain the client named; the cost of waiting is printed arithmetic tied to the dated events above.*

Benefit 1: reminder calls replaced by automatic SMS and email. Closes the pain of two people phoning clients all day.

The agency line is $2,600 a month [src: Ines Okafor email, 2026-10-29].

This is cash only if the agreement is ended, which is a condition in section 08.

Benefit 2: fewer missed appointments. Closes the pain of empty slots. Main Street's no-show rate fell from 13% to 9% [src: Dev Marchetti call, 2026-10-20].

That is one clinic, eight weeks, and Dev's own tally. The group-wide no-show rate is not measured [gap: 3 months of PMS no-show data, owner Dev Marchetti].

Each appointment is worth $95 in billed revenue [src: Ines Okafor email, 2026-10-29].

Applying the full 4-point gain to every clinic gives an illustrative upside:

  • 6,400 x 0.04 = 256 appointments recovered per month [computed: inputs C3, C9]
  • 256 x $95 = $24,320 per month of billed revenue [inferred: I1, low, extrapolates one clinic's pilot to six]

Dr Voss doubts the gain came from SMS. A one-point gain tests that doubt:

  • 6,400 x 0.01 = 64 appointments recovered per month [computed: inputs C3, I1]
  • 64 x $95 = $6,080 per month of billed revenue [inferred: I1, low, one-quarter of the pilot gain]

This is revenue, not margin, and a recovered slot only counts if it is not left empty. The first figure, $24,320, is not safe to quote as a forecast [inferred: I1, low, see assumptions register]. The second, $6,080, is the one to use in the room, labeled as an inference [inferred: I1, low, see assumptions register].

Benefit 3: clients can book online. Closes the pain of unanswered calls and voicemail booking requests. The benefit is stated qualitatively because no complaint or lost-booking count exists [gap: booking complaint count, owner Dev Marchetti].

Cost of waiting. Two computations, both from the agency agreement. They overlap, so they are not added together.

Computation 1, the renewal lock if approval waits for 2027-02-17 (notice deadline 2027-02-14):

  • $2,600 x 12 = $31,200 committed for months the project would have covered [computed: inputs C6, C4]

Computation 2, the minimum cost of the three-month gap between the two go-live dates (2027-01-27 and 2027-04-28):

  • $2,600 x 3 = $7,800 of agency cost paid after the system could have replaced it [computed: inputs C6, C5]

The no-show upside forgone in that gap would be $6,080 x 3 = $18,240 at the one-point case [computed: inputs I1, C3].

Investment for comparison. $54,000 fixed fee [quote: Q-CVV-0417]. At the one-point case, $6,080 a month over 12 months is $6,080 x 12 = $72,960 of billed revenue [computed: inputs I1]. That is a revenue figure on an inference, so it supports the case without carrying it.

05 The case against

*Bar: the cheapest alternative first, each objection at full strength, each answered with evidence or conceded.*

1. "Buy the ClinicBook add-on instead." Ines raised this before the meeting. The add-on is $240 per clinic per month and the vendor already supplies the PMS [src: Ines Okafor email, 2026-10-29].

It covers four clinics, because ClinicBook is installed at four of six [src: Dev Marchetti call, 2026-10-20].

  • 4 x $240 = $960 per month [computed: inputs C11]
  • $960 x 36 = $34,560 over three years [computed: inputs C11]

Our option over the same three years is a fee of $54,000 for year one plus 24 months of licence from month 13 [quote: Q-CVV-0417]:

  • $890 x 24 = $21,360 [computed: inputs C10]
  • $54,000 + $21,360 = $75,360 over three years, before SMS charges and the VetDesk 6 connection, which are unpriced [quote: Q-CVV-0417]

The add-on is cheaper by $75,360 - $34,560 = $40,800 over three years, and it is cheaper by more once unpriced items are added to ours [computed: inputs C10, C11].

We concede this. The case for the project does not rest on being cheaper than the add-on. It rests on three things the add-on does not do: online booking, reminders at Pike Street and Alder Lane, and a go-live early enough to give notice on the agency agreement. If the committee does not value online booking, the add-on is the better purchase for four clinics, and the agency agreement question stays open.

2. "The agency saving is not real unless we end the contract." Ines made this point directly [src: Ines Okafor email, 2026-10-29]. Conceded. The $2,600 a month only becomes savings if written notice is given by 2027-02-14 [src: Ines Okafor email, 2026-10-29]. Section 08 makes that a named decision with an owner, and the notice should follow two weeks of stable running (section 06).

3. "The Main Street result was the front desk, not the SMS." Dr Hannah Voss raised this [src: Dr Voss, relayed in Ines Okafor email, 2026-10-29]. Partly conceded. We have one clinic, one tally, no control. The answer is in the economics: the case uses a one-point gain, one quarter of the pilot, and is built to hold on the agency date and online booking if the no-show gain turns out to be small.

4. "Do nothing." Cheapest in cash this quarter. It leaves two people phoning clients, no online booking, and the agency agreement renewing for 12 months at $2,600 a month, which is $31,200 [computed: inputs C6, C4].

06 Risk

*Bar: each risk comes from friction in the sources, carries a severity, and has a mitigation that is an action.*

  1. VetDesk 6 clinics cannot be connected (Pike Street, Alder Lane). Severity: high. Source: quote exclusions. Mitigation: Dev Marchetti chooses between a nightly file export and migrating the two clinics to ClinicBook by 2026-12-04, and the vendor prices the choice before the first payment. If neither is chosen, go-live is limited to four clinics and the committee is told so.
  2. Agency staff are needed until the system is proven, so notice on 2027-02-14 may come too early. Severity: medium. Source: renewal date and go-live date. Mitigation: go-live 2027-01-27 leaves 18 days. Set a check on 2027-02-10; give notice only if reminders have run cleanly for two weeks, otherwise the committee takes the 12-month lock knowingly.

skills.markdown:
---
name: write-feature-spec
description: "Write a feature spec, PRD, development brief, or testable acceptance criteria from supplied product context. Use for explicit specification and scoping requests; routine code edits and bug fixes do not require a separate spec."
license: MIT
---


# Write feature spec

Write a spec that lets the next owner understand the requested behavior and verify it. Read the current brief, supplied sources, and existing decisions before drafting. Separate a confirmed requirement from a proposed choice or open decision.

Read [Spec decisions](references/spec-decisions.md) to choose the appropriate depth. A bounded change can use a compact development brief. A cross-system feature may need a fuller spec. A reproducible defect needs expected behavior and evidence of actual behavior, not a fabricated product strategy.

For UI, API or persistence detail, read [the detailed feature workflow](../specify-implementation/SKILL.md). Select the sections the requested feature needs; retain its state transitions and failure paths.

Use the audience's vocabulary. Describe the problem and intended outcome, the behavior in scope, and the constraints that affect implementation. Include exclusions only when they prevent a plausible misunderstanding. Give dependencies and unresolved decisions their actual owners when known.

Make acceptance criteria observable. Cover the main path and the edge cases that matter to this feature. Specify how to check the outcome at its real destination. Do not turn implementation preferences into product requirements without evidence.

Ask only for a missing decision that materially changes the spec or blocks useful work. Draft the supported portions while that decision is pending. Do not impose a fixed discovery questionnaire, require a universal “why now,” or invent a baseline, effort estimate, target, date, or owner to fill a template.

Use an existing work item when supplied. Preserve its ID and current state; drafting a spec does not close a Brain task or create a competing task system. Keep implementation and external release separate from specification unless the user requested those actions too.

Deliver the requested document at the depth its reader needs. Identify the decisions still needed to make its acceptance criteria executable. Existing source authority, claim checks, voice, brand, and completion rules govern the result.

examples.title: Spec for autosaving and resuming inspection drafts on poor signal
examples.markdown:
## Request

Can you write the feature spec for autosaving and resuming site inspection drafts in our inspector web app? My brief and the engineer's notes on the current API are in the inputs folder; the main thing is that inspectors on poor signal stop losing their work.

## Inputs

Run of the built `write-feature-spec` task package. The recording session invented this scenario, the request and the inputs below before running the skill. It had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so.

#### api-notes.md

#### Current API notes (from Kofi Adeyemi, backend engineer)

Written from memory; I have not re-read the code this week.

- `POST /api/inspections/submit` takes `{ session_id, site_id, items: [{ item_id, answer, note }] }`. Auth is the `requireInspector()` helper, which returns the inspector's user ID.
- `session_id` is the login session, not the visit. It changes when the inspector logs in again.
- Submit writes to `inspections` (one row) and `inspection_items`. I believe the items save does DELETE then INSERT for the inspection, so item row IDs change on every save.
- `inspection_items` has a unique key on (inspection_id, item_id) and a foreign key to `inspections`.
- Nothing reads a half-finished inspection today. I do not know of any GET endpoint for inspections an inspector owns; the supervisor list reads submitted rows only.
- Answers are `pass`, `fail`, `na`. A `fail` requires a note of at least 10 characters (validated client-side only).
- I have not checked whether `inspections` has a status column.

#### brief.md

#### Brief: inspection drafts (Tallow Row Facilities)

Author: Priya Nandakumar, product manager. Contact: priya@example.com

##### Problem
Inspectors complete a 40-to-60 item checklist on a phone, often in plant rooms and basements with weak signal. Today nothing is saved until they tap Submit. If the page reloads, the phone locks for long enough to drop the session, or Submit fails on a bad connection, the whole checklist is gone. Support logged 14 "lost inspection" tickets in October 2026.

##### Wanted
- The checklist saves automatically as the inspector works, without them tapping anything.
- If the connection drops, they keep working; changes are sent when the connection returns.
- Reopening the inspection later (same phone or another device) restores answers and notes.
- Submit still works as it does now and turns the draft into the final inspection.

##### Rules I am sure of
- Only the inspector who started an inspection can open or edit its draft. Supervisors can see submitted inspections only (existing behaviour).
- One draft per inspector per site visit.
- Photos are out of scope for this release; they upload separately and already work.

##### Not decided
- How long an abandoned draft is kept. Ask Operations (Tomasz Berg).
- Whether a supervisor may take over a draft when an inspector is off sick.
- Launch date.

##### Success
Fewer lost-inspection tickets. I have not agreed a target with support.

## Output

I've written the spec for inspection draft autosave and resume. It's ready for review, but not for implementation yet. Four decisions are open, and the first one changes how a draft is identified.

**File:** `out/inspection-draft-spec.md` (Markdown, write-feature-spec depth with API, data and states)

#### What the spec says

**Outcome.** Answers and notes are saved on the server as the inspector works. Edits made offline queue on the phone and send when signal returns. The inspector can reopen the draft on any device after a reload or re-login. Submit keeps working and turns the draft into the final inspection. Support logged 14 lost-inspection tickets in October 2026, and that is the only baseline in your material.

**Design points that come from Kofi's notes**
- `session_id` is the login session and changes on every login, so it can't identify a draft. The client creates an `inspection_id` (UUID) when the checklist opens. A resume list for the site lets a second device find it.
- Kofi believes the item save does DELETE then INSERT. Autosave must upsert on the existing (`inspection_id`, `item_id`) key and write only the changed items. Otherwise each save would replace item row IDs, and a partial request could wipe answers it didn't mention.
- No read path exists for unsubmitted inspections. The spec proposes three endpoints:
  - `PUT /api/inspections/{inspection_id}/draft` takes changed items and a `base_revision`. It returns the new `revision`, or 409 when the revision is stale.
  - `GET /api/inspections/{inspection_id}/draft` returns the owner's draft.
  - `GET /api/inspections/drafts?site_id=` lists the caller's own drafts.
- A draft owned by another inspector returns 404, so its existence isn't disclosed.
- `POST /api/inspections/submit` gains an optional `inspection_id`, so older app versions keep working. If a request carries both `session_id` and `inspection_id`, both must belong to the caller, or it is rejected with 409 and nothing is written. A submit can't move an existing inspection to another site or session. A repeated submit writes nothing new.
- After a timeout, a lost response is retried safely. A 409 on retry triggers a read-back. If the server already holds the pending edits, the save counts as done. Otherwise the inspector sees a conflict dialog.
- The 10-character rule for a `fail` note is client-side only today. Drafts accept short notes, and the rule moves server-side at Submit. Kofi should review that change.

**Interface states.** The spec covers New, Resume available, Saving, Saved, Offline, Conflict, Rejected and Submitting. Each has a trigger, what the inspector sees, and the next state. It also covers a polite live-region save indicator, focus handling for the two dialogs, and keyboard-only use.

**Data.** The changes are additive. `inspections` gets a `status` (default `'submitted'`, so existing rows are untouched), a `revision` and an `updated_at`. `inspection_items` needs no schema change. Supervisor queries must filter to submitted rows, and every query that reads `inspections` needs checking for that.

**Acceptance.** There are 15 criteria, each with an action, an observable result and a check method. They include:
- offline edits reaching the server
- resume after re-login
- the same item row ID after repeated saves
- a lost-response retry
- a two-device conflict
- denied access for another inspector
- supervisors not seeing drafts
- the old client still submitting
- screen-reader and keyboard checks

#### Decisions still open

| # | Decision | Owner | What it blocks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | What counts as one "site visit" | Priya | Draft identity. I assumed site plus the inspector's local calendar date, and marked it as an assumption. |
| 2 | How long an abandoned draft is kept | Tomasz Berg | Cleanup rule. The spec specifies no deletion. Discard marks a draft as discarded. |
| 3 | Whether a supervisor can take over a draft | Priya | Until decided, only the owner has access. |
| 4 | Whether `inspections` already has a status column | Kofi | Whether to reuse it or add one. |
| 5 | Launch date | Priya | Nothing in the behaviour. |

#### Gaps and limits
- I had no code access. Everything about current behaviour (DELETE then INSERT, no read path, client-only validation, the session ID's lifecycle) is Kofi's recollection from his notes. The spec lists what to read before building: the submit handler, `requireInspector()`, the `inspections` schema and the supervisor query.
- No success target is set. The spec proposes tracking lost-inspection tickets against October's 14, with a target and window agreed by you and support before launch.
- Nothing was implemented, migrated or run. The acceptance checks are planned, not executed.
- I couldn't run the bundled writing checker (`writing_check.py`). I did a manual read of the text instead, so no scanner result stands behind it.

### File: inspection-draft-spec.md

#### Inspection drafts: autosave and resume

Status: ready for review. Not ready for implementation until decisions 1 to 4 below are settled.
Source: Priya Nandakumar's brief and Kofi Adeyemi's API notes. No code was read, so every statement about current behaviour is Kofi's recollection and is marked as such.

##### Problem and outcome

Inspectors fill in a 40-to-60 item checklist on a phone, often with weak signal. Nothing is stored until they tap Submit, so a reload, a dropped login session or a failed Submit loses the whole checklist. Support logged 14 lost-inspection tickets in October 2026.

Outcome: answers and notes are stored on the server while the inspector works, work continues through a connection drop, and the inspector can reopen the draft later on any device and finish it. Submit keeps working and turns the draft into the final inspection.

No ticket-reduction target exists. Measurement work is proposed in the last section; this spec sets no target.

##### Confirmed requirements (from the brief)

- Autosave without an inspector action.
- Changes made offline are sent when the connection returns.
- A draft reopens on the same or another device with answers and notes restored.
- Only the inspector who started the draft can read or edit it. Supervisors see submitted inspections only.
- One draft per inspector per site visit.
- Photos are out of scope.

##### Open decisions

| # | Decision | Owner | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | What counts as one "site visit" | Priya Nandakumar | Sets the draft's identity. This spec assumes site plus the inspector's local calendar date. |
| 2 | Retention of an abandoned draft | Tomasz Berg (Operations) | Sets the cleanup rule and the resume list. No deletion is specified here. |
| 3 | Supervisor takeover of a draft | Priya Nandakumar | Until decided, only the owner has access. |
| 4 | Whether `inspections` has a status column | Kofi Adeyemi to check | Decides between reusing it and adding one (see Data). |
| 5 | Launch date | Priya Nandakumar | Does not block the behaviour below. |

##### Current behaviour (unverified, from Kofi's notes)

- `POST /api/inspections/submit` takes `{ session_id, site_id, items: [{ item_id, answer, note }] }`. Authentication is `requireInspector()`, which returns the user ID.
- `session_id` identifies the login session and changes on every new login. It cannot identify a visit.
- Items are probably saved by DELETE then INSERT, so `inspection_items` row IDs change on each save. The table has a unique key on (`inspection_id`, `item_id`) and a foreign key to `inspections`.
- No endpoint reads an unsubmitted inspection. The supervisor list reads submitted rows.
- The rule that a `fail` needs a note of 10 or more characters runs in the client only.

Consequence for the design: autosave must update items in place on (`inspection_id`, `item_id`), so repeated saves keep row IDs and never delete answers the request did not mention. The login `session_id` cannot key a draft, because the inspector would lose it on re-login.

##### Behaviour

###### Identity

The client creates an `inspection_id` (UUID) when the inspector opens a checklist for a site and stores it locally. The server accepts it only if it is new or already owned by the caller. A second device finds the draft through the resume list (below), which returns the existing `inspection_id`.

###### States

| State | Trigger | What the inspector sees | Next state |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| New | Opens a checklist for a site with no draft today | Empty checklist, indicator "Not saved yet" | Saving on first answer |
| Resume available | Opens a site where the caller has a draft for the same visit | Prompt: "Continue your draft from 09:42?" with Continue and Discard. Continue loads the draft. | Populated |
| Saving | Answer or note changes | Indicator "Saving…". Inputs stay enabled. Changes are batched, at most one request in flight. | Saved, Offline or Rejected |
| Saved | Server acknowledges | Indicator "Saved 09:44" | Saving on next edit |
| Offline | Request fails or no connectivity | Indicator "Offline. Changes kept on this phone." Inputs stay enabled and edits queue locally. | Saving when connection returns |
| Conflict | Server reports a newer revision | Dialog: "This draft was changed on another device." Actions: Load latest, which discards queued local edits for the items that differ, or Keep mine, which resends them on top of the latest revision. | Saved |
| Rejected | Server returns 4xx other than 409 | Indicator "Could not save" with the reason; local edits stay on screen. | Saving on retry |
| Submitting | Tap Submit | Submit disabled until the response. | Submitted, or back to Saved with errors |

Discard in the resume prompt asks for confirmation and then marks the draft as discarded. It is not a hard delete until decision 2 is made.

###### Accessibility

- The save indicator is a text element in a polite live region. Changes between Saving, Saved and Offline are announced; "Saving…" is not announced on every keystroke, only when it has lasted over 2 seconds.
- The conflict dialog and resume prompt take focus on open, trap it, and return focus to the control that opened them (or to the first checklist item for the resume prompt) on close.
- Both dialogs work with the keyboard alone, and every button has a text name.
- Failed-item validation messages at Submit are linked to their fields.

##### API (proposed)

All endpoints use `requireInspector()`. The caller must own the `inspection_id`; a draft owned by someone else returns 404, not 403, so its existence is not disclosed.

###### PUT /api/inspections/{inspection_id}/draft

Request:

```json
{
  "site_id": "string",
  "base_revision": 0,
  "items": [{ "item_id": "string", "answer": "pass|fail|na|null", "note": "string|null" }]
}
```

- `items` holds only changed items. Each is upserted on (`inspection_id`, `item_id`). Items not listed are untouched.
- `base_revision` is the last revision the client received; 0 for a new draft.
- Notes shorter than 10 characters on a `fail` are accepted in a draft.
- 200: `{ "inspection_id", "revision", "saved_at" }`. Revision increases by 1 per accepted request.
- 400: unknown `item_id`, answer outside the allowed set, or missing `site_id`.
- 409: `base_revision` is behind the server. Response carries the current `revision` and the items changed since.
- 409 with code `already_submitted`: the inspection is final; drafts cannot be edited.
- 403: `inspection_id` exists with a different `site_id` for the caller. Site never changes after creation.
- 503 or timeout: dependency unavailable; the client treats it as Offline.
- Retry safety: item upserts are idempotent. If the first attempt committed but the response was lost, the retry returns 409. The client then reads the draft, and if the server's items equal its pending items it treats the save as done; otherwise it shows the Conflict state.

###### GET /api/inspections/{inspection_id}/draft

Returns `{ inspection_id, site_id, revision, saved_at, items: [...] }` for the owner. 404 if missing, discarded, submitted or owned by another user.

###### GET /api/inspections/drafts?site_id={site_id}

Returns the caller's own drafts, newest first, with `inspection_id`, `site_id`, `saved_at`. Empty list when none.

###### POST /api/inspections/submit (changed)

- Adds optional `inspection_id`. A caller that omits it behaves as today, so older app versions keep working.
- When both `session_id` and `inspection_id` are given, the session must belong to the caller and the draft must be owned by the caller; otherwise the request is rejected with 409 and no write occurs. An existing inspection keeps its original context; the request cannot move it to another site or session.
- Items from the request are upserted by (`inspection_id`, `item_id`) and the status moves to submitted in one transaction. Server-side validation of the 10-character `fail` note applies at submit (a change from client-only, flagged for Kofi's review). Failures return per-item errors and leave the draft as it was.
- Repeating a submit for an inspection that is already submitted returns the existing result and writes nothing.

##### Data (proposed, additive)

- `inspections`: if a status column exists, add `draft` and `discarded` values and check that existing rows read as submitted. If not, add `status` text not null default `'submitted'`, `revision` integer not null default 0, `updated_at` timestamptz. Existing rows need no backfill beyond the defaults. Adding columns is non-destructive; rollback is dropping the added columns before any draft rows exist.
- `inspection_items`: no schema change. Writes switch from DELETE and INSERT to upsert on the existing unique key.
- A uniqueness rule for decision 1: unique on (owner user ID, `site_id`, visit date) for rows with status `draft`. Final wording waits for decision 1.
- Access: draft rows are readable and writable by the owning user only. Supervisor queries must filter to `status = 'submitted'`; this needs a check in every query that reads `inspections`.

##### Read-back and ownership

Request

Can you write the feature spec for autosaving and resuming site inspection drafts in our inspector web app? My brief and the engineer's notes on the current API are in the inputs folder; the main thing is that inspectors on poor signal stop losing their work.

Inputs

Run of the built write-feature-spec task package. The recording session invented this scenario, the request and the inputs below before running the skill. It had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so.

api-notes.md
Current API notes (from Kofi Adeyemi, backend engineer)

Written from memory; I have not re-read the code this week.

  • POST /api/inspections/submit takes { session_id, site_id, items: [{ item_id, answer, note }] }. Auth is the requireInspector() helper, which returns the inspector's user ID.
  • session_id is the login session, not the visit. It changes when the inspector logs in again.
  • Submit writes to inspections (one row) and inspection_items. I believe the items save does DELETE then INSERT for the inspection, so item row IDs change on every save.
  • inspection_items has a unique key on (inspection_id, item_id) and a foreign key to inspections.
  • Nothing reads a half-finished inspection today. I do not know of any GET endpoint for inspections an inspector owns; the supervisor list reads submitted rows only.
  • Answers are pass, fail, na. A fail requires a note of at least 10 characters (validated client-side only).
  • I have not checked whether inspections has a status column.
brief.md
Brief: inspection drafts (Tallow Row Facilities)

Author: Priya Nandakumar, product manager. Contact: priya@example.com

Problem

Inspectors complete a 40-to-60 item checklist on a phone, often in plant rooms and basements with weak signal. Today nothing is saved until they tap Submit. If the page reloads, the phone locks for long enough to drop the session, or Submit fails on a bad connection, the whole checklist is gone. Support logged 14 "lost inspection" tickets in October 2026.

Wanted
  • The checklist saves automatically as the inspector works, without them tapping anything.
  • If the connection drops, they keep working; changes are sent when the connection returns.
  • Reopening the inspection later (same phone or another device) restores answers and notes.
  • Submit still works as it does now and turns the draft into the final inspection.
Rules I am sure of
  • Only the inspector who started an inspection can open or edit its draft. Supervisors can see submitted inspections only (existing behaviour).
  • One draft per inspector per site visit.
  • Photos are out of scope for this release; they upload separately and already work.
Not decided
  • How long an abandoned draft is kept. Ask Operations (Tomasz Berg).
  • Whether a supervisor may take over a draft when an inspector is off sick.
  • Launch date.
Success

Fewer lost-inspection tickets. I have not agreed a target with support.

Output

I've written the spec for inspection draft autosave and resume. It's ready for review, but not for implementation yet. Four decisions are open, and the first one changes how a draft is identified.

File: out/inspection-draft-spec.md (Markdown, write-feature-spec depth with API, data and states)

What the spec says

Outcome. Answers and notes are saved on the server as the inspector works. Edits made offline queue on the phone and send when signal returns. The inspector can reopen the draft on any device after a reload or re-login. Submit keeps working and turns the draft into the final inspection. Support logged 14 lost-inspection tickets in October 2026, and that is the only baseline in your material.

Design points that come from Kofi's notes

  • session_id is the login session and changes on every login, so it can't identify a draft. The client creates an inspection_id (UUID) when the checklist opens. A resume list for the site lets a second device find it.
  • Kofi believes the item save does DELETE then INSERT. Autosave must upsert on the existing (inspection_id, item_id) key and write only the changed items. Otherwise each save would replace item row IDs, and a partial request could wipe answers it didn't mention.
  • No read path exists for unsubmitted inspections. The spec proposes three endpoints:
  • PUT /api/inspections/{inspection_id}/draft takes changed items and a base_revision. It returns the new revision, or 409 when the revision is stale.
  • GET /api/inspections/{inspection_id}/draft returns the owner's draft.
  • GET /api/inspections/drafts?site_id= lists the caller's own drafts.
  • A draft owned by another inspector returns 404, so its existence isn't disclosed.
  • POST /api/inspections/submit gains an optional inspection_id, so older app versions keep working. If a request carries both session_id and inspection_id, both must belong to the caller, or it is rejected with 409 and nothing is written. A submit can't move an existing inspection to another site or session. A repeated submit writes nothing new.
  • After a timeout, a lost response is retried safely. A 409 on retry triggers a read-back. If the server already holds the pending edits, the save counts as done. Otherwise the inspector sees a conflict dialog.
  • The 10-character rule for a fail note is client-side only today. Drafts accept short notes, and the rule moves server-side at Submit. Kofi should review that change.

Interface states. The spec covers New, Resume available, Saving, Saved, Offline, Conflict, Rejected and Submitting. Each has a trigger, what the inspector sees, and the next state. It also covers a polite live-region save indicator, focus handling for the two dialogs, and keyboard-only use.

Data. The changes are additive. inspections gets a status (default 'submitted', so existing rows are untouched), a revision and an updated_at. inspection_items needs no schema change. Supervisor queries must filter to submitted rows, and every query that reads inspections needs checking for that.

Acceptance. There are 15 criteria, each with an action, an observable result and a check method. They include:

  • offline edits reaching the server
  • resume after re-login
  • the same item row ID after repeated saves
  • a lost-response retry
  • a two-device conflict
  • denied access for another inspector
  • supervisors not seeing drafts
  • the old client still submitting
  • screen-reader and keyboard checks
Decisions still open
#DecisionOwnerWhat it blocks
1What counts as one "site visit"PriyaDraft identity. I assumed site plus the inspector's local calendar date, and marked it as an assumption.
2How long an abandoned draft is keptTomasz BergCleanup rule. The spec specifies no deletion. Discard marks a draft as discarded.
3Whether a supervisor can take over a draftPriyaUntil decided, only the owner has access.
4Whether inspections already has a status columnKofiWhether to reuse it or add one.
5Launch datePriyaNothing in the behaviour.
Gaps and limits
  • I had no code access. Everything about current behaviour (DELETE then INSERT, no read path, client-only validation, the session ID's lifecycle) is Kofi's recollection from his notes. The spec lists what to read before building: the submit handler, requireInspector(), the inspections schema and the supervisor query.
  • No success target is set. The spec proposes tracking lost-inspection tickets against October's 14, with a target and window agreed by you and support before launch.
  • Nothing was implemented, migrated or run. The acceptance checks are planned, not executed.
  • I couldn't run the bundled writing checker (writing_check.py). I did a manual read of the text instead, so no scanner result stands behind it.

File: inspection-draft-spec.md

Inspection drafts: autosave and resume

Status: ready for review. Not ready for implementation until decisions 1 to 4 below are settled. Source: Priya Nandakumar's brief and Kofi Adeyemi's API notes. No code was read, so every statement about current behaviour is Kofi's recollection and is marked as such.

Problem and outcome

Inspectors fill in a 40-to-60 item checklist on a phone, often with weak signal. Nothing is stored until they tap Submit, so a reload, a dropped login session or a failed Submit loses the whole checklist. Support logged 14 lost-inspection tickets in October 2026.

Outcome: answers and notes are stored on the server while the inspector works, work continues through a connection drop, and the inspector can reopen the draft later on any device and finish it. Submit keeps working and turns the draft into the final inspection.

No ticket-reduction target exists. Measurement work is proposed in the last section; this spec sets no target.

Confirmed requirements (from the brief)
  • Autosave without an inspector action.
  • Changes made offline are sent when the connection returns.
  • A draft reopens on the same or another device with answers and notes restored.
  • Only the inspector who started the draft can read or edit it. Supervisors see submitted inspections only.
  • One draft per inspector per site visit.
  • Photos are out of scope.
Open decisions
#DecisionOwnerEffect
1What counts as one "site visit"Priya NandakumarSets the draft's identity. This spec assumes site plus the inspector's local calendar date.
2Retention of an abandoned draftTomasz Berg (Operations)Sets the cleanup rule and the resume list. No deletion is specified here.
3Supervisor takeover of a draftPriya NandakumarUntil decided, only the owner has access.
4Whether inspections has a status columnKofi Adeyemi to checkDecides between reusing it and adding one (see Data).
5Launch datePriya NandakumarDoes not block the behaviour below.
Current behaviour (unverified, from Kofi's notes)
  • POST /api/inspections/submit takes { session_id, site_id, items: [{ item_id, answer, note }] }. Authentication is requireInspector(), which returns the user ID.
  • session_id identifies the login session and changes on every new login. It cannot identify a visit.
  • Items are probably saved by DELETE then INSERT, so inspection_items row IDs change on each save. The table has a unique key on (inspection_id, item_id) and a foreign key to inspections.
  • No endpoint reads an unsubmitted inspection. The supervisor list reads submitted rows.
  • The rule that a fail needs a note of 10 or more characters runs in the client only.

Consequence for the design: autosave must update items in place on (inspection_id, item_id), so repeated saves keep row IDs and never delete answers the request did not mention. The login session_id cannot key a draft, because the inspector would lose it on re-login.

Behaviour
Identity

The client creates an inspection_id (UUID) when the inspector opens a checklist for a site and stores it locally. The server accepts it only if it is new or already owned by the caller. A second device finds the draft through the resume list (below), which returns the existing inspection_id.

States
StateTriggerWhat the inspector seesNext state
NewOpens a checklist for a site with no draft todayEmpty checklist, indicator "Not saved yet"Saving on first answer
Resume availableOpens a site where the caller has a draft for the same visitPrompt: "Continue your draft from 09:42?" with Continue and Discard. Continue loads the draft.Populated
SavingAnswer or note changesIndicator "Saving…". Inputs stay enabled. Changes are batched, at most one request in flight.Saved, Offline or Rejected
SavedServer acknowledgesIndicator "Saved 09:44"Saving on next edit
OfflineRequest fails or no connectivityIndicator "Offline. Changes kept on this phone." Inputs stay enabled and edits queue locally.Saving when connection returns
ConflictServer reports a newer revisionDialog: "This draft was changed on another device." Actions: Load latest, which discards queued local edits for the items that differ, or Keep mine, which resends them on top of the latest revision.Saved
RejectedServer returns 4xx other than 409Indicator "Could not save" with the reason; local edits stay on screen.Saving on retry
SubmittingTap SubmitSubmit disabled until the response.Submitted, or back to Saved with errors

Discard in the resume prompt asks for confirmation and then marks the draft as discarded. It is not a hard delete until decision 2 is made.

Accessibility
  • The save indicator is a text element in a polite live region. Changes between Saving, Saved and Offline are announced; "Saving…" is not announced on every keystroke, only when it has lasted over 2 seconds.
  • The conflict dialog and resume prompt take focus on open, trap it, and return focus to the control that opened them (or to the first checklist item for the resume prompt) on close.
  • Both dialogs work with the keyboard alone, and every button has a text name.
  • Failed-item validation messages at Submit are linked to their fields.
API (proposed)

All endpoints use requireInspector(). The caller must own the inspection_id; a draft owned by someone else returns 404, not 403, so its existence is not disclosed.

PUT /api/inspections/{inspection_id}/draft

Request:

{
  "site_id": "string",
  "base_revision": 0,
  "items": [{ "item_id": "string", "answer": "pass|fail|na|null", "note": "string|null" }]
}
  • items holds only changed items. Each is upserted on (inspection_id, item_id). Items not listed are untouched.
  • base_revision is the last revision the client received; 0 for a new draft.
  • Notes shorter than 10 characters on a fail are accepted in a draft.
  • 200: { "inspection_id", "revision", "saved_at" }. Revision increases by 1 per accepted request.
  • 400: unknown item_id, answer outside the allowed set, or missing site_id.
  • 409: base_revision is behind the server. Response carries the current revision and the items changed since.
  • 409 with code already_submitted: the inspection is final; drafts cannot be edited.
  • 403: inspection_id exists with a different site_id for the caller. Site never changes after creation.
  • 503 or timeout: dependency unavailable; the client treats it as Offline.
  • Retry safety: item upserts are idempotent. If the first attempt committed but the response was lost, the retry returns 409. The client then reads the draft, and if the server's items equal its pending items it treats the save as done; otherwise it shows the Conflict state.
GET /api/inspections/{inspection_id}/draft

Returns { inspection_id, site_id, revision, saved_at, items: [...] } for the owner. 404 if missing, discarded, submitted or owned by another user.

GET /api/inspections/drafts?site_id={site_id}

Returns the caller's own drafts, newest first, with inspection_id, site_id, saved_at. Empty list when none.

POST /api/inspections/submit (changed)
  • Adds optional inspection_id. A caller that omits it behaves as today, so older app versions keep working.
  • When both session_id and inspection_id are given, the session must belong to the caller and the draft must be owned by the caller; otherwise the request is rejected with 409 and no write occurs. An existing inspection keeps its original context; the request cannot move it to another site or session.
  • Items from the request are upserted by (inspection_id, item_id) and the status moves to submitted in one transaction. Server-side validation of the 10-character fail note applies at submit (a change from client-only, flagged for Kofi's review). Failures return per-item errors and leave the draft as it was.
  • Repeating a submit for an inspection that is already submitted returns the existing result and writes nothing.
Data (proposed, additive)
  • inspections: if a status column exists, add draft and discarded values and check that existing rows read as submitted. If not, add status text not null default 'submitted', revision integer not null default 0, updated_at timestamptz. Existing rows need no backfill beyond the defaults. Adding columns is non-destructive; rollback is dropping the added columns before any draft rows exist.
  • inspection_items: no schema change. Writes switch from DELETE and INSERT to upsert on the existing unique key.
  • A uniqueness rule for decision 1: unique on (owner user ID, site_id, visit date) for rows with status draft. Final wording waits for decision 1.
  • Access: draft rows are readable and writable by the owning user only. Supervisor queries must filter to status = 'submitted'; this needs a check in every query that reads inspections.
Read-back and ownership

skills.markdown:
---
name: write-portfolio-case-study
description: "Turn a piece of the candidate's work into a sanitized, evidence-checked portfolio case study (working + publish copy) using the candidate’s template and publish gate."
---


# Write portfolio case study

Use only the candidate identity, career records, thresholds, author profile and destinations explicitly supplied or authorized for this task. Record names below describe a suggested source map; resolve them under the confirmed career root or accept equivalent supplied records. None is a bundled personal default. Missing optional context does not block a bounded draft from supplied facts.

Turn any project, product, or engagement of the candidate's into a portfolio case study that is consistent, sanitized, and safe to publish. Produce two copies every time: a **working copy** (evidence labels and proof notes visible, for the candidate) and a **publish copy** (clean first-person prose, for the site).

The split is the point. Evidence control lives in the working copy. The publish copy states what happened with confidence and contains no labels, caveat sentences, or status notes.

## Before you start
- Confirm the subject, ownership and publication authority from the current claims and rights ledger supplied for this task. A historical employer relationship does not itself authorize reuse. Client names, logos, data, rate-card numbers, margins and quote identifiers require explicit disclosure authority.
- Use the candidate’s supplied program records and evidence ledger for figures. Do not invent or round beyond their supported precision.
- Never invent a fact, number, client, or quote to make a study read better. Missing detail: bracket it in the working copy and flag it to the candidate in chat; do not fill the gap.

## Skeleton (fill for each study)
- **Title** — what the candidate built or did, plain, no client name.
- **Client (sanitized)** — industry + size band only; never name, logo, or identifying detail. If it's the candidate’s own product, say so.
- **Problem** — the business problem, one short paragraph.
- **What I did** — the approach and the system or artifacts the candidate actually built.
- **How it works** — the mechanism (the differentiator; show the build, not just the result).
- **Outcome** — what happened, stated plainly.
- **My role** — what the candidate personally did versus the team.
- **What it becomes** — the reusable method, offer, or skill it maps to.

Write each study in first person, as the candidate. Use the confirmed author profile for voice and structure. Omit a closing summary when it merely repeats the case; retain a conclusion when it advances the requested decision.

## Evidence labels (working copy only)
- **[verified]** — source is showable (a record, a computed figure).
- **[reported]** — a real engagement figure not independently re-verified.
- **[estimated]** — a modeled/opportunity number.
- **[in progress]** — built, not yet in production use.
An untagged number does not ship.

## Resolving labels into the publish copy
Labels come off. Caveat sentences do not replace them.
- [verified] → state it.
- [estimated] → keep the single word inside the claim: "an estimated $20K–$30K in this synthetic example." Nothing more.
- [reported] → use it only if the candidate would say it plainly ("a synthetic review process fell from six hours to two hours"). Otherwise cut it. Never append "directional" or "not a controlled study."
- [in progress] → describe what the candidate built and what it does. Do not add "not in production," "not verified," or "not claimed." Don't imply it runs live; just don't say either way.
- Lost or open deals → one word in the outcome ("lost," "open") when the outcome matters to the story. No status sentence.

Banned in the publish copy: "not verified," "unverified," "not claimed," "I don't claim," "does not prove," "directional," "not a controlled study," "Where it stood," "remained outside," "no sold deal was recorded," any sentence explaining what a number is not, and any state or publication note. Preserve material uncertainty and necessary qualifications. If a claim cannot be stated accurately for its audience, omit it rather than concealing the qualification.

## Voice — use the confirmed author profile
The publish copy is the candidate's own first-person voice, so gate it against the `apply-author-style` with an explicitly supplied confirmed profile skill before it ships. Apply confirmed author preferences alongside these general review checks:
- Trust the reader — never restate a point or explain the previous sentence.
- No empty "builder" constructions ("I build systems that turn X into Y"). Name the actual thing: a deal-intelligence system, a discovery-to-requirements engine, the playbook catalog.
- No X-not-Y antithesis ("systems, not slideware"; "deprecate deliberately, not delete"). State the positive directly.
- No defensive disclaimers (rule 6).
- No origin-story throat-clearing; no banned phrases ("at the intersection of," "proven ability to," "whether it's X or Y," "at the end of the day," and the rest in the candidate’s profile).
- Concrete nouns, real numbers, named systems in every sentence. Short sentences mixed with long. End flat and confident on the last true thing.

## Publish gate (all six before it goes public)
1. **Sanitized** — no client name, logo, stakeholder, internal identifier, or their dollar figures unless the candidate cleared them.
2. **Owned** — methods and products the candidate may show; no rate card or margin.
3. **Sourced** — every number in the working copy carries a label; nothing in the publish copy overstates its label.
4. **Separation** — no internal resourcing, rate card, margin, or staffing detail.
5. **In the candidate’s voice and clean** — passes `apply-author-style` with an explicitly supplied confirmed profile; a scan for the banned disclaimer phrases returns nothing.
6. **Two versions** — working copy (labels, proof notes) + publish copy (clean prose).

## Metadata block (top of the working copy only)
```
Study:            <name>
Maps to offer:    <offer / skill>
Evidence status:  <verified | mostly reported | mostly estimated>
Sanitization:     <done | pending>
Ownership check:  <clear | needs generic rebuild>
Publish-ready:    <yes | no — blocked on: ...>
```
The metadata block never appears in the publish copy.

## Output
Deliver the study as a markdown file: metadata block, then working copy, then publish copy. Save durable versions to the project. Report bracketed gaps and figures that need the candidate's confirmation in chat, not in the publish copy.

mentions.name: apply-author-style
mentions.context:
## Voice — use the confirmed author profile
The publish copy is the candidate's own first-person voice, so gate it against the `apply-author-style` with an explicitly supplied confirmed profile skill before it ships. Apply confirmed author preferences alongside these general review checks:
- Trust the reader — never restate a point or explain the previous sentence.
- No empty "builder" constructions ("I build systems that turn X into Y"). Name the actual thing: a deal-intelligence system, a discovery-to-requirements engine, the playbook catalog.
- No X-not-Y antithesis ("systems, not slideware"; "deprecate deliberately, not delete"). State the positive directly.
- No defensive disclaimers (rule 6).
- No origin-story throat-clearing; no banned phrases ("at the intersection of," "proven ability to," "whether it's X or Y," "at the end of the day," and the rest in the candidate’s profile).
- Concrete nouns, real numbers, named systems in every sentence. Short sentences mixed with long. End flat and confident on the last true thing.

examples.title: Portfolio case study for a three-way invoice matching tool
examples.markdown:
## Request

Can you turn my Harbourline invoice-matching project into a portfolio case study for my site? My notes, the figures ledger and the client's permission email are attached. I want a working copy and a publish copy.

## Inputs

Run of the built `write-portfolio-case-study` task package. The recording session invented this scenario, the request and the inputs below before running the skill. It had no connectors, accounts or network access and could not execute scripts, so any scripted step was done by hand and the answer says so.

#### figures-ledger-and-permission.md

#### Figures ledger

| Figure | Source | Status |
|---|---|---|
| ~4,000 invoices/month | Harbourline AP volume report, May 2026 | checked against report |
| Auto-approve rate 71.4% | Pilot run log, June batch (3,962 invoices, 2,829 auto-approved) | computed from log |
| 11 duplicates caught, Jun–Jul | Hold-queue export | in export |
| Matching time 3 days → under 1 day at close | Dana's verbal comment, not measured | reported |
| "Pays for itself in a quarter" | Verbal, tone unclear | not usable |
| Estimated annual duplicate-payment exposure avoided: 38,000 | My model: 11 caught x avg invoice 3,450, extrapolated over 12 months | modeled |

#### Permission email (from Dana Okoye, 14 Oct 2026, dana.okoye@example.com)

"Happy for you to write up the matching tool as a case study. Please don't use our name or logo, and please keep supplier names, our invoice volumes by supplier and your fees out of it. Describing us as a regional food distributor is fine. You own the code you wrote; just keep our data out of any demo."

#### project-notes.md

#### Harbourline Foods – invoice matching (my notes)

Client: Harbourline Foods, regional food distributor, about 220 staff. Accounts payable team of 6 handled roughly 4,000 supplier invoices a month. Contact was Dana Okoye, finance controller.

Problem: AP clerks matched each supplier invoice against the purchase order and the goods-received note by hand in spreadsheets. Mismatches (price, quantity, missing receipt) surfaced late, often after the payment run was scheduled, and caused duplicate-payment risk and supplier disputes.

What I did (Mar–Jun 2026, solo, 14 weeks, billed at my day rate of 640 per day): built a three-way matching tool in Python and SQLite. It reads the ERP export of POs, the receiving log CSV and the invoice batch. Rules: exact PO number match first, then fuzzy match on supplier + amount + date window of 10 days when the PO number is missing or mistyped. Price tolerance of 2% or 15 currency units, whichever is lower. Each invoice lands in one of three queues: auto-approve, review (with the reason code), hold (no receipt or duplicate suspected). Duplicate check hashes supplier ID + invoice number + amount. Clerks work only the review and hold queues through a simple web page I wrote with Flask. Two AP clerks helped me write the reason codes; Dana signed off on tolerances.

Results as I remember: clerks used to spend about 3 days per month-end close on matching, now under 1 day. Auto-approve rate about 70% in the pilot. Caught 11 duplicate invoices in the first two months. Dana said it paid for itself in a quarter, I think? Might have been a joke.

The tool is running in production for the monthly batch since June. The email-alert feature for holds is built but they haven't switched it on yet.

Reusable: I have since turned the matching rules into a generic template I can reuse (own code, no Harbourline data).

## Output

I've written the case study with a working copy and a publish copy. It isn't ready to post yet. It needs your OK on two items below, and I couldn't run the voice check.

**File:** `./out/invoice-matching-case-study.md`. It holds the metadata block, the working copy with evidence labels, the publish copy, and a short checks record.

#### What the publish copy says
- **Client:** a regional food distributor with roughly 200 staff. There is no name, logo or contact. The permission email allowed "regional food distributor" and nothing identifying.
- **Problem:** six AP clerks matched about 4,000 invoices a month by hand in spreadsheets. Mismatches surfaced after the payment run was scheduled.
- **How it works:**
  - The tool is built in Python, SQLite and Flask.
  - It does an exact PO match first. If that fails, it does a fuzzy match on supplier, amount and a 10-day window.
  - The price tolerance is 2% or 15 currency units, whichever is lower.
  - Invoices land in an auto-approve, review or hold queue. Duplicates are caught by hashing supplier ID, invoice number and amount.
  - A hold alert by email is built into the tool. I described it without saying whether it is switched on.
- **Outcome:** in the June batch, 2,829 of 3,962 invoices (71.4%) were auto-approved. The tool caught 11 duplicates in June and July, and has run the monthly batch since June.
- **Your role and what it becomes:** you were the sole developer. The matching rules are now a generic template you reuse.

#### What I left out, and why
- **Fees and day rate:** the client asked for these to be kept out.
- **Supplier names, per-supplier volumes and the average invoice value (3,450):** the client asked for supplier names and per-supplier volumes to be kept out. I treated invoice value as client financial data.
- **Controller's name:** I used the role only.
- **"3 days to under 1 day" at month-end close:** this was a verbal comment from the client and was never measured. You weren't sure of it in your notes, so I labelled it [reported] and cut it. If you would say it plainly as your own observation, I can restore it.
- **"Pays for itself in a quarter":** tone unclear, so I excluded it.
- **38,000 estimated annual exposure avoided:** I cut it from the publish copy, for these reasons:
  - The ledger says this is 11 caught duplicates × 3,450 average, extrapolated over 12 months. But 11 × 3,450 is 37,950, which is the two-month total with no extrapolation. A 12-month extrapolation would be about 227,700.
  - No currency is given.
  - Caught duplicates may never have been paid, so "exposure avoided" may overstate it.
  - Tell me which calculation you meant and I can restore it as "an estimated …".

#### Needs your confirmation
1. **Tolerance figures (2% / 15 units).** Your controller signed these off, but the permission email doesn't mention them. They show how the tool works, so I included them. Say if you'd rather keep them generic.
2. **Invoice volume (about 4,000 a month).** The client barred per-supplier volumes, not total volume. I read that as allowed. Please confirm.
3. **"In use since June."** This comes from your notes only, and I labelled it [reported]. Confirm it is still accurate.
4. **Size band.** Your notes say about 220 staff. I wrote "roughly 200".

#### Gaps in my checks
- **Publish gate, voice:** no confirmed apply-author-style profile was supplied, so gate 5 is open. The metadata marks the study "Publish-ready: no".
- **`writing_check.py`:** I can't run scripts here. I did the banned-phrase scan and the read-through by hand and found nothing. Please run the real checker before you publish.
- **Arithmetic:** I checked 2,829 / 3,962 = 71.4%.
- **Layer reached:** the files are prepared locally. Nothing has been posted to your site.

#### Files
- `./out/invoice-matching-case-study.md`
- `./out/answer.md`

### File: invoice-matching-case-study.md

```
Study:            Three-way invoice matching for a regional food distributor
Maps to offer:    Finance-operations automation (matching and exception-queue builds)
Evidence status:  verified (reported and estimated figures held back from the publish copy)
Sanitization:     done
Ownership check:  clear (own code; client permission email of 14 Oct 2026; client data excluded)
Publish-ready:    no — blocked on: confirmed apply-author-style profile (gate 5); candidate OK on the tolerance figures
```

#### WORKING COPY

##### Title
Three-way invoice matching for a regional food distributor

##### Client (sanitized)
Regional food distributor, roughly 200 staff. Accounts payable team of six. [verified: ~220 staff in notes; banded]

##### Problem
Clerks matched every supplier invoice to its purchase order and goods-received note by hand in spreadsheets. About 4,000 invoices a month [verified: AP volume report, May 2026]. Mismatches in price, quantity or receipt surfaced after the payment run was scheduled, which created duplicate-payment risk and supplier disputes.

##### What I did
Solo build, March to June 2026 (14 weeks). A three-way matching tool in Python and SQLite, plus a small Flask page for the clerks. Two AP clerks helped write the reason codes. The client's finance controller signed off the tolerances.

##### How it works
- Inputs: ERP export of purchase orders, receiving log CSV, invoice batch.
- Pass 1: exact match on PO number.
- Pass 2 (PO number missing or mistyped): fuzzy match on supplier + amount + a 10-day date window.
- Price tolerance: 2% or 15 currency units, whichever is lower. [reported: from notes; confirm OK to publish]
- Three queues: auto-approve, review (with reason code), hold (no receipt or suspected duplicate).
- Duplicate check: hash of supplier ID + invoice number + amount.
- Clerks work only the review and hold queues.
- Email alert for holds: built, not switched on by the client. [in progress]

##### Outcome
- June batch: 2,829 of 3,962 invoices auto-approved, 71.4%. [verified: pilot run log, computed]
- 11 duplicate invoices caught, June–July. [verified: hold-queue export]
- In use for the monthly batch since June. [reported: candidate's notes]
- Month-end matching time fell from about 3 days to under 1 day. [reported: client's verbal comment, never measured] — held back from the publish copy; see chat.
- Estimated annual duplicate exposure avoided: 38,000. [estimated] — held back; see chat.
- "Pays for itself in a quarter." Not usable (tone unclear). Excluded.

##### My role
Sole developer and designer: requirements, rules, code, queue page, rollout to the monthly batch. Clerks contributed reason codes; the controller approved tolerances.

##### What it becomes
The matching rules are now a generic template in my own code with no client data. Offer: three-way matching and exception-queue builds for AP teams.

##### Excluded on purpose
Client name and logo, controller's name, day rate and any fee figure, supplier names, per-supplier volumes, average invoice value (client financial data).

---

#### PUBLISH COPY

#### Three-way invoice matching for a regional food distributor

**Client:** A regional food distributor with roughly 200 staff.

##### Problem
The accounts payable team of six matched about 4,000 supplier invoices a month against purchase orders and goods-received notes by hand, in spreadsheets. Price, quantity and missing-receipt mismatches showed up after the payment run was scheduled. That meant duplicate-payment risk and disputes with suppliers.

##### What I did
Between March and June 2026 I built a three-way matching tool in Python and SQLite, with a Flask page for the clerks. I worked with two AP clerks to write the reason codes, and the finance controller approved the tolerances.

##### How it works
The tool reads the ERP purchase-order export, the receiving log and the invoice batch. It first matches on exact PO number. When the number is missing or mistyped, it falls back to a fuzzy match on supplier, amount and a 10-day date window. Price differences pass within 2% or 15 currency units, whichever is lower.

Every invoice lands in one of three queues. Auto-approve needs no attention. Review carries a reason code that tells the clerk what to check. Hold collects invoices with no receipt or a suspected duplicate, found by hashing supplier ID, invoice number and amount. Clerks work the review and hold queues only. A hold alert by email is built into the tool.

##### Outcome
In the June batch, 2,829 of 3,962 invoices, 71.4%, went through auto-approve. The tool caught 11 duplicate invoices in June and July. It has run the monthly batch since June.

##### My role
I was the only developer. I gathered the requirements, designed the matching rules, wrote the code and the queue page, and moved it onto the monthly batch. The clerks shaped the reason codes and the controller set the tolerances.

##### What it becomes
I have rebuilt the matching rules as a generic template with no client data. I use it for three-way matching and exception-queue projects in accounts payable.

---

#### CHECKS (working record)
- Banned-phrase scan of the publish copy by hand ("not verified", "unverified", "not claimed", "directional", "does not prove", "Where it stood", etc.): none found. `writing_check.py` could not be run here; I did a manual read for X-not-Y constructions, filler and closing restatement and found none.
- Arithmetic: 2,829 / 3,962 = 71.4%.
- Gate: 1 sanitized ✔; 2 owned ✔ (no rate card or margin); 3 sourced ✔; 4 separation ✔; 5 voice — pending a confirmed author profile; 6 two versions ✔.

skills.title: Statement of work
skills.description: Generate Statements of Work (.docx) from a confirmed quote JSON and a selected contract profile, in Waterfall (fixed scope), Agile (adaptive scope), and Assess (advisory, readout-gated) variants. Use when asked to generate the SOW, draft the SOW from the quote, build the SOW for a Q-number, or turn a quote into a Statement of Work. The quote is the source of truth; this skill renders it, does not price (the Pricing System prices), and does not author scope language (scope-project does). It builds the .docx, resolves placeholders with an audit trail, verifies the required-clause gate, and hands off to the embedded contract review mode. For authoring quality review, select the embedded contract scope and obligation review mode; DDOC remains a deck workflow.

guide.what: Draft a statement of work from confirmed scope.
guide.when: A fixed-scope, adaptive, or assessment agreement needs drafting.
guide.inputs: The confirmed quote model and the project’s approved contract and brand profiles.
guide.outputs: A reconciled Word document and checks against the selected scope and terms.
guide.example: Draft the selected SOW variant from this confirmed quote and approved contract profile.
guide.expect: It reads one confirmed quote revision, picks the SOW variant from the engagement shape, and renders a .docx only after the hours and revenue tie out. A figure that does not reconcile stops the build and is returned to the quote owner, missing values stay visible as flagged fields, and the document is never treated as approved or sent.
guide.overview: It reads one confirmed quote revision, picks the SOW variant from the engagement shape, and renders a .docx only after the hours and revenue tie out. A figure that does not reconcile stops the build and is returned to the quote owner, missing values stay visible as flagged fields, and the document is never treated as approved or sent.
guide.value: Translate an agreed quote into a consistent statement of work with scope, obligations and commercial figures tied together. It checks hours and revenue before rendering the Word document.

preparation.where: Provide one confirmed quote revision and the project's approved contract profile. The profile is the authorized clause/template set and contract choices, supplied by the agreement owner; no former employer's terms are assumed. A brand profile controls appearance and can use neutral defaults.
preparation.missing: Missing approved terms or unreconciled figures prevent a complete contract build. Unknown values remain visible rather than invented. A draft document is not legal approval, acceptance, signature or delivery to the client.

reuse.label: General use
reuse.reason: The method accepts the user’s project sources and takes private context as an explicit input.
reuse.setup: Requires a confirmed quote model, the project’s approved contract profile, and the document runtime.
reuse.basis: Source classification and automated reference scan; cross-environment execution has not been tested.

profile.setup: Requires a confirmed quote model, the project’s approved contract profile, and the document runtime.
profile.expect: It reads one confirmed quote revision, picks the SOW variant from the engagement shape, and renders a .docx only after the hours and revenue tie out. A figure that does not reconcile stops the build and is returned to the quote owner, missing values stay visible as flagged fields, and the document is never treated as approved or sent.
